cars.description: Another Maserati highlight, an aerodynamic test vehicle, was unveiled at the 1952 Turin Motor Show. Based on a FIAT platform, the car showcased strikingly original styling by Franco Scaglione and was powered by a 1.5-liter engine tuned by Abarth to deliver 73 HP. The only example ever built was later shown at the Pebble Beach Concours d’Elegance in recent years, where it earned the prestigious Gran Turismo trophy.
cars.hero: A futuristic-looking design featuring a large central headlight, this Abarth was first shown at the 1952 Turin Motor Show.

cars.description: This was a factory-tuned version of the FIAT 500, developed by the iconic Italian performance brand Abarth, which returned to the scene in 2007. Powered by a turbocharged 1.4-liter DOHC engine delivering 133.1 HP and 151.9 ft-lb of torque. Tipping the scales at just 2447 lbs, the car accelerated from zero to 62.1 mph in 7.9 seconds and reached a top speed of 127.4 mph. The design carried the unmistakable presence of an Abarth, with aggressive bumpers, flared side skirts, and a roof-mounted spoiler.
cars.hero: The Abarth returned yet again with bolder looks and performance, this time in the form of the timeless "500."

cars.description: The FIAT Abarth 595 made its debut in 1963. It was derived from the second-generation FIAT 500 tuned by Abarth. An even more potent variant of the 595 later emerged as the 595 Esseesse. While it retained the same engine displacement, engineers raised compression to boost output to 31.6 HP. Thanks to this added performance, the 595 lineup made its mark in European racing, dominating the under 600 cc category.
cars.hero: A hardcore sports version of the FIAT 500.

cars.description: The AFEELA 1 was unveiled at CES® 2025. This production model was offered in two distinct trims—Origin and Signature. The cabin was envisioned as a Creative Entertainment Space that challenged traditional notions of what travel could be. Advanced technologies were embedded throughout the BEV, including an array of external sensing devices and an intelligent personal agent capable of holding natural, conversational dialogue.
cars.hero: A new era of mobility that reimagines transportation.

cars.description: The AFEELA Prototype 2024 was a BEV introduced by Sony Honda Mobility during CES® 2024. An array of sensing technologies delivered intuitive driver assistance, while dashboard and rear-seat displays offered abundant in-car entertainment. AFEELA turned the notion of waiting during travel into an enjoyable experience.
cars.hero: A revolutionary "mobility device" set to change how we spend time commuting.

cars.description: The 155 2.5 V6 TI was Alfa Romeo’s answer to the increasingly advanced Deutsche Tourenwagen Masters (DTM), which, by 1993, allowed significant car modifications. Based on the 1992 155 sedan, it featured a 60-degree 2.5-liter V-6 powerplant producing 414.2 HP and a full-time 4-wheel-drive system. The car won 12 of 20 rounds and secured the championship.
cars.hero: This champion race car won 12 out of 20 races in the super-competitive DTM race series.

cars.description: Alfa Romeo’s first mass-produced mid-engine sports car, the 4C made its debut in 2013. Its design paid tribute to the timeless lines of the Tipo 33/2 Stradale. The 1742 cc 4-cylinder engine, producing 236.7 HP and 253.2 ft-lb of torque, was paired with an exceptionally lightweight body, enabling the car to accelerate from zero to 62.1 mph in just 4.5 seconds and reach a top speed of 160.3 mph. A special "Launch Edition" was also released, limited to just 1,000 units worldwide.
cars.hero: The launch edition of the 4C, limited to 1000 units, sold out almost immediately after going on sale.

cars.description: The 4C Gr.3 is a Gran Turismo original model based on Alfa Romeo's new-generation mid-engine sports car, the 4C, modified to meet Gr.3 standards. To boost stability and aerodynamics, its wheelbase has been lengthened by 4.3 inches and its revised front overhang grew 1.2 inches. The Gr.4 4C is essentially a refined, tuned variant of the base model. Although less powerful, it exploited its light weight and small footprint to remain competitive in corners.
cars.hero: The launch edition of the 4C, limited to 1000 units, sold out almost immediately after going on sale.

cars.description: The 4C Gr.3 is a homologation version of Alfa Romeo’s 4C mid-engine sports car that was developed to meet Gr.3 standards. The already agile base model has been transformed with a wider body, and the engine's power was boosted from 200 to 450 horsepower.
cars.hero: This road car version of the Gr.3 4C sold 1000 units as soon as it was released to the public.

cars.description: The 4C Gr.4 is a Gran Turismo original model based on Alfa Romeo's new-generation mid-engine sports car, the 4C, modified to meet Gr.4 standards. Essentially a refined version of the production model, it may have lacked outright power, but its compact footprint and sharp handling gives it a distinct edge on technical circuits.
cars.hero: The launch edition of the 4C, limited to 1000 units, sold out almost immediately after going on sale.

cars.description: As its name suggested, the Alfa Romeo 8C 2900B Touring Berlinetta was a stunning coupe, its body hand-shaped by Carrozzeria Touring using the lightweight superleggera method. The "8C" badge referred to the car’s 8-cylinder engine. Designed by the legendary Vittorio Jano, the water-cooled inline-8 delivered performance that placed the machine firmly in race-car territory. It's believed that only five examples were ever produced.
cars.hero: Equipped with DOHC V-8, this exquisite coupe was produced by Alfa Romeo in the pre-war period.

cars.description: The original 8C took its name from the 8-cylinder engine designed by the legendary Vittorio Jano. Beneath its timeless bodywork lay a 4.7-liter V-8, tuned by Alfa Romeo to deliver 443.8 HP. With a top speed of 180.2 mph and a 0–62.1 mph sprint time of under 4.2 seconds, it rivaled—and in some cases surpassed—contemporary supercars. Limited to just 500 units worldwide, the car sold out almost immediately upon its release.
cars.hero: This car marked Alfa Romeo's return to the rear-drive coupe and possessed a top speed of 180.2 mph plus.

cars.description: In 2020, Alfa Romeo marked their 110th anniversary with the release of the special Giulia GTA and GTAm models. The twin-turbo 2.9-liter V-6 saw its output raised to 532.5 HP, accompanied by weight reduction and a wider track for enhanced performance. The GTAm, built with circuit driving in mind, featured a large front splitter, carbon fiber rear wing, and integrated roll bars—delivering a truly hardcore setup.
cars.hero: The top-of-the-line model in the Giulia lineup celebrated 110 years of Alfa Romeo.

cars.description: Introduced in 1962, Alfa Romeo’s first Giulia series began as a 4-door sedan, with the Sprint GT coupe joining the lineup in 1963. Designed by Giugiaro, the body featured elegant lines and subtly curved surfaces. The Sprint GT quickly gained popularity as a high-performance sports coupe and remained in production until 1977.
cars.hero: An iconic 1960s high-performance coupe from Alfa Romeo
cars.name_long: Alfa Romeo Giulia Sprint GT Veloce '67

cars.description: This racing machine was the result of a collaborative effort between Alfa Romeo and Carrozzeria Zagato. Based on the TZ, its body shell was replaced with lightweight FRP, while the nose and roof were lowered to enhance aerodynamic performance. Under the hood, it featured the twin-ignition cylinder head from the Giulia GTA, allowing it to produce 162.7 HP and reach a top speed of 152.2 mph.
cars.hero: Both in style and substance, this car represented all that was good about sports cars in the 1960s.
cars.name_long: Alfa Romeo GIULIA TZ2 carrozzata da ZAGATO '65

cars.description: This 3-door hatchback was released in the B-segment as a replacement for Alfa Romeo’s previous entry-level model, the 147. Its name was inspired by Milan and Torino—two cities central to Alfa Romeo’s history. The standard powerplant was a turbocharged 1.4-liter DOHC, with the 1.4 Sport variant producing 152.9 HP and 166.4 ft-lb of torque, paired with a 6-speed manual transmission. With a top speed of 133.6 mph and a zero-62.1 mph time of 8.0 seconds, it delivered more than respectable performance for its class.
cars.hero: Alfa Romeo's MiTo hatchback brings a dash of Italian flair to the compact car segment.

cars.description: The original Alpine A110 proved itself across the globe, performing admirably in rally competition. In 2017, Renault revived the Alpine name to carry the torch forward, revealing the modern Alpine A110. This new version, clad in an aluminum body echoing the original, featured a mid-mounted turbocharged 1.8-liter 4-cylinder engine producing 248.5 HP and 231.5 ft-lb of torque. A special Première Édition was created, with production limited to 1,955 units worldwide.
cars.hero: This lightweight sports car from the reborn Alpine brand combined elegance with performance.

cars.description: The Alpine A110 was a classic French sports car with a celebrated heritage in rally racing. With its rear-engine layout and lightweight construction, it delivered superb traction and quickly rose to prominence in international rally events, claiming numerous victories. First introduced in 1963 with a 1.1-liter engine, the A110 saw gradual increases in displacement to remain competitive over time. The pinnacle of the lineup was arguably the 1600S, which came equipped with a 1.6-liter engine.
cars.hero: The swoopy rear-engined Alpine was powered by a Renault engine.

cars.description: While Alpine earned fame through rallying success with the A110, the 1960s also saw the marque build competitive prototype racers that achieved results on the track. Among them, the A220 stood as Alpine’s strongest contender for overall victory at the 24 Hours of Le Mans, making its debut in 1968. Although the car was beset by mechanical issues and failed to deliver the expected result, it remained a fan favorite and a cherished part of Alpine’s legacy.
cars.hero: Not only a maker of dominant rally cars, the noted French car company also forayed into road machines.

cars.description: This was a single-seater sports car created by the renowned French marque Alpine, developed specifically for Gran Turismo players. Its styling followed Alpine’s core philosophy of “speed and excitement, embodied in style,” while paying tribute to the brand’s storied past. This groundbreaking machine bridged the divide between road and track, and between the digital world and physical reality.
cars.hero: A legendary brand's glimpse of the ultimate future sports car.

cars.description: This was a single-seater concept created by the famed French marque Alpine, developed specifically for Gran Turismo players. Its design reflected Alpine’s core philosophy of “speed and excitement, embodied in style,” while simultaneously paying tribute to the brand’s iconic past. The result was a groundbreaking machine that blended road and track, and bridged the divide between the virtual and the real.
cars.hero: A legendary brand's glimpse of the ultimate future sports car.

cars.description: This was a single-seater sports car developed by the celebrated French brand Alpine, crafted specifically for Gran Turismo players. Its styling followed Alpine’s core philosophy of “speed and excitement, embodied in style,” while paying tribute to the brand’s storied past. This groundbreaking machine bridged the divide between road and track, and between the digital world and physical reality.
cars.hero: A legendary brand's glimpse of the ultimate future sports car.
cars.name_long: Alpine Vision Gran Turismo Race Mode

cars.description: Mercedes-AMG created this touring car in its early years. The 300 SEL 6.3 was already quick, but AMG bored the engine out to 6.8 liters and re-tuned it, raising output from 246.5 HP to 422.1 HP. At the 1971 24 Hours of Spa, it took 1st in class and 2nd overall—an early showcase of AMG’s racing pedigree.
cars.hero: This legendary race car put AMG on the map after its class victory at the 1971 24 Hours of Spa.

cars.description: This high-performance model joined the third-generation A-Class lineup one year after the platform's debut. Powered by a turbocharged 2.0-liter engine tuned by AMG, it delivered 355 HP and 325.5 ft-lb of torque. It accelerated from zero to 62.1 mph in 4.6 seconds and reached its electronically limited top speed of 155.3 mph. To manage its power, the car employed a 7-speed dual-clutch transmission routed through a 4-wheel-drive system. Both the braking system and suspension were also upgraded.
cars.hero: The ultimate hot hatch based on the third-generation A Class.

cars.description: This was the high-performance variant of the fourth-generation C-Class. While it carried the familiar C63 name, it introduced significant changes, most notably replacing the naturally-aspirated 6.2-liter V-8 with a more compact and efficient twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V-8. Shared with the AMG GT, the engine was specially tuned, featuring increased maximum torque and a broader low-end range to better suit the C63’s weight and everyday performance needs. The C63 S Coupé is a circuit-focused performance model.
cars.hero: The most powerful model of the fourth-generation C-Class boasts a twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V-8.

cars.description: It represents one of the ultimate evolutions derived from the AMG GT lineage since its debut in 2014. Its 4.0-liter V-8 has been specially tuned to deliver an impressive 719.9 HP and 800 Nm (590.0 ft-lb) of torque. The suspension system has been completely reengineered with upgraded materials and construction, optimizing handling and cornering precision. Adding to its appeal is aggressive, race-inspired bodywork.
cars.hero: This ultimate version of the AMG GT is laden with Formula 1 technology.

cars.description: This was a true “road-going race car” derived from the AMG GT. Its aggressive wide-body design included flared fenders and an active aerodynamic system, while the front grille featured bold vertical slats that echoed AMG’s motorsport DNA. Under the hood, the twin-turbo 4.0-liter V-8 had been tuned to deliver an impressive 576.9 HP and 515.7 ft-lb of torque. It also marked a technical milestone, becoming the first Mercedes-AMG model to feature 4-wheel steering.
cars.hero: This 'road-legal race car' evokes the image of the much-celebrated 300SL sports car.

cars.description: The AMG GT was a supercar introduced in 2014 by Mercedes-Benz. Beneath its signature long-nose design sat a rigid aluminum space frame, housing the M178 3982 cc twin-turbo V-8 engine. The high-performance "S" variant pushed output to 502 HP, pairing that power with stiffer suspension and wider tires.
cars.hero: With a 192.6 mph top speed, this Mercedes-Benz is a race car in street-car clothes.

cars.description: The AMG GT was a supercar introduced in 2014 by Mercedes-Benz. Beneath its signature long-nose design sat a rigid aluminum space frame, housing the M178 3982 cc twin-turbo V-8 engine. The high-performance "S" variant pushed output to 502 HP. This particular model was modified as a Safety Car.
cars.hero: With a 192.6 mph top speed, this Mercedes-Benz is a race car in street-car clothes.

cars.description: The AMG GT3 was Mercedes-Benz’s dedicated GT3 race car. It was introduced in 2016 and designed for global GT3 category competition. It quickly proved its worth by securing a remarkable 1-2-3-4 finish in its debut race at the Nürburgring 24 Hours. One of its most successful campaigns came through HTP Motorsport, a top contender in the Blancpain GT Series.
cars.hero: This race car dominated the 24 Hours of Nürburgring in its very first outing.

cars.description: This FIA-homologated GT3 race car was based on the AMG GT. While performance and aerodynamics were improved, development also prioritized reducing running costs for client teams. This led to longer engine life, improved radiator protection, and several other enhancements. In 2020, the EVO model was introduced alongside a facelift for the road car, bringing with it a host of new features.
cars.hero: An improved and more cost effective GT3 machine

cars.description: This vehicle marked the launch of the "Vision Gran Turismo" project. Its elegant silhouette was inspired by a feline on the hunt, and it featured a hybrid structure of an aluminum space frame and carbon fiber. At just 2994 lbs, it remained relatively lightweight and was powered by an AMG twin-turbo 5.0-liter V-8 producing 430kW (576.9 HP) and 800Nm (590.2 ft-lb) of torque. Specialists also tuned the engine sound, making this machine as thrilling to hear as it was to behold.
cars.hero: The start of something very special: The very first "Vision Gran Turismo."

cars.description: This is a racing version of the Mercedes-Benz AMG Vision Gran Turismo. All interior comforts were removed to bring the weight down to 2866 lbs, while a large fixed rear wing increases downforce for circuit use. The AMG twin-turbo 5.5-liter V-8 has been tuned to produce 591.7 HP. The transmission has been upgraded from the 7-speed dual-clutch to a full sequential system for optimal performance on the track.
cars.hero: Another "Mercedes-Benz AMG Vision Gran Turismo" ready for competitive racing.
cars.name_long: Mercedes-Benz AMG Vision Gran Turismo Racing Series

cars.description: Unveiled at the 2009 Frankfurt Motor Show, this striking sports car was distinguished by its signature gull-wing doors. Beneath its all-aluminum body was a newly developed 6.3-liter V-8 engine, producing 563.1 HP and 477.4 ft-lb of torque. The 7-speed dual-clutch transmission was integrated with the rear differential, offering five selectable driving modes. Performance was formidable, with a zero-to-62.1 mph acceleration in just 3.8 seconds and a top speed of 197 mph.
cars.hero: With the SLS AMG, Mercedes-Benz recreates the 300 SL for the modern era.

cars.description: The SLS supercar paid tribute to Mercedes-Benz’s storied design heritage. This Gr.4 variant is a Gran Turismo Original. Fitted with a GT3-style roll cage, its long-nose, short-deck proportions echo the legendary 300SL, contributing to impressive cornering stability. Yet it’s not all about handling—the classic V-8 engine delivers formidable straight-line speed that’s equally hard to overlook.
cars.hero: With the SLS AMG, Mercedes-Benz recreates the 300 SL for the modern era.

cars.description: The SLS AMG GT3 was a race machine based on the road-going SLS AMG. It retained the same fundamental powerplant as the production model. Although official output figures were never released, estimates placed it at over 591.7 HP. Entering full-scale competition in 2011, the car secured 25 victories out of the 101 races it contested that year.
cars.hero: This race car version of Mercedes-Benz's supercar was tailored to FIA GT3 regulations.

cars.description: The Version NISMO Type 380RS was a fully tuned Z33 Fairlady Z developed by NISMO. Power House Amuse took it a step further, crafting the Amuse NISMO 380RS Super Leggera. The standout upgrade was its weight reduction of 309 lbs, a nod to the Super Leggera name—Italian for "super light."
cars.hero: Modified by Amuse, this Z car not only looked great, but also underwent a major weight reduction.

cars.description: While Power House Amuse was well known for tuning the S2000, its most refined build was the S2000 GT1. Its body kit was constructed with carbon fiber developed in collaboration with Polyphony Digital. Despite an increase in width to 72.0 inches, the car’s overall weight dropped to around 2469 lbs. Performance was further enhanced with engine upgrades, resulting in a remarkable power-to-weight ratio of just 4 lbs per 1 horsepower.
cars.hero: Development engineers of Gran Turismo contributed with Amuse to build this ultimate S2000.

cars.description: Unveiled at the 2016 Geneva Motor Show, the DB11 represented the quintessential Aston Martin. While retaining the brand’s signature silhouette, it distinguished itself from its predecessors with modern design cues. At its heart was a newly developed twin-turbo 5.2-liter V-12 producing 599.6 HP and 513.5 ft-lb of torque, paired with a ZF 8-speed automatic transmission, allowing the car to accelerate from zero to 62.1 mph in just 3.9 seconds and reaching a top speed of 206.3 mph.
cars.hero: Aston Martin's successor to the DB9 featured a new futuristic design theme.

cars.description: This car was a staple of the 1950s race scene. Starting with the base DB3, this car underwent extensive modifications, including a shortened wheelbase, reduced body weight, and refined aerodynamics. Its inline-6 engine, which originally produced 224.9 HP, was later tuned to deliver up to 239.6 HP. It was awarded the Gran Turismo Trophy at Pebble Beach in 2013.
cars.hero: This historic 1950s race car won the Pebble Beach Gran Turismo Trophy.

cars.description: The DB5 was a sports car introduced by Aston Martin in 1963. Designed by Italy’s Carrozzeria Touring, it featured superleggera construction that helped reduce overall weight. The standard model’s engine produced 282 horsepower (281.1 HP), while the Vantage variant delivered 314 horsepower (313.6 HP). It was praised as one of the standout sports cars of the early 1960s. It also gained iconic status as one of the original “Bond cars,” famously appearing in the James Bond 007 film series.
cars.hero: This classic sports car from the 1960s, as well as its most famous driver, James Bond, put Aston Martin on the international sports-car map.

cars.description: The Aston Martin DBR9 GT1 was developed by Aston Martin Racing in 2005 for competition in the GT1 category, based on the road-going DB9. Its body was significantly lightened using carbon-fiber construction, and it was powered by a 5.9-liter V-12 engine paired with a 6-speed sequential transmission. The DBR9 made an immediate impact, winning its debut race at the 12 Hours of Sebring. It went on to secure GT1 class victories at the 24 Hours of Le Mans in both 2007 and 2008.
cars.hero: This GT1 race car based on the Aston Martin DB9, commemorated the marque's return to international motorsports.

cars.description: The Vision Gran Turismo model was conceived by Marek Reichman’s design team at Aston Martin. It was developed using the same processes as Aston Martin’s production models, at the company’s Gaydon facility in Warwickshire. Power came from a twin-turbo V-12 producing 800 BHP (799.8 HP). The DP-100 also functioned as a testbed for Aston Martin’s future design language and advanced technologies.
cars.hero: A glimpse of the ultimate British sports car of the future.
cars.name_long: Aston Martin DP-100 Vision Gran Turismo

cars.description: This was Aston Martin’s new flagship model, unveiled in 2009. Although it shared visual cues with the DB9 and DBS, it was, in fact, a bespoke creation developed almost entirely from the ground up. At its heart lay a 7.3-liter V-12 engine, co-developed with Cosworth, producing 749.5 HP and 549.7 ft-lb of torque, making it the most powerful naturally aspirated engine ever fitted to a production car. Initially priced at £1,200,000 in the UK, all 77 units were spoken for within a year of deliveries commencing in early 2011.
cars.hero: This handsome supercar was limited to 77 units, and could very well be the most desirable British car ever.

cars.description: This was a purpose-built racing machine that began competing in GT events in 2012, continuing the proud legacy established by its predecessors, the DBR9 and DBRS9. Based on the V8 Vantage platform, it featured widened fenders and a prominent rear wing, while its weight was reduced to just 2756 lbs. The V-12 engine was tuned to deliver 591.7 HP and 513.5 ft-lb of torque, paired with an XTrac sequential transmission with paddle shifters. The car would go on to deliver exceptional performances at circuits across the globe.
cars.hero: A well-balanced, high-performance car that immediately became a familiar presence on race podiums.

cars.description: This Gran Turismo Original takes Aston Martin’s mid-range Vantage sports car and reimagines it to comply with Gr.4 race regulations. Its spirited V-8 engine delivers strong straight-line performance, while the car’s near-perfect weight distribution contributes to superb cornering dynamics, resulting in a highly capable racing machine.
cars.hero: Aston Martin's Porsche 911 fighter: The new Vantage.

cars.description: The "Baby Aston" was developed with the goal of delivering top-tier performance. This front-engine/rear-wheel-drive sports car first appeared in 2005, powered by a 4.3-liter V-8 engine. In 2008, displacement was increased to 4.7 liters, resulting in improved performance across the board. The Vantage S was a special high-performance variant introduced in 2011. In addition to its uprated engine, it featured a stiffer suspension setup and a quicker steering ratio, delivering a sharper driving experience.
cars.hero: Aston Martin's Porsche 911 fighter: The new Vantage.

cars.description: The Valkyrie hypercar was the result of a collaboration between Red Bull Racing and Aston Martin. Its front wing was suspended beneath a high-nose front section, while the entire underbody functioned as an aerodynamic tunnel, generating immense downforce. Power came from a naturally-aspirated 6.5-liter V-12 paired with a KERS hybrid system. With a total system output of 1139 HP, the Valkyrie delivered performance on par with top-tier racing machines.
cars.hero: A uniquely shaped hypercar with F1-derived aerodynamics.

cars.description: The Vantage proved to be a success as a performance-focused, rear-wheel-drive sports car. The model introduced in 2017 shared much of its construction with the DB11 V8, but featured a shorter wheelbase and was approximately 265 lbs lighter. These changes earned it widespread acclaim, with many praising it as the best-handling Aston Martin to date. The engine was a Mercedes-AMG–derived twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V-8, capable of reaching a top speed of 195.1 mph (195 mph).
cars.hero: This lightweight cornering machine has been hailed as the finest Aston Martin ever.

cars.description: A special circuit-only model limited to 24 units, this car was developed using the knowledge and experience gained from the One-77 project. Its front mid-mounted 7.0-liter V-12 produced 799.8 HP, delivered through a transaxle for optimal weight distribution. Damping, ABS, and traction control could all be fine-tuned to suit the driver’s preferences. Each fortunate owner received full technical support from Aston Martin, along with access to a dedicated circuit driving program.
cars.hero: With a mere 24 units produced, this hypercar shined on the track and became an instant collector's item.

cars.description: Audi Design created an all-electric Vision Gran Turismo concept. Throughout its body, design cues from the legendary 90 IMSA GTO are prominently featured. The vehicle employed a 4-wheel-drive layout powered by three electric motors—one at the front and two at the rear—delivering a total system output of 600kW (803.7 HP). Audi Sport developed a fully functional e-tron prototype, which went on to demonstrate its formidable performance at tracks worldwide.
cars.hero: This Vision Gran Turismo is a thrilling embodiment of Audi's electric mobility initiative.

cars.description: A Vision Gran Turismo model was developed by Audi Design. Two versions were conceived: one hybrid, the other fully electric. In the hybrid, a turbocharged 3.4-liter V-6 drove the rear wheels, while the front wheels were powered by an electric motor/generator unit, together delivering an impressive 950kW (1274.2 HP). The design of the car paid tribute to the iconic Audi 90 IMSA GTO race machine.
cars.hero: Taking cues from its IMSA race cars, this Vision Gran Turismo machine represents the future of Audi.

cars.description: The Audi R18 was engineered to compete in the 2016 World Endurance Championship (WEC). Its aerodynamics underwent a complete redesign, adopting a F1-inspired narrow nose with integrated wing, while the hybrid system’s regenerative energy capacity was increased from 4MJ to 6MJ. Although Audi secured 2nd place in the Constructors’ Championship, the brand made the difficult decision to withdraw from the WEC at year’s end.
cars.hero: Audi's history-making LMP1 car dominated the World Endurance Championship in the 2010s.

cars.description: This prototype race car was developed by Audi. While it shared lineage with the diesel-powered R10 and R15, the R18 was Audi’s first closed-cockpit design since the R8C of 1999. Its engine produced a modest 532.5 HP—less than its recent predecessors—but compensated with aggressive weight reduction and the aerodynamic efficiency afforded by its enclosed bodywork. In 2011, the R18 claimed overall victory at Le Mans.
cars.hero: This diesel-powered R18 TDI scored yet another victory for Audi at the 24 Hours of Le Mans in 2011.

cars.description: Although derived from the "Le Mans quattro" concept, the production version of this sports car took its name from Audi’s R8 race cars, which had earned a solid reputation with dominant performances at Le Mans. Built around Audi’s ultra-lightweight aluminum space frame, the car featured a 4.2-liter V-8 producing 414.2 HP, delivering power to all four wheels via the quattro system, which employed viscous couplings. In 2009, the lineup was expanded with the addition of the 5.2 FSI model, powered by a 5.2-liter V-10 generating 517.7 HP.
cars.hero: Engineered to the finest detail, this Audi supercar features welds measured in microns.

cars.description: The second-generation model of Audi’s road car, bearing the name of its renowned Le Mans prototype, continued the legacy of performance and innovation. While preserving the silhouette of its predecessor, the new model introduced a revised Audi Space Frame for improved rigidity and reduced weight, alongside an updated quattro all-wheel-drive system. The V10 Plus represented the high-performance model, with its 5.2-liter V-10 engine further refined to deliver an impressive 601.6 HP. It came equipped with a fixed rear wing and a mechanical LSD as standard.
cars.hero: Audi's second-generation sports car based on the Le Mans-conquering R8.

cars.description: In 2015, the production Audi R8 underwent a full model change, and with it came the debut of the updated R8 LMS, built to FIA GT3 specifications. This new generation brought significant advancements in both safety and aerodynamics, while the transmission and traction control systems were replaced with newly developed, race-focused components. Mere moments after its unveiling, the R8 LMS proved its capabilities by taking overall victory in its debut outing at the Nürburgring 24 Hours.
cars.hero: This updated version of a champion race car won the Nürburgring 24 Hour Race immediately after its debut.

cars.description: This was the evolution model of the R8 LMS. Cooling efficiency and aerodynamic performance saw notable improvements over its predecessor, while the entire drivetrain was upgraded to boost reliability under the demands of endurance racing. Although engine output remained unchanged, a 55 lbs reduction in body weight allowed greater flexibility in weight distribution through ballast adjustment. Making its debut in the autumn of 2018, the car demonstrated its potential with a victory at the Gulf 12 Hours later that year.
cars.hero: This evolved version of Audi's R8 LMS competed in various GT3 events across the globe.

cars.description: This was a 2019 Deutsche Tourenwagen Masters (DTM) machine. In line with the series’ engine downsizing rules, the previous 4.0-liter V-8 was replaced with a turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-4. Remarkably, the new engine produced more power than its predecessor, while also weighing less, with improved weight distribution. In the 2019 season, Audi’s ace driver René Rast captured the championship title, alongside securing the team championship.
cars.hero: A DTM machine with two victories in the Class 1 era.

cars.description: Audi shook the rallying world in 1981 with the debut of its full-time 4-wheel-drive system in the World Rally Championship. This particular variant, a modified version of the Sport quattro S1, was tailored specifically for hill climb competitions, equipped with radical ground effects that pushed the limits of aerodynamics. In 1987, Walter Röhrl piloted this machine to a record-breaking triumph at the Pikes Peak International Hill Climb.
cars.hero: The 1987 winner of the Pikes Peak that also set a new record that year.
cars.name_long: Audi Sport quattro S1 Pikes Peak '87

cars.description: The Audi TT was a sports coupe introduced in 1998. The base model came equipped with the same 177.5 HP turbocharged 1.8-liter DOHC inline-4 found in the Audi A3 and A4, while higher trims featured more powerful versions of the same powerplant. In 2003, the 3.2 quattro variant joined the lineup, powered by a 3.2-liter V-6 engine producing 246.5 HP. It was paired with Audi’s next-generation two-pedal manual, the DSG (Direct Shift Gearbox), offering lightning-fast gear changes.
cars.hero: With its ground-breaking exterior design, this agile coupe took the sports car world by storm.

cars.description: This racing machine was based on the Audi TT and developed specifically for the Audi Sport TT Cup one-make series. Sections of the body shell were replaced with carbon fiber, and all driver comforts were stripped away, reducing the car’s weight to just 2480 lbs. It was powered by a 305.7 HP 2.0-liter 4-cylinder engine, the same unit found in the standard TTS, but enhanced with a "push to pass" system that temporarily boosted output by an additional 29.6 HP.
cars.hero: These TTs were produced specifically for the "Audi Sport TT Cup" one-make race.

cars.description: The TTS was the high-performance variant of the TT series, introduced in 2008. Its powertrain featured a 2.0-liter direct-injection turbocharged engine paired with either a 6-speed manual or a 6-speed S-Tronic transmission. The engine block, pistons, and connecting rods were uniquely developed for the TTS, and the turbocharger was upgraded to handle the increased output. Power was delivered through Audi’s proprietary full-time 4-wheel-drive system, enabling a zero-62.1 mph acceleration time of 5.2 seconds with the S-Tronic model, and 5.4 seconds with the manual.
cars.hero: A high-performance model, aggressively evolved from the TT.

cars.description: The third-generation TT made its debut in 2014. While it retained the core design philosophy of its predecessors, it adopted a more aggressive look, highlighted by a larger single-frame grille and headlights inspired by the R8. At the top of the range sat the TTS, the flagship sports variant, equipped with a 2.0 TFSI turbocharged 4-cylinder engine tuned to produce 309.7 HP and 274.9 ft-lb of torque in the German domestic model. Paired with a 6-speed manual transmission and Audi’s quattro all-wheel-drive system, it delivered a truly exhilarating driving experience.
cars.hero: With more power, the sporty version of the third-gen TT took a good thing and made it even better.

cars.description: The A112 Abarth, introduced in 1971, was widely regarded as one of the original hot hatches. Based on the Autobianchi A112, the car was tuned by Abarth. Continuously refined throughout its production run, the car's engine displacement was increased in 1975, raising output to 70 HP, and in 1979, a 5-speed transmission was added. Although production ended in 1985, the A112 Abarth maintained a loyal following among enthusiasts drawn to its lively character.
cars.hero: The original hot hatch, with excellent power and agile handling, paved the way for a new genre.

cars.description: Built by Britain’s Briggs Automotive Company, this car was designed to deliver “the most authentic and pure driving experience” on the road. Its single-seat layout is built around a tubular chassis wrapped in a carbon-fiber shell, and it’s powered by a Cosworth-tuned 2.5-liter Ford Duratec engine. Weighing just 1279 lbs, the car rockets from 0-60 mph in a blistering 2.8 seconds, and reaches a top speed of 170.3 mph—performance figures on par with a Formula 3 car.
cars.hero: Simple yet effective, this single-seat sports car is reminiscent of formula cars from a bygone era.

cars.description: In 1968, BMW introduced the 2800 CS sports coupe, powered by a robust 2.8-liter inline-6 engine. By 1971, the 3.0 CS arrived, an updated version with a larger engine. To compete in motorsport, BMW created a lightweight homologation model based on the 3.0 CS, naming it the 3.0 CSL. The "L" in CSL stood for “light,” reflecting the car’s reduced weight for racing.
cars.hero: This lightweight model of the 3.0 CS was stripped of all creature comforts to maximize performance.

cars.description: Unveiled in 1971, the 3.0 CSL served as the homologation version of the BMW 3.0 CS, featuring a powerful 3.0-liter inline-6 engine. Engine displacement grew from 2985 cc to 3003 cc in 1972, and to 3155 cc in 1973 for the evolution models, which achieved remarkable success on the European touring car stage.
cars.hero: This lightweight model of the BMW 3.0 CS was developed to compete in touring car racing.

cars.description: This modern road racer was developed by BMW’s design team. Its exterior was sculpted to convey a striking sense of speed, even at a standstill. Power came from a 3.0-liter inline-6 delivering 404kW and 680Nm of torque (541.4 HP/499.1 ft-lb). Remarkably lightweight at just 2601 lbs, the car also achieved ideal 50:50 front-to-rear weight distribution. This Vision Gran Turismo represents a striking blend of BMW’s racing heritage and advanced technology.
cars.hero: The ultimate road racer that draws its heritage from the glorious touring cars of the '70s.

cars.description: This electric vehicle was unveiled by BMW in 2013. Its distinctive, boxy 4-door body featured small, pillarless rear doors, and weighed just 2634 lbs, thanks to an aluminum alloy chassis paired with a carbon-fiber cabin. The electric motor produced 167.7 HP and 180.8 ft-lb of torque, enabling the car to accelerate from zero to 37.3 mph in 3.7 seconds, and to 62.1 mph in 7.2 seconds. With a top speed exceeding 93.2 mph, it proved it can compete with its internal combustion-powered counterparts.
cars.hero: BMW’s first mass-produced production vehicle has a sports-car heart.

cars.description: This cutting-edge Le Mans Daytona h (LMDh) prototype used a Dallara-built carbon-fiber monocoque and a hybrid system built around the DTM-derived P66/3, a twin-turbo 4.0-liter V-8 engine. During the 2025 season, the car competed in both the IMSA WeatherTech SportsCar Championship and the FIA World Endurance Championship, highlighted by a 1-2 finish at Road America in the eighth round of IMSA In the WEC, it also showed strong pace at rounds such as Imola, proving itself at the highest level of endurance racing.
cars.hero: A new category sports prototype that carries the lineage of the celebrated V12 LMR.

cars.description: This ferocious beast housed the S55 twin-turbo 3.0-liter inline-6 from the M3 and M4 within the compact body of the 2 Series coupe. Its flared fenders hinted at the performance lurking beneath, and a brief press of the throttle was all it took to unleash the full force as the turbochargers came alive. The suspension incorporated aluminum components to reduce unsprung weight. Meanwhile, the torque-vectoring Active M Differential allowed it to tackle any corner with confidence and precision.
cars.hero: A hardboiled FR that hides the power of a demon in its compact body.

cars.description: The third-generation M3 was introduced with the E46 3 Series. Its 3.2-liter S54 Inline-6 delivered more than 98.6 HP per liter, peaking at 338.3 HP at 7900 rpm. In 2003, the high-performance CSL variant was launched. It featured a carbon-fiber roof to reduce weight and a retuned engine pushing output to 355 HP. This model went on to achieve significant success in touring car racing and various other motorsport events.
cars.hero: Featuring BMW's high-revving engine technology, this sports car represented the epitome of the E46 3 Series.

cars.description: Across multiple generations of the 3 Series, the M3 has consistently been positioned as a high-performance variant with a deep motorsports heritage. The E92 M3 paired a 7-speed dual-clutch transmission (DCT) with a high-revving 4.0-liter V-8 delivering 414.2 HP. Despite its larger body, extensive weight-saving measures kept the road car’s weight down to just 3593 lbs. It could sprint from zero to 62.1 mph in 4.8 seconds.
cars.hero: Based on the E92 3 Series coupe, this 4th-gen M3 featured a 414.2 HP V8.

cars.description: This homologation model was developed from the 3 Series platform of its time, specifically to compete in touring car racing. Built on the 2-door sedan, it featured a widened track and aerodynamic enhancements, including an adjustable rear wing to improve performance. It initially came with a 2.3-liter DOHC inline-4 engine, with continuous yearly refinements leading to the 2.5-liter Sport Evolution model.
cars.hero: A virtual race car for the street, this homologation model once claimed victory in the DTM.

cars.description: The second-generation M3 was based on the E36 3 Series. It marked a shift from pure motorsport focus to a more refined grand tourer. This model offered a broader appeal with multiple body styles, including a 2-door coupe, 4-door sedan, and cabriolet. Originally equipped with a 3.0-liter engine, the M3 received an upgrade in 1995 to a 3.2-liter unit, along with the introduction of a 6-speed manual and an optional 2-pedal SMG (Sequential Manual Gearbox).
cars.hero: From race car to luxury grand tourer, the second-generation M3.

cars.description: The GT version, developed from this high-performance base, was extensively modified for racing. Many body panels were replaced with carbon fiber, cutting weight down to 2745 lbs, while the fenders were flared, widening the body by 4.3 inches. Even with a restrictor in place, the 4.0-liter V-8 still produced an impressive 493.1 HP.
cars.hero: BMW's M3 GT2 raced in premier endurance contests including the ALMS and ILMC series as well as the 24 Hours of Nürburgring.

cars.description: This coupe was designed for touring car racing and developed by BMW M, based on the E30 3 Series. It featured blistered fenders, front and rear spoilers, and distinctive side skirts, giving it a bold, aggressive appearance. The Sport Evolution was the final version of this M3 generation. Its enlarged 2.5-liter engine produced 234.7 HP and 173.6 ft-lb of torque, making it a formidable force on the circuit.
cars.hero: This highly modified homologation version of the E30 3 Series served as a small hint of what was to come from BMW.

cars.description: The 3 Series coupe and cabriolet models were split off to form the new 4 Series lineup, with this car serving as the flagship. While its sleek 2-door coupe proportions made it visually striking, its true emphasis was on performance. Under the hood was a twin-turbocharged inline-6 producing 425 HP and 405.8 ft-lb of torque. Paired with an active M differential, adaptive M suspension, and M-specific DSC, it delivered a driving experience worthy of the M badge.
cars.hero: The BMW M4 becomes the 2-door version of the daunting M3.

cars.description: This Gran Turismo Original reimagines BMW’s new-generation high-performance M4 coupe as a Gr.4-spec machine. Although styled like a touring car, it retains the precise cornering ability and rock-solid stability that define BMW’s performance legacy. Its well-balanced handling and approachable dynamics make it an ideal choice even for novice drivers.
cars.hero: This Gran Turismo original Gr.4 race car maximizes the performance of the M4.

cars.description: This Gran Turismo Original safety car is based on BMW’s latest-generation high-performance M4 coupe. Building on the M Performance Edition, it features a range of specially designed components, including a front lip spoiler, hood pins, grille garnishes, a rear spoiler, and a rear diffuser.
cars.hero: A special safety-car version of the BMW M4.

cars.description: BMW announced its entry into the FIA GT3 category with the M6 GT3, beginning in the 2016 season. At 16.4 ft long and 6.6 ft wide, it presented a noticeably larger footprint compared to its predecessor, the compact Z4 GT3. Gran Turismo series producer Kazunori Yamauchi competed in the Nürburgring 24 Hours behind the wheel of the Walkenhorst Motorsport M6 GT3, finishing the race and placing 22nd overall.
cars.hero: The car driven by Kazunori Yamauchi in the 2016 24 Hours of Nürburgring.

cars.description: This car succeeded the Z4 GT3, which had been BMW’s flagship GT3 racer since 2010. In stark contrast to the compact Z4, it featured a commanding presence, measuring nearly 16.4 ft long and more than 6.6 ft wide. Under the hood, a twin-turbo 4.4-liter V-8 delivered 576.9 HP in its stock configuration. Built primarily from carbon fiber, the car also featured a completely redesigned frame and suspension, setting it far apart from the production M6.
cars.hero: A powerful GT3 race machine with a 4.4-liter twin-turbocharged V8.

cars.description: Masterminded by Gordon Murray, this car is the racing evolution of the high-performance road-going McLaren F1. After its debut in 1995, the car underwent continuous development, culminating in the introduction of this aerodynamically enhanced Long Tail version in 1997. The F1 GTR enjoyed a long racing career, remaining at the forefront of GT competition under privateer teams all the way through to 2003.
cars.hero: This F1 GTR race car took many racing titles around the world, including the 24 Hours of Le Mans.
cars.name_long: BMW McLaren F1 GTR Race Car '97

cars.description: The Z4 was a convertible sports car that made its debut in 2002 as the successor to the Z3. Its design was distinguished by clean fender lines and a signature Z-shaped press line just ahead of the door. Torsional rigidity was improved by nearly threefold compared to the Z3, while overall weight was reduced by 55 lbs. It also introduced several new technologies, becoming the first BMW to feature electric power steering.
cars.hero: An elegant convertible with an inline-6 engine lurking under its elongated hood.

cars.description: Based on the E89-generation Z4, BMW’s GT3 race machine began competition in 2010. Weight was reduced by 661 lbs through extensive modifications, including the replacement of the retractable roof with a fixed panel. The engine was also changed to a 4.0-liter V-8. In 2011, the car was further refined with wider fenders and a larger 4.4-liter engine producing 507.9 HP. Paired with an upgraded paddle-shift transmission, this Z4 achieved a series of remarkable results in some of the world’s most fiercely contested GT races.
cars.hero: Starting the 2011 24 Hours of Spa from the 49th position on the grid, this BMW Z4 GT3 crossed the finish line in a remarkable 2nd place.

cars.description: This luxury convertible sports car drew inspiration from the iconic BMW 507 of the 1950s. Its aluminum space frame housed the same 5.0-liter V-8 and 6-speed manual transmission found in the E39 M5, producing 394.5 HP and capable of accelerating from zero to 62.1 mph in just 4.7 seconds. It also earned cinematic fame as the featured Bond car in a 007 movie.
cars.hero: BMW's contemporary Z8 roadster has the distinction of being one of James Bond's rare non-British vehicles.

cars.description: This machine was conceived as a tribute to Bugatti’s storied racing heritage. Designers and engineers collaborated to craft the vehicle using cutting-edge technologies and advanced aerodynamic theory. Powered by a W16 engine with four turbochargers, it produced an astonishing 1230kW and 1580Nm of torque (1649.9 HP/1165.2 ft-lb), enabling it to exceed 248.5 mph in four sections of Circuit de la Sarthe, home of the 24 Hours of Le Mans. This immense power allowed the car to achieve a top speed of 278.1 mph.
cars.hero: This Vision Gran Turismo machine pays homage to the Type 57 Tank, one of the glorious cars that define Bugatti's history.

cars.description: A version of the Bugatti Vision Gran Turismo concept car has been developed in collaboration with Gran Turismo and adapted to meet Gr.1 regulations. Thanks to its wide track and 4-wheel-drive system, the base platform delivers excellent stability, resulting in a surprisingly approachable race car.
cars.hero: A dream machine made to be the pinnacle of race cars and a true Bugatti.

cars.description: The Chiron is a super sports car by Bugatti, introduced in 2016. Limited to a global production run of just 500 units, it serves as the spiritual successor to the groundbreaking Veyron. Built around a carbon-fiber chassis with rigidity comparable to that of an LMP1 race car, the Chiron is powered by the Veyron’s quad-turbo 8.0-liter W16, tuned to produce 1479.3 HP and 1179.7 ft-lb of torque. It can accelerate from zero to 62.1 mph in just 2.5 seconds, and a prototype version recorded a top speed of 304.8 mph.
cars.hero: The successor to the ultra-high-performance Veyron.

cars.description: This car was the ultimate expression of a modern super sports machine. First unveiled at the 2005 Tokyo Motor Show, it delivered figures rarely seen even among elite supercars: 987.2 HP, a top speed of 252.9 mph, and a price tag of one million euros. Its engine was an 8.0-liter W-16 equipped with four turbochargers, paired with a 7-speed DSG transmission. To access its maximum velocity, a special key was required to activate top-speed mode, allowing the car to exceed 233 mph.
cars.hero: With a little help from a special key, this remarkable automobile reached speeds of over 233 mph.

cars.description: Bugatti’s Veyron supercar has been reimagined to meet Gr.4 regulations for this Gran Turismo Original. Although its power output was reduced from that of the standard model to comply with class rules, it can still hold its own against rivals with impressive straight-line speed. Its 4-wheel-drive system also provides a distinct advantage in cornering, offering exceptional stability through turns.
cars.hero: With a little help from a special key, this remarkable automobile reached speeds of over 233 mph.

cars.description: The BVLGARI Aluminium Vision Gran Turismo draws its inspiration from the "BVLGARI Aluminium," a watch that reshaped the industry in 1998, carrying the same spirit—sporty, intelligent, essential and precise. Its design remains timeless and distinctive, reflecting a bold, conceptual approach while staying true to BVLGARI’s design DNA, rising above fleeting trends and fashion cycles.
cars.hero: A digital concept car infused with the DNA of BVLGARI.

cars.description: This car was produced by Caterham in 1996, more than two decades after the company inherited production rights to the Seven from Lotus in 1973. As the Superlight name implied, weight was trimmed throughout the car, making it between 77 lbs and 110 lbs lighter than the standard Seven, depending on trim. The later models from 2008 and after, were powered by a 2.0-liter Ford engine producing 262.3 HP, giving it 0-to-62.1 mph acceleration of 2.88 seconds and performance that could rival supercars.
cars.hero: The ultimate version of the extremely lightweight Caterham.

cars.description: The Chaparral 2J was a highly unconventional race car that competed in the 1970 SCCA Can-Am series. Nicknamed the “vacuum cleaner,” it featured a groundbreaking design with two fans mounted at the rear of the car. Powered by a separate secondary engine, these fans created powerful suction by extracting air from beneath the chassis. In effect, it became the world’s first active ground-effect race car. However, for the 1971 season, a change in SCCA regulations banned the use of auxiliary engines, leading to the retirement of the 2J.
cars.hero: Dubbed by some as "the vacuum cleaner," this car became an American racing icon.

cars.description: Chaparral is a legendary name in motorsport, known for producing unique race cars, and the 2X is unlike anything that came before it. The driver is enclosed within a carbon fiber body, positioned headfirst in a prone posture, as if hovering just centimeters above the track. Power comes from a radical laser pulse propulsion system, which generates thrust and downforce through the rapid expansion of air.
cars.hero: Experience rocket-like speed produced by laser pulse shock waves!

cars.description: The Chevrolet Camaro 1968 Race-Mod was Gran Turismo’s modern interpretation of the Camaro Z28, a car originally developed for homologation in the SCCA’s Trans-Am Series. Adorned with carbon black trim, the exterior featured a wide-mouth bumper, a large ducktail spoiler, and a center-exit exhaust. The interior featured a sequential shifter and roll cage, along with Alcantara bucket seats.
cars.hero: This is a restomod of the classic Trans-Am hero Camaro Z28.

cars.description: The sixth-generation Camaro made its debut in 2015. While the exterior continued the retro-modern theme of its predecessor, the underlying structure featured an entirely new design. Built on the new Alpha platform, the car employed aluminum extensively, resulting in 28 percent more rigidity and a weight reduction of 198 lbs. The SS performance model came equipped with a 6.2-liter V-8 engine, and included 20-inch wheels and Brembo brakes as standard.
cars.hero: The sports grade model of the 6th generation Camaro with the 6.2-liter LT1 engine.

cars.description: The original Ford Mustang was an unprecedented success upon its debut as a compact sports coupe. In response, Chevrolet set out to surpass Ford’s achievement, unveiling the Camaro as a direct competitor in the autumn of 1966. The Z28 represented the Camaro at its performance peak. This special variant featured a larger-displacement engine and an enhanced chassis, developed to meet the regulations of the Trans-Am production-based race category.
cars.hero: The Z28 is one of the most popular muscle cars ever, thanks to its good looks and high performance.

cars.description: The sixth-generation Chevrolet Camaro made its debut in 2015. At the top of the lineup stood the ZL1, powered by the same supercharged 5.7-liter LT4 V-8 engine found in the Corvette Z06. It delivered an impressive 649.9 HP and 649.5 ft-lb of torque. In 2018, a version equipped with the 1LE performance package—which included upgrades to the suspension and drivetrain—recorded a Nürburgring lap time of 7:16.04, outperforming a number of supercars.
cars.hero: This version of the sixth-generation Camaro lived up to the hype, thanks in part to its 649.9 HP LT1 engine.

cars.description: The Chevelle was introduced in 1964 as Chevrolet’s first intermediate-size model. The Chevelle also offered the "SS" performance trim, which reached its peak with the introduction of the 1970 model. That year saw the debut of the SS 454, powered by the LS6 engine, the most powerful production engine listed in any American car catalog at the time. It's no wonder that the SS 454 quickly became one of the most formidable and dependable contenders on the drag racing circuit.
cars.hero: A massive engine that produced plenty of power made this car a favorite for drag racing.

cars.description: In the early 1950s, the American sports car market was largely ruled by European imports. It was during this time that Chevrolet introduced the original Corvette. The first models featured a forward-thinking design, combining a steel frame with lightweight fiberglass body panels. Power came from a 3.8-liter inline-6 producing 149.9 HP. Initially built as a limited run of just 300 units, the Corvette quickly captured public interest, leading to full-scale production beginning in 1954. That year, output was increased slightly to 152.9 HP, and by 1958, the Corvette gained distinctive quad headlights.
cars.hero: The origin of the American sports car: the glorious first-generation Corvette.

cars.description: This generation played a pivotal role in cementing the Corvette’s reputation as the king of American sports cars. Its futuristic yet refined design captivated audiences worldwide. Its performance was equally impressive, thanks to a 5.4-liter OHV V-8 engine producing more than 295.9 HP, combined with 4-wheel independent suspension and a short wheelbase.
cars.hero: This second-generation Corvette sports car was based on the Stingray race machine.
cars.name_long: Chevrolet Corvette Sting Ray Sport Coupe (C2) '63

cars.description:
The Stingray name returned with the launch of the seventh-generation Corvette. Built using lightweight materials, the car maintained a nearly perfect 50:50 front-to-rear weight distribution, even with its powerful 6.2-liter LT1 V-8, matching the benchmark set by the world’s finest sports cars. \r
Equipped with the Z51 performance package, with features such as an electronic LSD, dry sump lubrication, and high-performance brakes, the car was able to accelerate from zero to 60 mph in just 3.8 seconds.
cars.hero: The seventh-generation Corvette is the first to wear the "Stingray" badge since the 1976 third-generation model.

cars.description: This Gran Turismo Original took the final front-engine Corvette—the C7—and transformed it to meet Gr.3 regulations. Its exterior has been purpose-built for endurance racing, featuring prominent fog lamps and a distinctively shaped rear wing. Underneath, the raw acceleration of the large-displacement V-8 combined with the sharp, balanced handling of a front-mid-engine layout showcases what a front-engine/rear-drive race car should be.
cars.hero: The daunting Stingray moniker was resurrected with the seventh-generation Chevrolet Corvette.

cars.description: A homologation model of the C7 Gr.3, a race-prepped version of the final front-engine Corvette, meets Gr.3 competition standards. Visually, it stands out with a bold design that pushes right up to the 80.7 inches width limit allowed in the category. Despite its broad stance, the car is exceptionally agile, with race-spec suspension allowing for quick and precise cornering, revealing its true identity as a purpose-built performance machine
cars.hero: The daunting Stingray badge returns with the 7th-gen Chevrolet Corvette.
cars.name_long: Chevrolet Corvette C7 Gr.3 Road Car

cars.description: This Gran Turismo Original reimagines the C7—the final front-engine Corvette—to meet Gr.4 regulations. It retains the base car’s predictable cornering behavior, resulting in a confidence-inspiring driving experience. With impressive straight-line speed to match, it allows drivers to stay competitive across every section of the track.
cars.hero: The daunting Stingray badge returns with the 7th-gen Chevrolet Corvette.

cars.description: The ZR1 was introduced near the end of the C7 Corvette’s production run, becoming the most powerful version of the generation. Under the hood, the supercharged 6.2-liter LT5 V-8 delivered 754.4 HP and 969 Nm (714.6 ft-lb) of torque. Its aerodynamic components were developed in collaboration with Pratt & Miller Engineering, which campaigned the C7 in GT racing. Buyers could choose between a model focused on lap times, or one maximizing top speed. A ZR1 equipped with the high-speed package was capable of reaching an impressive 214.9 mph.
cars.hero: One of the last of the C7 Corvettes and also the most powerful.

cars.description: Released in 2019, the eighth-generation Corvette became the first in the lineup to adopt a mid-engine layout—a major departure from the traditional front-engine design. At its core was the new 6.2-liter LT2 V-8, producing 495.1 HP and 470.1 ft-lb of torque, paired with an 8-speed dual-clutch gearbox. Although it left behind the Corvette’s signature long-nose silhouette, the C8 delivered outstanding performance, particularly in GT racing.
cars.hero: A new generation mid-engine Corvette.

cars.description: The third-generation Corvette made its debut in the fall of 1967. Heavily inspired by Chevrolet’s 1965 show car, the Mako Shark II, it introduced a bold new coupe design, characterized by its curvaceous “coke bottle” silhouette, which instantly turned heads. Initially launched simply as the Corvette, the model brought back the Stingray name in 1969, along with a larger engine that added greater versatility and performance.
cars.hero: Taking design cues from the Mako Shark II concept, this 3rd-gen Corvette was known for its distinctive character.

cars.description: The Corvette CX Concept was an all-wheel drive electric hypercar. At its core was a fan-powered downforce system, using fighter jet–style thrust vectoring to precisely balance aerodynamic forces between the front and rear.  This advanced setup allowed for more than 2,000 horsepower generated by four electric motors. Engineered to feel equally at home on both road and track, the CX Concept represented a bold new vision for the Corvette legacy.
cars.hero: An electric hypercar that offered a glimpse into the future of the Corvette.

cars.description: The Corvette CX.R Vision Gran Turismo Concept is a track-only model based on the Corvette CX Concept. With enhanced aerodynamics and a dramatically lower ride height, it offers even greater performance capability. Under the skin, a hybrid powertrain combines electric motors with an e-fuel–driven engine, delivering the speed, endurance, and efficiency demanded by endurance racing.
cars.hero: A futuristic GT racer born from the Corvette lineage.
cars.name_long: Chevrolet Corvette CX.R Vision Gran Turismo Concept

cars.description: The 1968 Corvette Stingray drew its design inspiration from the Mako Shark II concept, which reimagined the Corvette as a sleek grand tourer. In 1969, the base engine displacement was increased from 327 to 350 cubic inches, although output remained at 295.9 HP. The following year, Chevrolet introduced the LT1 engine, producing 364.9 HP. This version earned praise for being the best handling C3 Corvette.
cars.hero: The Stingray version of the alluring 3rd-gen Corvette translated to more performance all around.

cars.description: The original Chevrolet Corvette earned numerous race victories. The Corvette SS, a purpose-built race car developed under the direction of GM engineer Zora Arkus-Duntov, featured a 364.9 HP fuel-injected 283 cubic inch engine, and was capable of reaching a top speed of 181.4 mph. However, following a major incident in NASCAR, the AMA imposed a ban on factory-backed race programs. The Stingray Racer was introduced as the successor to the Corvette SS and went on to win the SCCA Class C Modified title in 1959 and 1960.
cars.hero: The '59 concept embodied a styling that swept the world and remains a part of Corvette history.

cars.description: The Corvette C5 lineup expanded in 1999 with the addition of a hardtop model, which increased body rigidity and improved performance. Even more appealing to enthusiasts was its lower price point compared to the standard model, which helped it gain strong support. In 2001, Chevrolet pushed the C5 platform even further with the Z06. Inspired by the spirit of the C2, it delivered outstanding performance and held the highest top speed of any production Corvette of its time.
cars.hero: The top-of-the-line variant of the fifth-generation Corvette revives the classic Z06 moniker.

cars.description: The ZR-1 name first appeared in 1990 as a special high-performance package for the Corvette. At its heart was the LT5 engine, which featured an aluminum alloy block and a DOHC 4-valve head co-developed by Chevrolet and Lotus. While the standard Corvette engine produced 246.5 HP, the LT5 delivered 374.8 HP. Despite its price tag—twice that of a base Corvette—it’s said that Chevrolet made very little profit from the model, underscoring its role as a halo car rather than a volume seller.
cars.hero: The daunting ZR1 badge on the 4th-gen Corvette assured world-beating performance.

cars.description: From the debut of the C6 Z06 in 2005, the Chevrolet Corvette began to show not only the styling but also the performance credentials of a true supercar. By 2008, the ZR1 had taken things even further, matching its high-end rivals from Ferrari and Lamborghini in raw performance. Its supercharged 6.2-liter V-8 produced 638.1 HP, and with a curb weight of just 3325 lbs, it posted a Nürburgring lap time faster than that of the Nissan GT-R.
cars.hero: The 6th-gen Corvette ZR1 set one of the fastest lap times ever for a production car at the Nürburgring.

cars.description: It's an imaginative custom hot rod that made its debut at SEMA 2013. Based on a 1967 Chevrolet Nova body, it was outfitted with the supercharged 6.2-liter LS9 engine from the Corvette, paired with racing-grade components across the braking and suspension systems. It took home the prestigious GT Award that year.
cars.hero: This monster Nova was a 2013 GT Award winner, equipped with the highest quality performance parts available.

cars.description: France's world-famous economy car, the 2 CV remained in production for 42 years after its introduction in 1948. Introduced in 1980, the Charleston was a special-edition model featuring a two-tone body and a more luxurious interior. At its heart was an air-cooled flat-2 engine that had grown to 602 cc over the generations, and while it produced just 28.6 HP, that was enough to propel the extremely lightweight body with ease.
cars.hero: A masterpiece of the French people's car with a two-tone color scheme.

cars.description: The BX made its debut at the 1982 Paris Salon. It carried forward the spirit of Citroën’s iconic GS and CX models while introducing a modern, geometric design language. The styling was penned by Marcello Gandini during his tenure at Bertone. True to Citroën tradition, the car featured the brand’s signature hydropneumatic suspension system. The 19 TRS model featured here was a grand tourer-style variant powered by a 1.9-liter gasoline engine.
cars.hero: Citroën’s versatile tourer receives a modern makeover.

cars.description: The Citroën DS made its debut at the 1955 Paris Salon, introduced as a groundbreaking front-wheel-drive vehicle that combined a sleek aerodynamic profile with advanced hydropneumatic suspension. It quickly earned the nickname “flying saucer” for its appearance. Development was led by André Lefèbvre, while the striking body was the work of designer Flaminio Bertoni. In 1964, Citroën introduced the upscale Pallas trim, followed by the addition of quad headlights in 1967. The DS 21 Pallas delivered refined performance from its 2.1-liter engine and remained in production for two decades.
cars.hero: A historic vision of the future from France.

cars.description: Designed for competition in the Gr.4 category, this race car is a modified version of the GT by Citroën, originally unveiled at the 2008 Paris Motor Show. The updates were overseen by Takumi Yamamoto, the designer behind the original concept. Its exterior features a striking six-color livery and a prominent rear wing. Also, the interior has been revised with a new steering wheel and updated HUD to suit its motorsports focus.
cars.hero: This concept car for the virtual world was developed in collaboration with Citroën.

cars.description: A Gran Turismo Original, this Gr.3-spec version of the GT by Citroën is born from a unique collaboration between Gran Turismo and Citroën. Unlike the stock model, its aggressive exterior—reminiscent of a battle-ready machine—leaves a striking impression. Fitted with multiple aerodynamic winglets across the body, it delivers exceptional downforce.
cars.hero: This concept car for the virtual world was developed in collaboration with Citroën.

cars.description: Based on the GT by Citroën, first shown at the 2008 Paris Motor Show, this model has been reimagined as the ultimate road-going version. The most significant change lay in the powertrain, transformed from a high-performance EV into a V-8-powered, mid-engine sports car. Its distinctive, armor-like styling was preserved, creating a uniquely striking and high-performance machine built for the road.
cars.hero: From dream to reality, the supercar concept developed by Citroën and Gran Turismo becomes a V8-powered mid-engine sports car.

cars.description: First unveiled as the Kopen at the 1999 Tokyo Motor Show, this model entered production in 2002 as the Daihatsu Copen, becoming the company’s first fully convertible kei-class car. With a rigid yet lightweight body and a specially tuned suspension, the Copen delivered sharp and responsive handling. It also drew significant attention for being the first kei-car in the world to feature a power-operated retractable hardtop. Its unique charm led to exports to markets such as the UK and Australia.
cars.hero: A kei car with a sports car heart, this little convertible was at home on the racetrack.

cars.description: The Daihatsu Copen is a compact convertible that delivers a full sports car experience while staying within Japan’s kei-car regulations. The Copen RJ Vision Gran Turismo is based on the second-generation model, which debuted in 2014. While it retains the kei-standard 660 cc engine, boost efficiency has been significantly improved, allowing it to produce 146.9 HP and 149.0 ft-lb of torque. Further weight reduction brings the car down to just 1323 lbs, enabling it to perform on par with larger-displacement sports cars. This bold, aspirational machine carried forward Daihatsu’s fighting spirit.
cars.hero: A Vision Gran Turismo that represents the potential of kei cars.
cars.name_long: DAIHATSU COPEN RJ Vision Gran Turismo

cars.description: This was De Tomaso’s second production mid-engine sports car. To address the lack of power in the earlier Vallelunga, it was fitted with a Ford V-8 engine. Weighing approximately 1.3 tons, the car could reach a top speed of 155.3 mph, thanks to its lightweight construction. The exterior, notable for its gullwing-opening rear section, was designed by Giorgetto Giugiaro during his time at Carrozzeria Ghia. Production was limited to just 401 units.
cars.hero: This mid-engine sports car set the stage for the famous Pantera.

cars.description: This was the third model created by De Tomaso. Its sleek body, crafted by Carrozzeria Ghia, was paired with a robust 5.8-liter OHV V-8 sourced from Ford. This striking combination delivered performance on par with its more expensive contemporaries.
cars.hero: This extremely rare supercar combined vivid Italian design with no-nonsense American power.

cars.description: Formerly a vice president at GM, John Z. DeLorean struck out on his own to establish DeLorean Motor Company (DMC). The company’s first and only production model, the DMC-12, stood out with its bold stainless-steel body. Its signature gullwing doors quickly made it an icon, but despite its distinctive styling, the company went bankrupt in 1983. The owner of the newly reformed DMC, now dedicated to servicing and restoring original DeLoreans, answered the call from fans by releasing the Series 2 DeLorean, equipped with a 197.2 HP powerplant.
cars.hero: At the request of DeLorean owners, the tuned-up Series 2 was created.

cars.description: This Dodge sports coupe was introduced in 1970, built on the same E-body chassis as the Plymouth Barracuda. Targeting the booming pony car segment favored by younger drivers, it was offered in both hardtop and convertible variants. The high-performance R/T (Road/Track) trim sat at the top of the range, positioned above the standard inline-6 and V-8 models.
cars.hero: The top-grade model of the Challenger, which impressed with its performance and bold styling.

cars.description: In 2008, Dodge revived the Challenger nameplate for a new third generation, honoring the legacy of the original muscle car icon. Since its return, several high-performance variants have been introduced, but the standout came in 2018. The SRT Demon was an uncompromising machine built for drag racing dominance. Tuned to deliver 840.2 HP on 100-octane or higher fuel, the Demon could storm through the quarter mile in a jaw-dropping 9.65 seconds.
cars.hero: A Demon born simply to run the quarter mile as fast as possible.

cars.description: Introduced in 1966, the Dodge Charger was Chrysler’s response to the muscle car wave that swept across the United States during the 1960s. It quickly gained popularity for its laid-back styling and the widespread availability of powerful, large-displacement V-8s across the lineup. In 1968, the high-performance R/T (Road/Track) variant was introduced, featuring upgraded suspension and brakes, along with the option of the legendary 426 Hemi engine.
cars.hero: This true 1960s muscle car is the envy of collectors everywhere.

cars.description: The car shown here represents the most extreme performance version of the third-generation Charger, which originally launched in 2005. Developed by SRT, Chrysler’s high-performance division, the Charger SRT Hellcat adds a supercharger to the 6.2-liter Hemi V-8, resulting in 707.1 HP and 585.9 ft-lb of torque. Capable of accelerating from zero to 60 mph in just 3.7 seconds and reaching a top speed of 203.8 mph, it briefly held the title of the world’s fastest 4-door sedan.
cars.hero: Dodge pulls no punches with the Charger SRT Hellcat, one of the most potent sedans in the world.

cars.description: Introduced in 2014, the Charger SRT Hellcat stands as one of the most powerful and extreme models in the Charger’s long-running legacy, which dates back to 1966. Developed by SRT, Chrysler’s high-performance division, the car produces 707.1 HP and reaches a top speed of 204 mph. This safety car version is a Gran Turismo Original model.
cars.hero: This ultra high performance Charger set a world speed record, going 222 mph on the Bonneville Salt Flats.
cars.name_long: Dodge Charger SRT Hellcat Safety Car

cars.description: This was a car of the future, blending uncompromising, unrestrained performance with a striking, futuristic design. This mid-engine, all-wheel-drive single-seater featured a body constructed from advanced composite materials. The engine was a 6.98-liter V-10 producing 1,000 horsepower, supported by a pneumatic sub-system. The GTS-R was the dedicated racing variant of the Tomahawk. Drivers were equipped with a specialized racing suit designed to cope with the extraordinary G-forces this machine can generate.
cars.hero: A lightweight racing version of the visionary near-future single-seater concept.
cars.name_long: Dodge SRT Tomahawk GTS-R Vision Gran Turismo

cars.description: This was a car of the future, blending uncompromising, unrestrained performance with a striking, futuristic design. A mid-engine, 4-wheel-drive single-seater, its body was crafted from cutting-edge composite materials. The engine was a 6.98-liter V-10 producing 1,000 horsepower, supported by a pneumatic sub-system. The "S" variant represented a more grounded interpretation of the Tomahawk, designed with considerations for open-road drivability. However, unlocking its full potential demanded near-superhuman reflexes from the driver.
cars.hero: Featuring more than 1000 horsepower from a V-10 and compressed air unit with near-future technology.
cars.name_long: Dodge SRT Tomahawk S Vision Gran Turismo

cars.description: A Gran Turismo Original, this Gr.1-spec version of the Dodge SRT Tomahawk Vision Gran Turismo was the result of a collaboration between Gran Turismo and Dodge. To ensure that its 700 horsepower-plus was effectively translated to the ground, the car was outfitted with aerodynamic enhancements. These included an extended front splitter, a prominent rear wing, and four canards.
cars.hero: A mid-engine rear-wheel drive version of the Tomahawk for Gr.1 competition.
cars.name_long: Dodge SRT Tomahawk Vision Gran Turismo (Gr.1)

cars.description: This was a car of the future, blending uncompromising, unrestrained performance with a striking, futuristic design. A mid-engine, 4-wheel-drive single-seater, its body was crafted from cutting-edge composite materials. The engine was a 6.98-liter V-10 producing 1,000 horsepower, supported by a pneumatic sub-system. The "X" was the ultimate expression reserved only for drivers deemed capable of handling its 2465.5 HP total output.
cars.hero: Power exceeding 2500 horsepower and with unrivaled handling, this machine belongs in the hands of only a chosen few.
cars.name_long: Dodge SRT Tomahawk X Vision Gran Turismo

cars.description: The Dodge Super Bee was introduced in 1968 as a performance-focused yet affordable muscle car. It offered a range of powerful engine options, with the 7.0-liter V-8 producing 425 HP at the top of the lineup. True to its purpose, the car came with minimal comfort features. A facelifted version appeared in 1970, followed by the second-generation model in 1971, which was based on the Charger.
cars.hero: A Coronet, equipped with a 7.0-liter V8 Hemi, this was one of the standout cars in the muscle-car era.

cars.description: This Gran Turismo Original took Dodge’s high-performance Viper and modified it to comply with Gr.4 regulations. Its exterior features an aggressive front splitter, aerodynamic canards, and a prominent rear wing to generate substantial downforce. The result is a machine that delivered impressive straight-line speed while offering significant potential through the corners as well.
cars.hero: The third-generation Viper boasted extreme performance that was developed by the SRT division.

cars.description: This coupe was developed to fully exploit the Viper’s performance potential. While its basic structure, suspension, and V-10 engine remained largely unchanged from the RT/10 roadster, power output was increased to 449.7 HP. The addition of a fixed roof allowed the car to reach a top speed of 185 mph—approximately 183.9 mph—surpassing the roadster’s 165-mph limit. Introduced alongside it, the GTS-R race version appeared in endurance events across the globe, where it consistently demonstrated its superior capabilities.
cars.hero: With its monstrous levels of power and grip, this venerable machine could arguably be called America's first supercar.

cars.description: The third-generation Viper made its debut in 2012. A key highlight of this new model was that it was released under SRT, Chrysler’s high-performance brand. Although the V-10 engine retained its 8.4-liter displacement, numerous internal upgrades boosted output to 640 HP and 600.3 ft-lb of torque. As with previous generations, the chassis featured a steel tube frame, though torsional rigidity was improved by 50 percent. At the top of the range, the GTS offered an active suspension system.
cars.hero: This third-generation Viper is now marketed under Dodge's extreme performance SRT brand.

cars.description: When the third-generation Viper appeared in 2012, it was accompanied by the announcement of a racing variant—the GTS-R. From that foundation, the GT3-R was developed as a customer-focused race machine for private teams. Created through a collaboration between SRT, Chrysler’s high-performance division, and Riley Technologies, it featured significant weight reduction and a host of aerodynamic upgrades. It quickly demonstrated its competitiveness, proving its racing potential in GT events across America and around the world.
cars.hero: A machine for private racers, carrying on the bloodline of the GTS-R.

cars.description: This coupe was introduced during the Viper’s second generation, marking the car’s continued evolution as a true sports machine.
