While its design featured sleek, flowing lines, the front and rear overhangs were shortened to accommodate a front mid-engine layout with 2+2 seating. A mix of lightweight materials was used throughout the body, achieving a balance of reduced weight and high structural rigidity.
cars.hero: This stylish sports coupe attracted plenty of attention with its low nose and short overhang design.

cars.description: The Lexus LF-LC GT Vision Gran Turismo is a dream car crafted by Lexus with aspirations for competition in Super GT and the 24 Hours of Nürburgring. Inspired by the LF-LC luxury coupe concept, it merges CALTY DESIGN’s design philosophy with the technical practicality of Lexus Racing.
cars.hero: A beautiful high performance machine for participation in the Nürburgring 24 hour race.

cars.description: This ultimate sports car aimed to carry forward the spirit and performance legacy of the Toyota 2000GT. Its carbon-fiber body was produced through automated processes, and the transaxle and radiator were mounted at the rear to achieve a near-perfect 48:52 front-to-rear weight distribution. Under the hood was a 4.8-liter V-10 with a 72-degree bank angle. Its distinctive sound was tuned in collaboration with Yamaha. Only 500 units were produced, making it as rare as it was ambitious.
cars.hero: This ultra high-tech sports car achieved ultimate performance with mass-production quality.

cars.description: The RC F was unveiled by Lexus at the 2014 Detroit Auto Show. At its heart lay a refined version of the 5.0-liter V-8 from the IS F, producing 449.7 HP and 383.3 ft-lb of torque—an increase of 32.5 HP and 10.8 ft-lb more than the original engine. Paired with an 8-speed automatic transmission featuring paddle shifters, the RC F delivered both power and precision. Excluding the LFA, it stood as the most sports-focused model ever introduced in the Lexus lineup.
cars.hero: Even beginners can experience dynamic driving performance with a range of electronic aids.

cars.description: This Gran Turismo Original is a race-prepared version of the Lexus RC F coupe, specifically modified for Gr.4 competition. Harnessing the immense torque of its large-displacement V-8, the car delivers exceptional straight-line acceleration. Its base color is finished in the signature orange used by Lexus for its exclusive special models.
cars.hero: This version of the highly refined Lexus RC F production coupe was modified for Gr.4.

cars.description: Beginning in 2015, Lexus initiated test competition with a purpose-built race car based on the RC F, using the data and experience gained to refine and evolve the machine. This development culminated in the debut of the RC F GT3 in 2017. Emil Frey Racing, who played a key role in the car's development, campaigned the RC F GT3 in the International GT Open. Its efforts were rewarded with a 3rd-place finish in the team standings.
cars.hero: Emil Frey Racing was one of the first teams to compete with a GT3 version of the Lexus RC F.

cars.description: The RC F GT3 is a GT3-spec race car developed from the Lexus RC F, created as a prototype prior to official homologation to evaluate and refine its performance. In its early testing phase, the car claimed victory in Round 9 of the VLN (Nürburgring Endurance Series). At the time, it competed in raw carbon-fiber bodywork, but the version shown here is adorned in the distinctive Emil Frey Racing livery.
cars.hero: This highly refined Lexus RC F coupe competed in the 2016 VLN as a GT3 race car.

cars.description: The Lexus RC F competed in the Super GT GT500 class from 2014 to 2016. New regulations introduced that year required the monocoque and key components to be shared with DTM counterparts. It ran the same turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-4 used in Super Formula competition. In 2016, the au TOM’S RC F scored points throughout the season, including a 2nd place finish in Round 6, ultimately placing 5th overall in the standings.
cars.hero: This Toyota/Lexus race car competed under joint regulations between the Super GT Series and DTM.

cars.description: This Super GT race car competed during the 2008 season. To enhance aerodynamic efficiency, both the front and rear overhangs were extended, and its compact body proved highly effective on high-speed circuits. Although it didn’t claim any outright wins, its consistent performance throughout the season earned enough points to secure the team title.
cars.hero: Won the Super GT team title with its stable performance on high-speed circuits.

cars.description: The Maserati A6GCS/53 Spyder earned the Gran Turismo Trophy at the 2014 Pebble Beach Concours d'Elegance. Its elegant aluminum bodywork was crafted by Carrozzeria Fantuzzi, while power came from a 167.7 HP engine designed by Gioacchino Colombo. Raced under the official Maserati factory team, it secured five class victories and three overall wins during the 1954 season.
cars.hero: A beautiful streamlined 2-seat sports car that won the Gran Turismo Trophy

cars.description: This was the high-performance variant of the GranTurismo, introduced at the 2008 Geneva Motor Show. Its DOHC V-8 engine had its displacement increased to 4.7 liters, while the transmission and rear differential were integrated into a transaxle layout. It also became the first in the series to adopt the two-pedal semi-automatic MC Shift system.
cars.hero: True to its Italian heritage, this grand tourer was defined by class, performance and elegance.

cars.description: This marked Maserati’s first mid-engine sports car in 15 years, following the MC12. Designed with Dallara, the streamlined body was engineered to generate significant downforce without relying heavily on external aerodynamic elements. At its core was a lightweight carbon monocoque chassis weighing less than 220 lbs, paired with a newly developed twin-turbo 3.0-liter V-6 engine, featuring F1–inspired pre-chamber combustion.
cars.hero: A special super car that embodies the tradition and passion of Maserati.

cars.description: This mid-engine sports car made its debut in 1972 as the sister to the Bora. While the Bora was equipped with a V-8, the Merak utilized a smaller 3.0-liter V-6 sourced from the Citroën SM, allowing a 2+2 seating layout by making use of the extra space freed up in the rear. The SS was a high-performance variant introduced in 1975. By increasing the engine’s compression ratio, output was boosted, raising the top speed from 139.8 mph to 155.3 mph.
cars.hero: This high-output model of the Merak has been tuned for even sharper performance.

cars.description: Mazda’s 787B completed the 1991 24 Hours of Le Mans without a single mechanical issue, making history as the first Japanese manufacturer to secure an overall win at the event. Mazda, which had entered Le Mans with rotary engines beginning in 1974, developed the 787 as its final bid for rotary-powered victory, before regulations would turn against such powertrains. Although the effort fell short at the 1990 race, the 787 underwent extensive revisions and emerged as the 787B.
cars.hero: The legendary Mazda 787B was the first Japanese-manufactured race car to win the 24 Hours of Le Mans.

cars.description: Mazda’s Atenza global sedan has been specifically modified for Gr.3 competition as part of this Gran Turismo Original. The exterior showcases aggressive yet refined aerodynamics shaped by Mazda’s "KODO" design philosophy. To boost structural rigidity, a bulkhead has been added behind the cockpit, along with a rearview camera to enhance visibility.
cars.hero: This is an original racing version of the Mazda6 for Gr.3 competition.

cars.description: This is a Gr.3 homologation model of the Atenza, derived from Mazda’s global market sedan and adapted to comply with Gr.3 racing regulations. Engineered as a true race machine, it has been transformed into a high-performance sedan producing more than 400 horsepower. Its design stands out for considering even the flow of reflections across the bodywork.
cars.hero: The third-generation Mazda6 featured a curvaceous body style and SkyActiv technology.

cars.description: Mazda’s Atenza global sedan has been tailored for Gr.3 use in this Gran Turismo Original. Utilizing a 4-wheel-drive platform, the car delivers exceptional traction. A Gr.3-style front grille and hood vents are fitted to assist the turbocharged 4-cylinder engine in producing its impressive 394.5 HP.
cars.hero: This is an original racing version of the Mazda6 for Gr.4 competition.

cars.description: The third-generation Atenza also came equipped with Mazda’s SKYACTIV-D diesel engine. Nicknamed XD (cross-d), it was offered in three trims, with the L package as the highest specification. Thanks to features like idle-stop and i-ELOOP regenerative braking, SKYACTIV-D models achieved fuel economy figures of 52.7 MPG under Japan’s JC08 test cycle.
cars.hero: The third-generation Mazda 6 features a flowing body style and SKYACTIV technology.
cars.name_long: Mazda Atenza Sedan XD L Package '15

cars.description: The CX-30 is a crossover SUV introduced to fill the gap between the CX-3 and CX-5. Although compact in size, it showcased Mazda's signature "KODO" design, evident in its sculpted front end and the way light flowed across its sleek body lines. In 2021, Mazda released the CX-30 X Smart Edition. This version featured the innovative SKYACTIV-X engine, paired with enhanced driver assistance systems and refined pedal feedback.
cars.hero: This crossover SUV from Mazda featured a revolutionary engine design.

cars.description: The Mazda Demio underwent a full model change in 2014, entering its fourth generation with a bold new direction. Adopting Mazda’s KODO design philosophy, it showcased styling sharp enough to rival its European counterparts. One of its standout features was the newly developed turbocharged 1.5-liter diesel engine, the SKYACTIV-D 1.5. Praised for its excellent fuel efficiency, the diesel variant quickly gained popularity, accounting for more than 60 percent of total orders.
cars.hero: This compact diesel model from Mazda offered more luxury than you would expect from a car in its class.

cars.description: This automotive masterpiece marked the revival of the lightweight sports car as the 20th century drew to a close. First introduced in 1989 with a 1.6-liter engine, the model saw its displacement increased to 1.8 liters in 1993. Its true appeal lay in its mechanical purity—the transmission and rear differential were unified by an aluminum powerplant frame, while double wishbone suspension and disc brakes at all four corners delivered precise, responsive handling.
cars.hero: Mazda's Eunos Roadster is credited with reviving the small fun-to-drive rear-drive convertible sports car.

cars.description: The Mazda LM55 Vision Gran Turismo was crafted as Mazda’s futuristic vision of endurance racing excellence, with its sights set on total victory at the 24 Hours of Le Mans. Its striking silhouette was shaped by Mazda’s KODO design philosophy, and the front grille echoes the modern face of Mazda’s production lineup with a bold reinterpretation.
cars.hero: A fusion of speed and elegance, born from the spirit of an unrelenting challenger.

cars.description: This Gr.1-spec evolution of the LM55 Vision Gran Turismo represents Mazda’s vision of a modern rotary-powered prototype. It delivers the razor-sharp cornering Mazda is known for, enhanced by the exceptional grip of a 4-wheel-drive system. With the ability to dart through corners and surge down straights, it stands as a true modern embodiment of the legendary "rotary rocket."
cars.hero: A fusion of speed and elegance, born from the spirit of an unrelenting challenger.

cars.description: This machine was created by Mazda Spirit Racing, an initiative launched in 2021 to embody Mazda’s motorsport ambitions. Although derived from the ND Roadster, it has a 2.0-liter block not typically offered on Japanese soft-top models, distinguished by specially developed camshafts, a bespoke cylinder head, forged pistons, and a custom exhaust manifold. This delivers an output of 197.2 HP, a figure that stands near the upper limit of what remains practical in a production car. Additional refinements were made throughout the chassis, drawing upon the wealth of expertise Mazda had accumulated through years of Super Endurance racing.
cars.hero: With only 200 units ever produced, this is the ultimate works-tuned roadster.

cars.description: The fourth-generation MAZDA3 made its debut in 2018. A standout addition to the lineup was the mild hybrid M Hybrid, which gained global attention for its SKYACTIV-X engine, utilizing spark-controlled compression ignition. The X Burgundy Selection is a limited-edition variant based on the X grade, featuring the advanced SKYACTIV-X powertrain paired with a rich burgundy interior, offering a mature sense of elegance.
cars.hero: An elegant fastback with a revolutionary combustion system.

cars.description: This GT Original draws inspiration from the MAZDA3 Bio concept that competed in the ST-Q class of Japan’s Super Endurance Series. It runs on next-generation 100-percent biodiesel fuel derived from waste cooking oil. The body also incorporates environmentally friendly hybrid materials. This ambitious project aims to merge carbon neutrality with top-tier race car performance.
cars.hero: Exploring the potential of internal combustion, a next-generation bio-diesel-powered race car.

cars.description: This motorsport-focused base model was introduced as part of the fourth-generation Roadster lineup. Its drivetrain was upgraded to meet the demands of track use, complemented by a larger radiator and enhanced disc brakes. The suspension featured height-adjustable dampers supplied by Bilstein. In 2022, the car received Kinematic Posture Control, designed to dramatically improve rear-end stability and cornering composure.
cars.hero: This motorsports-based model epitomizes the core concepts of the Roadster.

cars.description: The fourth-generation ND Roadster made its global debut in April 2014 at the New York Auto Show. Its compact dimensions, combined with a wide, low stance and elegantly sculpted curves, garnered widespread acclaim when the final design was revealed in September of the same year. Pre-orders commenced in March 2015. The entry-level S grade featured pared-down equipment, and at just 2183 lbs, it stood as the only variant with a curb weight under one ton.
cars.hero: The MX-5 Miata returns to its roots with a lightweight 2183 lbs body and dashing looks.

cars.description: The Eunos Roadster (NA Special Package) '89 has been specially tuned by Gran Turismo to create this original machine. While the engine and suspension have been enhanced and aerodynamic components added, it faithfully preserves the Roadster’s hallmark "Jinba Ittai," the feeling of unity between car and driver. This spartan lightweight can even hold its own in touring car races.
cars.hero: A first-generation Mazda Roadster, tuned to perfection by Gran Turismo.

cars.description: The FC3S, second generation of the RX-7, made its debut in October 1985. Sporting a sleek, futuristic design, it was shorter than its predecessor but both taller and wider. This new generation also carried an additional 441 lbs of weight. To offset the added weight, the FC3S was fitted with the newly developed 13B rotary engine. Each chamber was enlarged to 654 cc, and with the addition of a turbocharger, the engine delivered a peak output of 182.4 HP and 180.8 ft-lb of torque.
cars.hero: This version of the second-generation RX-7 offered better driver feedback and agility.

cars.description: The FD3S, the third generation of the RX-7, was introduced in December 1991. Its widened body accommodated broader tires for improved grip, while extensive use of aluminum components throughout the chassis brought the weight down to just under 2646 lbs. Although it retained the 13B engine from the FC3S, the FD3S introduced a sequential twin-turbo system, boosting output to 251.5 HP and 217.0 ft-lb of torque. The lightest variant, the Type S, achieved a power-to-weight ratio of 4.97 kg/HP, making it the most potent RX-7 ever produced.
cars.hero: This final version of the Mazda RX-7 marked the end of an excellent 25-year run for the model.
cars.name_long: Mazda RX-7 Spirit R Type A (FD) '02

cars.description: Introduced in 2011, this marked the final special edition of the Mazda RX-8. Built on the 6-speed manual Type RS—equipped with Bilstein dampers—and the 6-speed automatic Type E—offering upscale touches like leather seating—both variants received exclusive interior and exterior enhancements. Initially planned as a 1,000-unit production, strong demand following the announcement of the RX-8’s discontinuation in 2012 prompted Mazda to double the run with an additional 1,000 units.
cars.hero: The final version of the RX-8, Mazda's rotary engine sports car with a unique 4-door layout.

cars.description: This rotary sports-car concept was unveiled at the 2015 Tokyo Motor Show. Every unnecessary line and surface were meticulously carved away from its sleek long-nose, short-deck silhouette, revealing Mazda’s purest interpretation of the ideal rear-wheel-drive sports car. Powered by the next-generation SKYACTIV-R rotary engine, this concept offered a bold glimpse into the future of rotary performance.
cars.hero: This stunning concept provided a glimpse of a next-generation rotary-engine-powered car.

cars.description: The RX-VISION concept was introduced at the 2015 Tokyo Motor Show. The base car’s elegant proportions have been reimagined with a more aggressive, motorsport-focused edge. To meet the performance demands of the Gr.3 class, the lightweight body houses a 4-rotor engine, drawing inspiration from the legendary 787B powerplant, revived through cutting-edge SKYACTIV technology to deliver unprecedented levels of power and responsiveness.
cars.hero: Mazda's dream rotary race car.

cars.description: This was an evolution of the GT3 CONCEPT racing car based on the MAZDA RX-VISION, which was unveiled in 2015. The splitter, diffuser and rear wing were redesigned to improve aerodynamic performance and increase downforce. Front canards were added, along with revisions to the grille mesh and the shape of the rear body panels. The front tire size was also changed to significantly improve cornering ability, a crucial factor in racing.
cars.hero: The RX-VISION GT3 evolved for serious competition.

cars.description: This concept car was created to celebrate the 50th anniversary of Mazda’s founding. Its bullet-shaped body was mounted on a steel tube space frame and powered by a 10A-type rotary engine originally developed for the 24 Hours of Spa, delivering around 246.5 HP. Although it appeared publicly in three different body colors, later investigation revealed it was, in fact, a single car repainted for each appearance.
cars.hero: This ultra-exotic concept featured a rotary engine and cutting-edge technology.

cars.description: The third-generation FD3S RX-7 was introduced in December 1991. The Savanna name used on earlier models was retired, with the official name in Japan becoming the ɛ̃fini RX-7. The car carried over the 13B rotary engine from the second generation, but output increased to 251.5 HP with the introduction of a sequential twin-turbo system. Thanks to extensive use of aluminum in components such as the hood, spare wheel, jack and 4-wheel double-wishbone suspension, the FD3S achieved an impressively low curb weight of around 2778 lbs.
cars.hero: The debut model of the third-generation RX-7, a car developed to be the ultimate sports car.

cars.description: The McLaren 650S was introduced in 2014. Its twin-turbo 3.8-liter V-8, inherited from earlier models, was tuned to produce 641 HP and 499.1 ft-lb of torque to match its name. Paired with a 7-speed dual-clutch transmission for seamless gear changes, it accelerated from zero to 62.1 mph in 3.0 seconds, covered 1312.3 ft in 10.5, and reached a top speed of 206.9 mph.
cars.hero: The 650S supercar came loaded with F1 technology.

cars.description: In the virtual world, the 650S inspired a Gran Turismo Original—the Gr.4 version, modeled on McLaren’s mid-tier supercar. Finished in McLaren’s factory racing color, this virtual machine offered well-balanced handling and predictable behavior. Its cockpit elements, fuel cap, and jack points were faithfully modeled after GT3-level race equipment.
cars.hero: Here is the Gran Turismo original Gr.4 spec-version of the McLaren 650S super sports car.

cars.description: The 650S GT3 was developed as a full FIA-GT3 compliant race car, derived directly from the production McLaren 650S. While it retained the same twin-turbo 3.8-liter V-8, power output was reduced to 493.1 HP to comply with GT3 regulations, similar to the MP4-12C GT3. Additional upgrades included extensive endurance-focused refinements throughout the car. The 650S GT3 earned significant victories in 2015, winning at GT Asia and later claiming top honors at the 2016 Bathurst 12 Hour.
cars.hero: The GT3 successor to the remarkable MP4-12C race car.

cars.description: The McLaren F1 was a groundbreaking supercar conceived by legendary Formula 1 designer Gordon Murray. From its unique 3-seat configuration, with the driver positioned at the center, to its balanced weight distribution, the F1 introduced a host of innovations that redefined what a road car could be. Celebrated worldwide, it earned acclaim not only as the fastest production car of its time but also for its usability in everyday driving.
cars.hero: The ultra-exotic McLaren F1 exemplified the genius of its designer, Gordon Murray.

cars.description: This race version was based on McLaren’s first full-scale road car, the F1. At the rain-soaked 1995 24 Hours of Le Mans, the F1 GTR defied the odds, outperforming purpose-built prototype racers to claim overall victory. Car No. 59, backed by the factory and driven by Yannick Dalmas, Masanori Sekiya, and JJ Lehto, etched its name into motorsports history.
cars.hero: The ultimate automobile by McLaren would go on to win both the BPR series and the 24 Hours of Le Mans.

cars.description: This circuit-only version of the McLaren P1 was created to commemorate the 20th anniversary of the F1 GTR and its race career throughout the 1990s. The hybrid powertrain, combining electric motors with a twin-turbo V-8, was tuned to produce 986.2 HP. To further enhance its track performance, the car received extensive aerodynamic upgrades, including a prominent rear wing.
cars.hero: This track-only model further defines the potential of the P1 hybrid supercar.

cars.description: The McLaren Ultimate Vision Gran Turismo was developed as McLaren’s vision of high-performance motoring in 2030 and beyond. Behind the cabin, where the driver lay in a motorcycle-like position, resides a twin-turbo 4.0-liter V-8. The engine is assisted by high-performance electric motors housed in each of the front wheel pods, bringing the total output to 1134.1 HP.
cars.hero: Putting the driver before all else, this car is the ultimate realization of the McLaren philosophy.

cars.description: A Gran Turismo Original, this Gr.1 machine is based on the McLaren Ultimate Vision Gran Turismo, born from a collaboration between McLaren and Gran Turismo. While Gr.1 regulations restrict the use of active aerodynamic elements, the car still delivers exceptional cornering performance thanks to its inherently high-downforce body design and formidable mechanical grip.
cars.hero: This version of McLaren's future is realized in Gr.1 form with Vision Gran Turismo.

cars.description: Bearing the name MP4—a subtle nod to McLaren’s F1—the MP4-12C stood out for its advanced carbon-composite "MonoCell" chassis. This lightweight structure played a crucial role in reducing overall mass, allowing the car, despite its relatively modest power figures by McLaren standards, to equal or even surpass the performance of its chief rival, the Ferrari 458 Italia.
cars.hero: The MP4-12C was the first McLaren production car since the McLaren F1 road car.

cars.description: This McLaren race car contested the 1988 F1 World Championship. Its chassis, the work of Gordon Murray and Steve Nichols, was paired with the Honda RA168E powerplant. Dominating the season, it triumphed in 15 of the 16 races. Car No. 12, the MP4/4, was piloted by Ayrton Senna. Senna delivered a stellar performance, securing 13 pole positions and 8 victories en route to the drivers' championship title.
cars.hero: This legendary machine marked the end of the turbocharged era in Formula 1.

cars.description: Mercedes-Benz entered DTM with the 190 E 2.3-16 back in 1986. In 1990, it pushed development further with the 190 E 2.5-16 Evolution II. Its wide, muscular fenders gave the car a sporty flair, matched by a 2.5-liter engine tuned to 231.8 HP. Limited to 500 units, it delivered strong performances during the 1992 DTM season.
cars.hero: Born from touring racing, the ultimate evolution of the 190E.

cars.description: The 300 SL race car, known inhouse as W194, used a tubular frame with aluminum body panels, paired with modified mechanicals from the W186 300. The car’s debut at the 1952 24 Hours of Le Mans resulted in a landmark win for Mercedes-Benz. That success sparked public demand, ultimately leading to the production of the 300 SL road car.
cars.hero: The car that brought Mercedes-Benz its first victory at the 24 Hours of Le Mans.

cars.description: Daimler-Benz revealed the Mercedes-Benz 300 SL at the 1955 New York Auto Show. While its 161.6 mph top speed was impressive, its roof-hinged "gullwing" doors made it unforgettable, which allowed the car's doors to open upward. Only 1,400 gullwing Coupés were built from 1955 to 1957 before the model evolved into the 300 SL Roadster.
cars.hero: With its gullwing doors and other advanced technologies, the 1954 Mercedes-Benz 300 SL Coupe was a car way ahead of its time.

cars.description: To compete in the newly established FIA GT Championship in 1997, Mercedes-Benz and AMG developed the CLK-GTR in just 128 days. Equipped with a V-12 engine, the car proved immediately successful, securing both the team and driver championships in its debut season. The following year, Mercedes introduced the CLK-LM as an evolution model. It made its debut at the 24 Hours of Le Mans, going on to dominate the FIA GT Championship, winning all 10 rounds and clinching the season title.
cars.hero: Making the switch from a heavy V12 engine to a lighter V8 helped this Mercedes-Benz dominate the FIA GT championship.

cars.description: This car earned double honors at the 2017 Pebble Beach Concours d’Elegance, capturing both Best of Show and the Gran Turismo Trophy. Produced between 1926 and 1933, what many regard as Mercedes-Benz’s first true sports car was the vision of Ferdinand Porsche. Powered by a supercharged 7.0-liter inline-6, it was wrapped in elegant "boat tail" coachwork crafted by Barker.
cars.hero: This very unqiue sports car was the first from Mercedes-Benz and is known for its characteristic boat tail styling.

cars.description: The C9 was a Group C race car developed by Switzerland’s Sauber. Having supplied engines in earlier efforts, Mercedes officially brought Sauber under its factory racing umbrella in 1988. By 1989, the C9 appeared in a striking all-silver livery, evoking memories of the legendary Silver Arrows. In a stunning performance at the 24 Hours of Le Mans, car No. 63 claimed victory, followed by No. 61 in 2nd place and No. 62 in 5th.
cars.hero: The unbeatable group C car marked the return of the Mercedes-Benz Works racing team.

cars.description: The SLR McLaren was the production realization of the 1999 Mercedes-Benz Vision SLR concept. Its most distinctive feature was the carbon-fiber monocoque chassis, dramatically reducing weight while enhancing rigidity. Power came from a 5.5-liter SOHC V-8 equipped with a twin-screw supercharger, paired with a 5-speed automatic transmission offering sport, comfort, and manual modes.
cars.hero: The already aggressive-looking SLR McLaren looked even more ominous with optional 19-inch wheels.

cars.description: The Unimog was a commercial vehicle developed and sold by Daimler Truck. First produced in 1948, it went on to become a long-running success as a highly versatile, multi-purpose machine. Introduced in 1956, the 411 series served as its successor, featuring a more powerful engine and a reinforced body structure. With three available wheelbase options and a variety of body styles, the lineup included twelve distinct models, each of which could be further customized with a wide range of attachments.
cars.hero: The benchmark for versatile, high-mobility vehicles.

cars.description: The W 196 was developed by Mercedes-Benz in anticipation of the new F1 regulations shifting to 2.5-liter engines from 1954. The W 196 R variant was specifically constructed for competition in F1. Its 2496 cc inline-8 engine produced 285 HP and was capable of reaching a top speed of 180.2 mph. The car delivered outstanding results during the 1954 and 1955 Formula One World Championships, with driver Juan Manuel Fangio securing the drivers' title in both seasons.
cars.hero: A legendary F1 car that made motorsports history.

cars.description: Created by Mine’s, the BNR34 GT-R N1 base is a finely tuned expression of the R34 GT-R’s purity, capturing its beauty while remaining true to the spirit of a street car. From the refined RB26DETT engine to the lowered suspension and understated exterior, every detail reflected the philosophy of Mine’s CEO, Michizo Niikura — to create “a first-class street car.” This example was fully restored in 2021 by Garage Yoshida.
cars.hero: This legendary, fully tuned GT-R gained a new following after an ambitious restoration.

cars.description: This Vision Gran Turismo represents a MINI built purely for racing. Weighing just 2315 lbs and producing 389.5 HP, it launches from zero to 62.1 mph in a mere 3.5 seconds. Power is sent to all four wheels. Its low-slung silhouette—with the wheels pushed to the very edges—delivers the signature go-kart-like handling MINIs are known for. The result is an exhilarating, track-ready driving experience.
cars.hero: A race spec Clubman able to reach 0-62.1 mph in just 3.5 seconds, with a top speed of 180.2 mph.

cars.description: This was the hot hatch version of the new MINI developed after BMW’s takeover. Its 1.6-liter inline-4 was supercharged to produce 167.7 HP and 159.1 ft-lb of torque, an increase of 53.3 HP and 50.6 ft-lb over the base Cooper. Paired with an exclusive 6-speed manual transmission, the car delivered pure driving fun in a compact, spirited package.
cars.hero: This hopped-up MINI Cooper S featured a supercharged engine.

cars.description: To fully exploit the MINI’s outstanding handling characteristics, the British Motor Corporation joined forces with F1 constructor John Cooper to develop this high-performance variant. The 970 S emerged as a special version, its engine displacement reduced to 970 cc to comply with specific racing class regulations. Whereas the standard 848 cc engine delivered 33.5 HP, this tuned iteration generated an impressive 65.1 HP. Despite a limited production run of just 963 units, the car achieved remarkable success in touring car competitions.
cars.hero: Devised by Formula 1 legend John Cooper, this very special Mini was intended to excel on the race track.

cars.description: This Vision Gran Turismo was created by Mitsubishi Motors, a brand with a strong legacy in events like the Dakar Rally and World Rally Championship (WRC). Inspired by the Mitsubishi Concept XR-PHEV shown at the 2013 Tokyo Motor Show, the concept evolved into a purpose-built racing machine. As a plug-in hybrid EV, it combines electric motors with a conventional engine, delivering massive power to all four wheels through the advanced S-AWC vehicle dynamics control system.
cars.hero: A hybrid concept packed with know-how and spirit gained through motorsports.
cars.name_long: Mitsubishi Concept XR-PHEV EVOLUTION Vision Gran Turismo

cars.description: The FTO made its debut in 1994, marking a return 23 years after the release of the original model. Its body adopted mid-size proportions suited to the Japanese market—uncommon for its time—and stood out for its generous width and athletic stance. Three engine options were offered: the 4G93, a 1.8-liter inline-4 SOHC; the 6A12, a 2.0-liter DOHC V-6 , and a higher-tuned version of the same V-6, producing 197.2 HP. The GP Version R was a high-performance variant, featuring sport-tuned suspension, a limited-slip differential, and front and rear strut tower bars as standard equipment.
cars.hero: This high-powered front-wheel-drive sports car featured a number of new systems.

cars.description: Introduced in 1990, the GTO marked Mitsubishi’s return to the true sports car segment after many years. Its bold, wide-bodied styling was clearly aimed at the American market. The car packed a suite of advanced technologies for its time, including all-wheel control, 4-wheel steering, electronically controlled suspension, and active aerodynamic elements. Under the hood was a 3.0-liter V-6 engine, offered in both naturally-aspirated and twin-turbocharged forms. It was sold overseas as the 3000GT, where it gained popularity for its bold styling and aggressive performance.
cars.hero: This pure-bred sports car by Mitsubishi featured advanced AWD technology.

cars.description: Limited to just 1,000 units, this was the final edition of the Lancer Evolution X, although the X itself was omitted from the body, subtly suggesting its role as the last of the legendary line. Based on the 5-speed manual GSR model, it featured an upgraded engine producing 308.7 HP and 311.0 ft-lb of torque, equipped with sodium-filled exhaust valve stems for improved durability. It also came standard with the "high-performance package," which included Bilstein dampers and Eibach springs.
cars.hero: An icon bodes farewell with a special Final Edition model.

cars.description: This Gran Turismo Original reimagines Mitsubishi’s high-performance Lancer Evolution Final Edition as a machine built to meet Gr.3 racing regulations. Stripped of all non-essential elements, the design focuses purely on function. Slits on the front fenders channel turbulent air out of the wheel wells, while an array of winglets inside the fenders carefully manage airflow across the entire body.
cars.hero: Saying goodbye to the Evo was made easier by the awesome prowess of the "Final Edition" model.
cars.name_long: Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution Final Edition Gr.3

cars.description: This Gran Turismo Original reinterpreted Mitsubishi’s high-performance Lancer Evolution Final Edition for Gr.4 competition. Building on the Lancer’s proven success in real-world touring car racing, this version carries over the model’s advanced electronically controlled 4-wheel-drive system, delivering exceptional cornering performance and stability on the track.
cars.hero: This final model closed the curtain on a long and historic WRC career.
cars.name_long: Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution Final Edition Gr.4

cars.description: This Gran Turismo Original is a Gr.B-spec reinterpretation of Mitsubishi’s high-performance sedan, the Lancer Evolution Final Edition. Its white, silver, and red livery pays tribute to the iconic rally machines of Mitsubishi’s storied World Rally Championship past. Fitted with Gr.3-style aerodynamic components, it generates substantial downforce that can challenge even today’s WRC contenders.
cars.hero: An icon bodes farewell with a special Final Edition model.
cars.model: Lancer Evolution Final Gr.B Rally Car
cars.name_long: Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution Final Edition Gr.B Rally Car

cars.description: A homologation model of the Lancer Evolution Final Edition Gr.B, this version has been originally developed as a rally base car. Thanks to its near-perfect 50:50 weight distribution and extended rear wing, it delivers handling on paved roads that few other 4-wheel-drive vehicles could match.
cars.hero: This Gr.B rally machine is a highly tuned version of the final Lancer Evolution.
cars.model: Lancer Evolution Final Gr.B Road Car
cars.name_long: Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution Final Edition Gr.B Road Car

cars.description: The third-generation Lancer Evolution was introduced in January 1995. With a focus on improving racing performance, it received aerodynamic and cooling enhancements, including a wider front bumper intake and a prominent rear wing mounted on the trunk. The legendary 4G63 engine was further refined to produce 266.3 HP, delivering sharper response and increased power. In the 1996 World Rally Championship, Tommi Mäkinen drove this very model to victory, securing the drivers' title.
cars.hero: Improved aerodynamics and cooling make for the ultimate first-gen  "Evo."

cars.description: In August 1996, the second-generation Lancer was introduced, bringing with it the Lancer Evolution IV. The 4G63 engine was rotated 180 degrees compared to previous models and delivered 276.1 HP with a peak torque of 260.4 ft-lb. A major advancement came with the rear differential, where the traditional mechanical LSD was replaced by an electronically controlled AYC (Active Yaw Control) system—greatly enhancing handling precision.
cars.hero: The 4th-gen Evo's handling got a boost from electronic Active Yaw Control and power now up to 276.1 HP.

cars.description: The Lancer Evolution IX GSR bears the MR initials for Mitsubishi Racing. Performance was enhanced in every area. The MIVEC system was tuned to sharpen turbo response, while the suspension benefited from Eibach springs and an updated AYC calibration for improved cornering stability. Marking the final appearance of the legendary 4G63 engine, this model stood as the pinnacle of the third wave of Lancer Evolution cars.
cars.hero: The "9.5," the final 4G63-powered Lancer Evolution.
cars.name_long: Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution IX MR GSR '06

cars.description: The fifth-generation Lancer Evolution was introduced in January 1998. Developed with the World Rally Championship in mind, the body was widened and the 4G63 engine received further tuning to boost torque. The AYC system (Active Yaw Control) from the Evolution IV was retained, while new inverted dampers and a front helical LSD were added to further elevate performance and cornering ability.
cars.hero: The 5th-gen Evo impressed with its bolder-looking flared fenders and an engine that produced more torque.

cars.description: This special edition of the Lancer Evolution VI was introduced to celebrate Tommi Mäkinen’s remarkable achievement of four consecutive WRC drivers’ championships. Tailored for tarmac rallies, its ride height was lowered by 0.4 inches, and low-end torque was increased to enhance everyday drivability. Limited to 2,500 units, it featured an exclusive red body color and matching seats, special alloy wheels, and a large-diameter exhaust silencer, making it as distinctive as it was capable.
cars.hero: Optional body graphics stood out on this rare Tommi Mäkinen Edition Evo.
cars.model: Lancer Evolution VI GSR T.M. SCP '99
cars.name_long: Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution VI GSR T.M. EDITION Special Color Package '99

cars.description: The eighth-generation Lancer Evolution was introduced in January 2003. Refinements to the ACD (Active Center Differential) and AYC (Active Yaw Control) systems improved both handling and ride comfort. The 4G63 engine delivered up to 289.3 ft-lb of torque, and with the addition of a new 6-speed manual transmission, the car was better equipped than ever to perform in a wide range of driving conditions.
cars.hero: The final evolution of the Lancer Evo VIII with updated suspension and low center of gravity.
cars.name_long: Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution VIII MR GSR '04

cars.description: In an era when Japanese passenger cars were generally capped at 276.1 HP, NISMO defied convention with a fully tuned machine delivering 394.5 HP. At its heart was the RB-X GT2, an enlarged 2.8-liter evolution of the revered RB26, paired with an N1-spec turbocharger. The suspension setup featured Bilstein dampers, reinforced by upgraded stabilizers and bushings. Flared fenders accommodated the wider tires, offering a visual cue to the car’s formidable capabilities.
cars.hero: Boasting 394.5 HP and an extremely limited production run, this is the ultimate R33 GT-R from Nismo.

cars.description: The Nismp R34 GT-R Z-tune stood as the ultimate expression of Nissan’s tuning prowess — a fully re-engineered, limited-production masterpiece based on the R34 Skyline GT-R.  Under the hood, the standard RB26DETT engine was replaced with a 2.8-liter version of the RB26DETT Kai-Z2, derived from Nissan’s GT500 race program. Nismo reinforced the chassis with additional spot welds and strategically integrated carbon fiber components, while fine-tuning the suspension and braking systems to deliver razor-sharp performance. The result was a road-going GT-R with motorsport DNA baked into every detail. Including the original prototype, only 19 units were ever built, making the Z-tune one of the rarest and most revered GT-Rs ever created.
cars.hero: This GT-R bows out with the ultimate complete tuned model.

cars.description: The 180SX arrived in March 1989 as the liftback variant of the S13 Silvia. Initially set to end production alongside the S13, it was given new life as demand continued abroad. The U.S.-market 240SX, powered by a 2.4-liter engine, remained popular, prompting Nissan to decouple the 180SX from the Silvia lineage. The 180SX became a favorite among enthusiasts who personalized it to suit their tastes and style.
cars.hero: This front-engine/rear-wheel-drive specialty car was given a different character to its sister car, the Silvia.

cars.description: Making its debut in 1969, the Fairlady Z was among the first Japanese automobiles to make a mark on the international stage. The standout variant was the Z 432, which featured the S20 inline-6 DOHC engine—borrowed from the Prince R380—rather than the standard L-type unit. Producing just under 157.8 HP, it also proved its mettle in motorsports competition. The 240Z, the U.S.-spec version powered by a 2.4-liter engine, helped cement the Z’s reputation after strong showings in the Safari and Monte Carlo rallies.
cars.hero: With its 'G-nose' and fender flares, this car epitomized Japanese sports car cool in the 1970s.

cars.description: Unveiled in 2008, the sixth-generation Fairlady Z (Z34) was an all-new model, although it retained a strong resemblance to its Z33 predecessor. Built on the same platform as the V36 Skyline Coupé, it featured a lighter chassis paired with a series of performance enhancements. At its core was the VQ37VHR engine, delivering an impressive 331.4 HP. Suspension and braking systems were also finely tuned, underscoring the model’s performance-focused character.
cars.hero: A shortened wheelbase plus larger engine equals driving fun in this sixth-gen Z car.

cars.description: The fourth-generation Fairlady Z was designed for the global market, largely disregarding the size restrictions of the Japanese domestic segment. Its wider body allowed for a broader track, unlocking improved cornering capabilities. Mounted in the front was a 3.0-liter V-6, delivering 226.8 HP in the naturally-aspirated version and 276.1 HP in the twin-turbo model.
cars.hero: With its tidy exterior design, this 4th-gen Z car was a handsome sports car for the global market.

cars.description: Introduced in 1969 as the top-grade variant of the Fairlady Z, the Z 432 was powered by the S20 inline-6 DOHC engine, producing 157.8 HP. Based on the powerplant of Nissan’s R380 race car, the engine gave the car a zero-to-1312.3 ft time of 15.8 seconds and registered a top speed of 130.5 mph. The Z 432 also proved itself in competitive racing. A lightweight version—the Z 432 R—was produced in limited numbers, featuring fiberglass panels and acrylic components to shed weight.
cars.hero: This special Datsun Z was equipped with the same engine as the Skyline GT-R.

cars.description: An enhanced version of the Z33 Fairlady Z arrived in 2007. At its heart was the new VQ35HR engine, which raised output to 308.7 HP. A redesigned intake manifold and reduced internal friction refined the engine’s character, especially at high revs. Revised suspension settings further contributed to a flatter, more composed ride, while maintaining the car’s trademark agility.
cars.hero: This refined Z33 model came powered by the next-generation VQ35HR engine.

cars.description: In 2016, the Nissan GT-R underwent its most significant facelift since its 2007 debut. The updated exterior achieved a refined balance of aerodynamics, downforce, and cooling efficiency. Its twin-turbo 3.8-liter V-6 engine, now producing 565.1 HP, was paired with an improved 6-speed dual-clutch transmission, delivering smoother acceleration and sharper cornering performance. These deeper, more focused refinements embodied the essence of Japanese sports car engineering.
cars.hero: Despite a touch of maturity, the new GT-R still possessed the heart of a monster.

cars.description: Nissan’s "multi-performance" R35 GT-R has been adapted for Gr.4 competition in this Gran Turismo Original. Its 4-wheel-drive system delivered exceptional handling stability, while endurance racing features—such as integrated fog lamps—make it a well-rounded machine built for long-distance performance.
cars.hero: Despite a touch of maturity, the new GT-R still possessed the heart of a monster.

cars.description: Nissan’s "multi-performance" R35 GT-R has been reimagined for Gr.B competition in this Gran Turismo Original. The most striking exterior changes includes quad fog lamps mounted on the bonnet and large auxiliary lamps flanking the front bumper, perfect for illuminating night rally stages. Its already exceptional 4-wheel-drive system gives the GT-R a distinct advantage in the world of rallying.
cars.hero: This Gr.B design reimagines the Nissan GT-R as a dedicated off-road race machine.

cars.description: After a surprise return to competition, the Nissan GT-R made its debut in the 2008 Super GT Championship. In preparation for upcoming regulation changes, the car received a pipe frame chassis and equipped with the same 4.5-liter V-8 previously used in the Z. The XANAVI NISMO demonstrated remarkable pace from the opening round and ultimately secured the drivers’ championship title.
cars.hero: This very fast GT-R scored wins at Suzuki, Okayama, and Autopolis in the 2008 Super GT.

cars.description: This R34 GT-R took to the track in the 1999 All Japan GT Championship. Compared to the previous R33 model, its wheelbase was shortened by 2.2 inches, and the engine was repositioned using a shallow oil pan—enhancements that significantly boosted overall performance. At Round 4 held at Mine Circuit, Érik Comas and Satoshi Motoyama claimed a decisive victory in the Pennzoil NISMO GT-R, securing Comas his second consecutive drivers' title.
cars.hero: This JGTC machine gained its edge by lowering the center of gravity and shortening the wheelbase.

cars.description: In spring 2014, Nissan announced its return to the 24 Hours of Le Mans with a car bearing the GT-R nameplate. The GT-R LM NISMO broke convention with its radical front-engine/front-wheel-drive layout. Its carbon-fiber body, designed by Ben Bowlby—the mind behind the DeltaWing and ZEOD RC—housed a twin-turbo 3.0-liter V-6 paired with an energy recovery system. Weighing in at the minimum 1940 lbs, it contended for overall victory on motorsports' most demanding stage.
cars.hero: A front-wheel-drive prototype hybrid racer designed by Ben Bowlby.

cars.description: The 2017 GT-R NISMO featured a host of refinements throughout the car. While retaining its bonded body construction and engine specifications, the front window frame was reinforced to improve chassis rigidity. Comfort was also enhanced, making it more livable in urban settings while remaining sharp on the circuit. Aerodynamics saw notable improvements as well, and thanks to a comprehensive redesign, the body generated increased downforce at high speeds, further enhancing performance.
cars.hero: The 2017 GT-R was a smoother, more refined version of the previous model.

cars.description: In 2013, Gran Turismo series producer Kazunori Yamauchi partnered with Schulze Motorsport to take on the Nürburgring 24 Hours. The GT-R GT3 was specially prepared for the race, with support from Polyphony Digital’s technical team. Data gathered from the car’s performance was later used to enhance the realism of Gran Turismo’s simulation engine.
cars.hero: Kazunori Yamauchi and this GT-R NISMO GT3 fought hard in the Nürburgring race in 2013.

cars.description: The Nissan GT-R NISMO GT3 was a production-based race machine built to FIA GT3 regulations, derived from the R35 GT-R. Later iterations were based on the GT-R NISMO, incorporating a dry sump system to lower the center of gravity and optimize weight distribution. Enhanced front-end rigidity and a newly designed suspension setup improved handling response. A revised engine bay layout boosted cooling efficiency, contributing to greater stability at high speeds.
cars.hero: This racing spec version of the GT-R was created for GT3 category competition.

cars.description: The new regulations for 2014 required the GT500 car to share the same monocoque weight and key components with its DTM counterpart. As a result, the GT-R underwent significant revisions to meet GT500 specifications, with ongoing refinements continuing through to the 2016 model. During the 2014 and 2015 seasons, the MOTUL AUTECH GT-R secured back-to-back series championships. Aiming for a third consecutive title in 2016, the team ultimately concluded the season in third place overall.
cars.hero: This 2016 Super GT race car was driven by the team of Tsugio Matsuda and Ronnie Quintarelli.

cars.description: The arrival of the 2024 GT-R silenced speculation that production had ended with the 2022 model. A newly designed exhaust silencer allowed the car to meet noise regulations without compromising performance. Aerodynamic refinements enhanced downforce. Also, the addition of high-sensitivity G-sensors in the electronically controlled suspension improved both traction and ride comfort, elevating the GT-R’s performance and refinement to new heights.
cars.hero: News of the Nissan GT-R R35's demise was evidently greatly exaggerated.

cars.description: This Gran Turismo Original transformed the R35 GT-R supercar into a dedicated safety car. Equipped with roof-mounted LED patrol lights and additional light arrays on the front and rear bumpers, it offered significantly enhanced visibility. The center console was also fitted with exclusive switches unique to its safety car role.
cars.hero: This Nissan GT-R, converted into a safety car, was made to patrol the race track.

cars.description: This Vision Gran Turismo concept offered a glimpse into Nissan’s not-too-distant future, brought to life through a collaboration between a youthful team of British designers and Japanese engineers. Its powertrain fuses a twin-turbo V-6 with three electric motors, forming a high-performance hybrid FR-4WD system. With active suspension maximizing its aerodynamic potential, the car remains poised to deliver its full performance the instant the driver calls upon it.
cars.hero: A look into the future of performance-minded touring cars.

cars.description: Nissan’s Qashqai, a popular compact SUV that was introduced in 2006, entered its third generation with a bolder presence and a more refined design. Built on a larger platform, the new model showcased a more confident stance and featured Nissan’s innovative e-Power hybrid system. Unlike traditional hybrids, e-Power used a gasoline engine solely to generate electricity, which then powered the electric motors that drove the wheels, delivering an EV-like driving experience without the need to plug in. The Tekna trim came well-equipped, offering premium features such as larger alloy wheels, ambient interior lighting, and a sharp head-up display, all included as standard.
cars.hero: Nissan's compact SUV is even better with e-Power.

cars.description: This homologation model of the R32 Skyline GT-R was produced in a limited run of just 500 units. With Group A victory as its target, engineers implemented comprehensive cooling enhancements, replaced the turbocharger’s turbine with a more durable metal unit, and reworked the body to optimize aerodynamics while shedding unnecessary weight. The result was a marked increase in performance, propelling the car to numerous touring car victories not only in Japan, but also across Europe and Australia.
cars.hero: A homologation model with 500 cars produced for Group A racing

cars.description: The R32 Skyline GT-R marked the triumphant return of the GT-R name after a 16-year hiatus following the legendary "Kenmeri" model. At its heart was the newly developed RB26DETT engine, equipped with ceramic twin turbochargers to deliver 276.1 HP and 260.4 ft-lb of torque. Power was channeled through the innovative ATTESA E-TS all-wheel-drive system, engineered with a focus on handling precision. Introduced in 1994, the V-Spec II was a high-performance variant that came equipped with wider 245/45R17 tires.
cars.hero: This unique R32 GT-R came fitted with 17-inch BBS wheels, Brembo brakes and 45-series tires.

cars.description: The R33 GT-R made its debut in January 1995. Faced with the challenge of following a car often hailed as one of the greatest in automotive history, Nissan introduced the new model with the bold slogan, “Minus 21-Second Dream”—a nod to its Nürburgring lap time, where it outpaced the R32 by a remarkable 21 seconds. The RB26DETT engine returned with refined tuning that delivered improved throttle response and increased torque. The V-Spec variant came fitted with the advanced ATTESA E-TS Pro all-wheel-drive system as standard, offering integrated control of the active limited-slip differential and ABS.
cars.hero: This top-of-the-line GT-R R33 included the ATTESA ET-S Pro high-performance all-wheel drive system.

cars.description: The R34 GT-R was unveiled in January 1999. In contrast to the larger R33, the new model adopted a more compact, muscular profile—3.0 inches shorter in overall length with a wheelbase reduced by 2.2 inches. The now fully matured RB26DETT engine received a final round of enhancements, pushing torque to 289.3 ft-lb, while refinements to the chassis brought sharper control and more intuitive handling. Crowning the lineup was the limited-edition Nür, fitted with the N1-spec RB26DETT engine, marking the final evolution of the powerplant.
cars.hero: A limited-edition model signifying the end of production, the "Nür" stands for Nürburgring, where the car was developed.
cars.name_long: Nissan Skyline GT-R V･spec II Nür (R34) '02

cars.description: With the All Japan GT Championship extending its turbocharger regulations through 1992, Nissan pressed forward with development, culminating in the formidable R92CP. Capable of exceeding 248.5 mph on Fuji Speedway’s main straight and generating up to 3.5 tons of downforce, the R92CP proved unstoppable, winning every race that season and bringing the turbo era to a dominant close.
cars.hero: Appearing towards the end of Group C's turbo era, this car won every round of the final All-Japan Sports Prototype Championship.

cars.description: The 180SX was introduced as the liftback version of the S13 Silvia. Although it carried slightly more weight and had reduced rear-end rigidity compared to the Silvia, it quickly gained a following as aftermarket tuning parts became widely available. One of the most iconic customizations was the combination of the 180SX body with the front end of the Silvia, also known as “Sileighty.”
cars.hero: This Nissan blended the 180SX with the appealing front end of the Silvia.

cars.description: The S14 Silvia possessed a larger body than the S13 model. In 1996, it underwent a major facelift, incorporating menacing, slanted headlights and a prominent rear spoiler. The Aero package—available on both K’s and Q’s trims—added distinctive front and rear spoilers, exclusive bumpers, white-faced gauges, and a leather-wrapped steering wheel and shift knob as standard.
cars.hero: The top grade of the S14 adds a rear spoiler and leather wrapped steering wheel.

cars.description: Built between 1988 and 1993, the S13-generation Silvia won over enthusiasts with its nimble handling and well-balanced rear-wheel-drive layout. Among its various trims, the high-performance K’s stood out—powered by a turbocharged DOHC inline-4, the CA18ET—earning a strong reputation for its versatility and performance. Later, the “Dia Selection” was introduced as a more affordable variant.
cars.hero: This special S13 had many previously optional items now included as standard equipment.

cars.description: The broader stance of the S14-generation Silvia lent it a more upscale, refined presence. Under the hood, it retained the SR20 engine from the S13, with the top-grade K’s model receiving an added boost from an intercooled turbocharger. The suspension layout mirrored its predecessor’s, utilizing struts up front and a multi-link configuration at the rear. Super HICAS 4-wheel steering system was also offered on a select variant.
cars.hero: The sixth-generation Silvia emphasized heightened luxury in a wide body format.

cars.description: Produced between 1988 and 1993, the S13-generation Silvia earned a devoted following for its sharp, responsive handling and compact rear-wheel-drive layout. While the top-trim K’s came equipped with a turbocharged engine, the Q’s variant featured a naturally-aspirated 138.1 HP unit. Its suspension employed MacPherson struts up front and a multi-link setup at the rear, and select models were available with the advanced Super HICAS 4-wheel steering system.
cars.hero: A low price, excellent handling and naturally aspirated engine made this S13 quite attractive.

cars.description: The seventh-generation S15 Silvia marked a return to the more compact proportions of the S13, reestablishing itself as an accessible, rear-wheel-drive sports car. While it continued to use the SR20 engine from previous generations, its chassis and running gear underwent a comprehensive redesign. With improved body rigidity, upgraded brakes, a more aggressive suspension setup, and the addition of a helical LSD, the S15 delivered a higher level of performance than its predecessors.
cars.hero: This popular S15 model included side skirts and a rear spoiler.

cars.description: The seventh-generation S15 Silvia marked a return to the more compact proportions of the S13, reestablishing itself as an accessible, rear-wheel-drive sports car. While it continued to use the SR20 engine from previous generations, its chassis and running gear underwent a comprehensive redesign. With improved body rigidity, upgraded brakes, a more aggressive suspension setup, and the addition of a helical LSD, the S15 delivered a higher level of performance than its predecessors.
cars.hero: This popular S15 model included side skirts and a rear spoiler.
cars.name_long: Nissan Silvia spec-R Aero (S15) Touring Car

cars.description: This high-performance version of the fourth-generation C110 Skyline was built to carry on the legacy of the GT-R. Larger than its predecessor, it retained the same S20 inline-6 found in the iconic “Hakosuka” GT-R, and was upgraded with 4-wheel disc brakes for improved stopping power. Although it was designed with motorsport in mind, tightening emissions regulations forced its early retirement before it could compete in a single race. Only 197 were produced.
cars.hero: Only 197 examples of this GT-R were made before it was discontinued because of stricter emissions standards.

cars.description: This high-performance variant of the seventh-generation Skyline was introduced with Group A competition squarely in its sights. Its RB20DET engine was extensively reworked, featuring a stainless steel exhaust manifold and a T04E turbocharger, complemented by refinements to the suspension and a more aggressive exterior design. The car secured the 1989 All Japan Touring Car Championship season title, yet it sparked curiosity as to why it wasn't given the GT-R name.
cars.hero: An unlikely monster machine born from the elegant lines of the seventh-generation Skyline.

cars.description: This high-performance version of the C10 Skyline—affectionately known as the “Hakosuka”—was introduced in February 1969. It featured bolt-on overfenders and the S20 DOHC engine, derived from the R380 race car, bringing true motorsport pedigree to the street. Its racing success was extraordinary, claiming 52 victories—49 of them consecutively—before the factory team withdrew from competition. The legend of the Skyline began here.
cars.hero: This car, dubbed the "Hako-Suka," became a legend after winning 50 races in a row.

cars.description: The Skyline Super Silhouette was a silhouette formula race car—built using only the basic outline of the production model—based on the sixth-generation Skyline. Its aggressive bodywork featured flared front and rear fenders and a large rear wing, and powered by a turbocharged 2.1-liter LZ20B inline-4 race engine. Between 1982 and 1984, this car secured an impressive eight victories.
cars.hero: An extraordinary Skyline that stood out in races of the 1980s

cars.description: The production model of the seventh-generation Fairlady Z first appeared in prototype form in 2020. Eschewing electrification, Nissan opted for the VR30DDTT twin-turbo 3.0-liter V-6, paired with either a 6-speed manual transmission or a 9-speed automatic with manual shift mode. At a time when the automotive industry was shifting toward self-driving technology and electrification, this car pursued the timeless allure of a front-engine/rear-wheel-drive sports car.
cars.hero: The seventh-generation Z is a 21st century reinterpretation of the classic S30.

cars.description: The Opel Corsa GSE Vision Gran Turismo is a fully electric high-performance concept car that blends Opel’s respect for tradition with its passion for futuristic technology. Twin electric motors, one mounted on each axle, delivers a combined output of 588 kW (788 HP). This enables the car to accelerate from 0-62.1 mph in just two seconds and reach a top speed of 198.8 mph. Its aerodynamic performance is equally impressive, with an active aero diffuser and spoiler that ensures stability even at the highest speeds.
cars.hero: This Vision Gran Turismo embodies the electric spirit of Opel’s GSE sports car brand.
cars.name_long: Opel Corsa GSE Vision Gran Turismo

cars.description: Pagani introduced the Huayra in 2011 as the successor to the Zonda. Its monocoque chassis combined carbon fiber and titanium, delivering both exceptional strength and lightness, while gullwing doors added to its striking design. Powered by an AMG-built twin-turbo 6.0-liter V-12 paired with a 7-speed sequential transmission, the Huayra could accelerate from zero to 62.1 mph in just 3.2 seconds and reach a top speed of 234.9 mph.
cars.hero: A car with bold styling, a lavish interior and a 6.0-liter twin-turbo Mercedes-AMG V12.

cars.description: This was a track-only evolution of the Zonda, unveiled in 1999. Its mid-mounted AMG V-12 delivered 739.6 HP and 520.8 ft-lb of torque. To enhance stability, both the wheelbase and track width were extended. The car was capable of reaching a top speed of 217.5 mph and could accelerate from zero to 62.1 mph in just 2.7 seconds.
cars.hero: The Zonda R featured an adjustable rear wing and a sequential-shift 6-speed transmission.

cars.description: The Peugeot 2008 was introduced in 2013. This featured 2008 SUV is a second-generation model. It was built on the same platform as Peugeot’s 208 hatchback. The lighting elements featured motifs inspired by a lion’s claws and fangs. One of the most notable features of this compact SUV was the 3D i-Cockpit, which included a small-diameter steering wheel with flattened top and bottom sections, paired with a head-up digital instrument cluster positioned above it for optimal driver visibility.
cars.hero: This compact SUV showcases Peugeot design cues throughout.

cars.description: Peugeot introduced the 205 GTI as a spirited road-going counterpart to its 205 Turbo 16 WRC car. Its compact frame and punchy 1.6-liter SOHC engine delivered a thrilling, well-rounded driving experience. More than 300,000 units of this French masterpiece sold across Europe, securing its place in the pantheon of 1980s and 1990s car-culture history.
cars.hero: A masterpiece hot hatch from France that became a rally legend.

cars.description: The 205 Turbo 16 itself was Peugeot’s Group B contender for the World Rally Championship. It won three rallies in its 1984 debut and repeated the feat in 1985. Peugeot evolved the car with more power, less weight, and better aerodynamics to produce the Evolution 2. The updated version captured 7 of 12 victories in 1985 and 6 of 13 in 1986, taking both the drivers' and manufacturers' titles.
cars.hero: This 4-wheel-drive pocket rocket took the Group B racing world by storm.

cars.description: Peugeot’s 208 GTi continued the tradition, based on the popular 208 compact hatch. Smaller than its predecessor, the 207, it shed more than 220 lbs thanks to a redesigned structure and materials. Its 142.9 mph top speed and 0–62.1 mph acceleration time of 6.8 seconds placed it among the top-tier hot hatches.
cars.hero: An exciting hot hatch with a distinctive French character.

cars.description: Peugeot developed the 908 HDi FAP to compete at the highest level of prototype racing. During 2007 and 2008, it took part in events such as the Le Mans Series, serving as a platform for ongoing research and development. In 2009, the car finally triumphed over its chief rival—Audi’s diesel-powered R10—securing a dominant 1–2 finish at Le Mans. Although it was unable to repeat the feat in 2010, the 908 HDi FAP continued to deliver commendable results.
cars.hero: This Peugeot LMP took the top four spots in qualifying for the 2010 24 Hours of Le Mans, but not one finished the race.

cars.description: Peugeot returned to the top class of endurance racing under Le Mans Hypercar (LMH) regulations in 2022 after previously stepping away in 2011. Its return was marked by the arrival of the all-wheel-drive hybrid 9X8. The original aerodynamic concept eliminated the need for a rear wing, although one was introduced as part of the car’s 2024 evolution package. The 2025 version further refined those developments, resulting in the most complete form of the 9X8. It demonstrated its potential with a 2nd place finish at Fuji during the 2025 FIA World Endurance Championship season.
cars.hero: An electric hypercar that represents the racing spirit of Peugeot.

cars.description: This Vision Gran Turismo was created as a tribute to Peugeot’s historic triumph at the 1916 Indianapolis 500 Mile Race. Standing at just 3.3 ft tall, the car boasts a low-slung profile, with a gracefully tapered tail reminiscent of the Indy-winning L45 machine. Its powertrain features a hybrid setup, pairing a 1.6-liter turbocharged 4-cylinder engine with two electric motors, delivering a combined output of 493.1 HP and 730 Nm (535.2 ft-lb) of torque.
cars.hero: This Vision Gran Turismo pays homage to the legendary L45 race machine.
cars.name_long: Peugeot L500R HYbrid Vision Gran Turismo, 2017

cars.description: This is the competition version of the L500R HYbrid Vision Gran Turismo. The rev limiter on its 1.6-liter 4-cylinder engine has been raised to 10,000 rpm, boosting peak output to 571 HP. When combined with the 167.7 HP produced by the electric motors, total system output reaches an impressive 739.6 HP. Visually, the car features a prominent front under spoiler and a large rear wing, both added to generate increased downforce.
cars.hero: This Vision Gran Turismo pays homage to the legendary L45 race machine.
cars.name_long: Peugeot L750R HYbrid Vision Gran Turismo, 2017

cars.description: The PEUGEOT Vision Gran Turismo is the result of a collaboration between Peugeot’s design team and the engineers at Peugeot Sport. With a height of just 3.3 ft, its low-slung body hugs the ground. Powered by a turbocharged 3.2-liter V-6 producing 875 ch (874.8 HP), it's clear this machine was conceived to deliver the quintessential driving experience.
cars.hero: Experience pure steering response in a car that generates powerful downforces directly from its body panels.

cars.description: This Gran Turismo Original is a Gr.3-spec version of the PEUGEOT Vision Gran Turismo, developed through a collaboration between Peugeot and Gran Turismo. To enhance aerodynamic performance, the front splitter and rear diffuser have been enlarged, while a swan-neck rear wing was added.
cars.hero: Experience pure steering response in a car that generates powerful downforces directly from its body panels.

cars.description: A Gran Turismo Original, this is a race-prepared version of the RCZ—Peugeot’s elegantly contoured specialty coupe—adapted for Gr.3 regulations. To enhance weight distribution and overall performance, the drivetrain has been reconfigured from its original front-engine/front-wheel-drive setup to a mid-engine/rear-wheel-drive layout. With its extended 102.8 inches wheelbase, the RCZ provides an ideal foundation for transformation into a competitive race machine.
cars.hero: This is a Gr.3 race version of the stylish Peugeot RCZ compact coupe.

cars.description: This is the homologation model of the RCZ Gr.3, a race-spec version of Peugeot’s gracefully sculpted specialty coupe, adapted for Gr.3 regulations. Transformed into a mid-engine supercar, the design draws inspiration from the 2002 RC concept, one of the earliest visions that eventually gave rise to the RCZ.
cars.hero: This is a Gr.3 production version of the stylish Peugeot RCZ compact coupe.

cars.description: A Gran Turismo Original, this is a Gr.4-spec version of the RCZ, Peugeot’s gracefully styled specialty coupe. Maintaining a front-wheel-drive layout, this model features motorsports-inspired enhancements including a prominent front splitter, a rear wing, and redesigned aerodynamic front fenders.
cars.hero: This is a Gr.4 race car version of the stylish Peugeot RCZ compact coupe.

cars.description: A Gran Turismo Original, this Gr.B version of the RCZ reimagines Peugeot’s elegantly sculpted specialty coupe. Designed in the spirit of the extreme Pikes Peak hillclimb cars, it features an oversized front spoiler and a towering rear wing. The drivetrain has been completely reengineered, with the engine relocated behind the cockpit and mated to a 4-wheel-drive system.
cars.hero: This is an original Gr.B rally-tuned version of the Peugeot RCZ compact coupe.

cars.description: First capturing attention with its debut as a concept at the 2007 Frankfurt Motor Show, the Peugeot RCZ transitioned to production in 2010 with remarkably few changes from its original design. In 2015, the lineup was enhanced with the introduction of the GT Line model, which brought a new front grille, dual exhaust outlets, 19-inch alloy wheels, and a red-stitched black leather interior.
cars.hero: A unique car with a double-bubble rear roof.

cars.description: This homologation model was released by Plymouth, under the Chrysler umbrella, with the clear intention of dominating stock car racing. Based on the standard Road Runner, it received an extended nose and an enormous rear wing, creating an unmistakable silhouette. Standard power came from the 440 Super Commando engine, delivering 369.8 HP, while performance-minded buyers could opt for the 426 Hemi with more than 419.1 HP or a 384.6 HP Six Barrel setup. It was produced for a single year to meet homologation requirements.
cars.hero: This stock car for the street had a wedge-shaped front end and one of the tallest rear wings ever to grace a production car.

cars.description: This was a masterpiece roadster crafted by legendary designer Virgil Exner in 1960. Its asymmetrical styling, hood bulge, and dramatic aero fins gave the impression of Exner’s personal interpretation of a 1950s-era race car. It was awarded the Gran Turismo Trophy in 2011.
cars.hero: The Gran Turismo Trophy winner, with unique asymmetric styling.

cars.description: Created by the Scandinavian electric performance brand Polestar, the Polestar 5 is an all-wheel-drive electric sedan distinguished by its sleek, sub-five-meter profile and a glass roof that extends gracefully to the rear. Power came from a dual-motor setup, with one motor mounted on each axle. In Performance trim, it delivered an impressive 650 kW and 1,015 Nm of torque. Its 800-volt electrical architecture supported 350 kW rapid charging, replenishing the battery from 10 to 80 percent in just 22 minutes. Under WLTP testing, the dual-motor version achieved a maximum range of 416.3 miles.
cars.hero: Polestar's flagship model combines sustainability with high-performance.

cars.description: This was a quintessential example of a 1970s American muscle car. The bold firebird decal emblazoned across the hood became a cultural icon, especially popular among younger enthusiasts of the era. Although it shared its underpinnings with the Chevrolet Camaro, the top-tier Trans Am distinguished itself with an exclusive 6.6-liter engine, not offered on its Chevrolet sibling, making it the pride of Pontiac.
cars.hero: Made famous by Burt Reynolds in "Smokey and the Bandit," this was one of the leading '70s muscle cars.

cars.description: Introduced in 1968, the second-generation Pontiac GTO was hailed as a pioneer of the muscle car era, though it faced fierce competition. To silence the debate, Pontiac unveiled “The Judge." Equipped with a 6.6-liter Ram Air III V-8, a Hurst shifter, heavy-duty suspension, wide tires, and a rear spoiler, the package propelled the GTO back to the forefront of the muscle car wars.
cars.hero: The ultimate sports spec car that appeared towards the end of the GTO era, when muscle cars flourished.

cars.description: Launched in 1949, the 356 A was a refined successor to Porsche’s first production model, the 356. Two variants were offered, both using a detuned version of the 550 Spyder’s engine. The 1500 GS Carrera road-going version produced 98.6 HP, while the semi-competition 1500 GS GT delivered 108.5 HP. This model also introduced the "Carrera" name—now synonymous with Porsche performance.
cars.hero: A semi-race equipped model of the 356A, one of the cars that contributed to the Porsche mystique.

cars.description: Porsche’s first mass-produced sports car made its debut in 1949. From 1955 to 1959, these models were referred to as the 356 A, using an engine derived from the 550 Spyder. The semi-competition 1500 GS GT Carrera, producing 108.5 HP, marked the beginning of the Carrera legacy.
cars.hero: With the introduction of this model, Porsche became known as a maker of the world's finest sports cars.
cars.name_long: Porsche 356 A/1500 GS GT Carrera Speedster '56

cars.description: The first Porsche 911 to carry the RS badge was the 911 Carrera RS 2.7, released in 1973. The "RS" stood for Rennsport, meaning racing sport in German. Developed to meet FIA Group 4 homologation requirements, the car was designed with motorsports in mind. It quickly proved to be a hit—its initial production run of 500 units sold out immediately. Due to high demand, Porsche expanded production, ultimately building a total of 1,580 examples.
cars.hero: A first in Porsche 911 history, the elusive Rennsport.

cars.description: In 1989, Porsche introduced the third-generation 911, known internally as the Type 964. Although it retained the familiar shape of its predecessor, it was a major leap forward, with about 80 percent of its components being newly developed. The Carrera 4, featuring 4-wheel drive, debuted first, followed by the rear-wheel-drive Carrera 2 in 1990. The Carrera RS of this generation was a performance-tuned variant based on the Carrera 2.
cars.hero: This Porsche was a lighter version of the third-generation 911 Carrera 2 and came with a 3.6-liter flat-6.

cars.description: Porsche introduced the fourth-generation 911 in 1993 with the launch of the Type 993. Alongside revised styling, the model featured significant suspension improvements that enhanced handling. The most powerful variant of the series was the Carrera RS, released in 1995, which featured a more rigid yet lighter body. Powering the car was the final air-cooled engine used in the 911—a 3.8-liter flat-6 producing 295.9 HP. The track-focused Carrera RS Clubsport was also made available.
cars.hero: The most powerful version of the 993, the last air-cooled Porsche, came with a 3.8-liter flat-6 producing 295.9 HP.

cars.description: The fourth-generation Type 993 Porsche 911 was introduced as an all-new model in 1993. In 1995, the Carrera RS followed, featuring a lighter yet more rigid body and a 295.9 HP 3.8-liter flat-6 engine. The lineup also included the track-focused Carrera RS Clubsport. Specifically designed for circuit use, it came equipped with a large front spoiler, a prominent rear wing, and a welded roll cage.
cars.hero: This version of the Type 993, the final air-cooled Porsche 911, was designed specifically for the race track.

cars.description: Porsche also developed the 911 GT1 Strassenversion—a road-legal counterpart to the 911 GT1 race car built for GT competition between 1996 and 1998. While the headlights were updated to match those of the Type 996, the core construction of the car remained nearly identical to its racing sibling. To comply with emissions regulations, the engine was detuned to 536.5 HP, yet the car still managed a 0–62.1 mph sprint in just 3.7 seconds and reached a top speed of 191.4 mph.
cars.hero: A road-going version of the 911 GT1 was developed by Porsche to compete in GT racing.

cars.description: The 996-generation Porsche 911, introduced in 1997, was the first to feature a GT3 variant. Using the rigid Carrera 4 chassis as a foundation, it incorporated race-grade upgrades to the suspension and brakes, while the engine took on a GT1-spec crankcase for high-rev performance. A total of 1,889 units were produced.
cars.hero: The 911's first GT3 spec model was introduced for the Type 996. It proved to be very popular, selling 1889 units.

cars.description: In 2006, Porsche introduced the GT3 variant for the Type 997. As with its predecessor, it used the Carrera 4 platform, along with upgraded suspension and braking systems. The engine, originally a 3.6-liter unit, was enlarged to 3.8 liters in 2008, increasing output to 428 HP. Electronically controlled PASM dampers were included as standard equipment.
cars.hero: Featuring adjustable dampers as standard equipment, this GT3 version of the Type 997 made its debut in 2006.

cars.description: The 911 GT3 R was a pure racing machine developed from the 992-model 911, the eighth generation of Porsche’s everyday sports car. Introduced in 2022, this machine was equipped with a naturally aspirated 4.2-liter flat-6 engine, producing a maximum 557.2 HP. It also featured lightweight carbon body panels and aramid-fiber components, as well as the double-wishbone/multilink suspension setup derived from the 911 RSR.
cars.hero: This is a pure racing machine from the 8th generation 911 catalogue.

cars.description: This high-performance model served as a further evolution of the 991-generation Porsche 911 GT3.
