Starting with the wide-body shell of the 911 Turbo, Porsche increased front and rear track widths, while also implementing major weight reductions and aerodynamic enhancements. The engine, enlarged to 4.0 liters, produced 493.1 HP and enabled the car to record a Nürburgring Nordschleife lap time of 7 minutes and 20 seconds.
cars.hero: The ultimate 991, rebuilt from the ground up.

cars.description: The Porsche 911 GT3 RS (992) was a high-performance road car that incorporated aerodynamic components from the 911 GT3 R race car. It was fitted with a range of advanced aerodynamic systems, including a large swan-neck rear wing with DRS (drag reduction system) and an active diffuser that functioned as an air brake under hard braking.
cars.hero: A hyper-performance road car packed with race car features.

cars.description: This race-bred machine carried the spirit of the RSR. And it was developed through an entirely different process than the production 911 road car. Its 4.0-liter naturally-aspirated engine, the first in 911 history to be mid-mounted, delivered 502 HP. At the 2017 Nürburgring 24 Hours, the car delivered a standout performance, holding the top spot for much of the race.
cars.hero: This 911, the first in history to feature a mid-engine layout, is a full competition spec machine.

cars.description: Introduced in 1975, the 911 Turbo was the first production Porsche to wear the now-iconic "Turbo" badge. True to its name, the car’s 3.0L air-cooled flat-6 engine was equipped with a KKK turbocharger, producing 256.4 HP. This setup enabled the car to cruise at speeds of up to 155.3 mph—a remarkable feat for its era. Beginning in 1977, the engine’s displacement was increased to 3.3 liters and paired with an air-to-air intercooler, which further boosted performance.
cars.hero: This top-of-the-line version of the vaunted 911 possessed a more muscular look and a turbocharged engine.

cars.description: Having stood as the symbol of the Porsche brand since the 1960s, the 911 entered its eighth generation in 2018 with the Type 992. In April 2020, Porsche introduced the Turbo S variant to the 992 lineup as its top-performing model. Powered by a twin-turbocharged 3745 cc flat-6 engine, the Turbo S delivered 641 HP and 590.2 ft-lb of torque, channeled through all four wheels, enabling a 0–62.1 mph time of just 2.7 seconds and a top speed of 205.1 mph.
cars.hero: The top performance version of the eighth-generation 911.

cars.description: The 964 represented the third generation of the 911 series, following the Type 901 and 930. The lineup included a “Turbo” model for those seeking greater performance, as well as the 911 Turbo S Leichtbau, a special variant created to commemorate Porsche’s success in the 1993 IMSA series. True to its “Leichtbau” (lightweight) name, the Turbo S featured high-lift camshafts and a revised turbocharger with increased boost, producing 375.7 HP/361.6 ft-lb. Weight was also significantly reduced compared with the standard Turbo model.
cars.hero: The third-generation 911 Turbo was virtually all new with 80 percent new parts.

cars.description: This 992-generation Porsche 911 Turbo S was a virtual model created by Gran Turismo and reimagined as a safety car. Built on Porsche’s updated 911 platform, the wide-body design incorporated a higher percentage of aluminum components. Its exceptional traction and stability made the 911 Turbo ideally suited for leading the field as a safety car.
cars.hero: The 911 Turbo S reimagined as a safety car.

cars.description: The Porsche 917 earned a celebrated place in motorsport history by securing seven victories out of ten races during the 1970 World Sportscar Championship season. The Porsche 917 LIVING LEGEND was a hypercar concept inspired by the 917. Its classic exterior design masked cutting-edge technology beneath the surface. Its blend of top speed and aerodynamic downforce resulted in remarkable stability, even at speeds exceeding 186.4 mph.
cars.hero: This extreme hyper car is an updated version of the legendary 917, one of the most celebrated race cars in Porsche history.

cars.description: The 917K was a prototype race car developed by Porsche specifically for sports car competition. Despite weighing under 1764 lbs, the 1970 version was capable of producing up to 591.7 HP in its most powerful configuration. In its second year of competition, 1970, the 917K proved nearly unbeatable, winning seven out of ten rounds in the International Championship for Makes. It also delivered Porsche its long-awaited first overall victory at the 24 Hours of Le Mans.
cars.hero: This prototype race car that gave Porsche its first victory at the 24 Hours of Le Mans.

cars.description: The Porsche 918 Spyder was a high-performance sports car introduced in 2011. It succeeded the Carrera GT and was produced in a limited run of 918 units, in keeping with its name. Its most defining feature was its plug-in hybrid powertrain. The mid-mounted 4.6-liter V-8 engine, producing 599.6 HP, was paired with two electric motors on the front axle and one on the rear, delivering a combined system output of up to 873.8 HP.
cars.hero: This super sports car represents the first plug-in hybrid flagship from the famed German car maker.

cars.description: This prototype sports car was developed specifically to compete in the World Endurance Championship (WEC) and at Le Mans. It utilized a turbocharged 2.0-liter V-4 as part of a hybrid system that included energy recovery technology, with a total output of 887.6 HP. From 2015 through 2017, it dominated the WEC, capturing both the constructors’ and drivers’ championships in those years.
cars.hero: The consecutive Le Mans champion & hybrid prototype sports car.

cars.description: The Porsche 959 was the production evolution of the original Gruppe B prototype, which Porsche had engineered for competition in Group B, the top category of the WRC at the time. It featured an advanced, electronically controlled 4-wheel-drive system that allowed drivers to adjust drivetrain settings to suit various conditions, delivering exceptional stability and ride comfort. Although Group B was disbanded before the car could compete in the WRC, the 959 still achieved remarkable success in other forms of motorsports.
cars.hero: A four-wheel-drive road car that shines bright in automotive history.

cars.description: The Porsche 962 C was a prototype race car that made its debut in the World Endurance Championship (WEC) in 1985. Over the course of its career, the car delivered Porsche numerous race victories and championship titles. In its debut WEC season, it won seven out of ten races. The following year, in 1986, it claimed four wins from nine rounds in the newly renamed World Sports Prototype Championship (WSPC). At the 1987 WSPC, it secured a win at Le Mans and followed it up with a 2nd-place finish the year after.
cars.hero: These Group C cars scored numerous endurance racing championships for Porsche.

cars.description: Porsche’s Le Mans Daytona h (LMDh) contender, the 963, carried forward the legacy of the legendary 962 and 919 Hybrid. After making its debut at the 2023 24 Hours of Daytona, it quickly amassed victories and podiums in IMSA and the WEC before Porsche claimed both the Drivers’ and Manufacturers’ titles in the 2024 IMSA season. For 2025, the car received further development in its suspension and rear aerodynamic package to improve balance and stability on any circuit.
cars.hero: A new category LMDh hypercar created by Porsche, the masters of endurance.

cars.description: The Porsche Carrera GT was a mid-engine super sports car produced from 2003 to 2006, with a total of 1,270 units built. Its chassis centered on a lightweight yet rigid carbon-fiber monocoque, complemented by carbon fiber subframes supporting the engine and rear suspension. Power came from a naturally-aspirated 5.7-liter V-10, derived from a race engine, producing 603.5 HP. This was paired with a 6-speed manual gearbox.
cars.hero: Only 1270 examples of this mid-engine supercar were produced from 2003 to 2006.

cars.description: In 1963, Porsche developed the Carrera GTS in response to the World Sportscar Championship regulations of the era. To meet the 100-unit production homologation requirement, the car employed a ladder-frame chassis paired with a lightweight fiberglass body. It delivered strong performance and achieved numerous victories, beginning with the Targa Florio, ultimately becoming the foundation of Porsche’s GT racing efforts throughout the 1960s.
cars.hero: A masterpiece that brought great success to Porsche's GT race efforts in the 1960s

cars.description: The Cayman GT4 joined the Porsche Cayman lineup in 2015 as a motorsports-focused model. It was powered by a 3.8-liter flat-6 derived from the 911 Carrera S, paired with a 6-speed manual transmission. With an output of 379.7 HP, it surpassed the base 911 Carrera in performance and incorporated braking and suspension components from the 991-generation 911 GT3. Optional equipment included a roll cage and 6-point harnesses.
cars.hero: A Cayman designed for motorsports and possessing all the competitive flair of the 911.

cars.description: A pure racing version was also introduced for the Cayman’s GT4 class. While it retained the same 379.7 HP 3.8-liter flat-6, it was fully optimized for competition, stripped of all comfort features and fitted with components from the 911 GT3 Cup car to maximize track performance.
cars.hero: The highest performance model of the Cayman series in its naturally aspirated flat 6 generation.

cars.description: This all-electric hypercar was unveiled on June 8, 2023—exactly 75 years after the original Porsche 356 "No.1" Roadster received approval. Its exterior design incorporated motifs from Porsche’s storied racing heritage, while the cockpit focused entirely on the driver experience. This car achieved a power-to-weight ratio of 1 horsepower per 2 lbs and downforce far exceeding that of the 992-generation 911 GT3 RS.
cars.hero: A hypercar concept to celebrate the 75th anniversary of Porsche.

cars.description: This lightweight, hyper-performance machine honored Porsche’s storied legacy while offering a glimpse into the future of sports cars. Its exterior and interior flowed together in perfect harmony, delivering an exceptionally immersive driving experience. Power came from twin electric motors, while an innovative active aerodynamic system adjusted in real time to deliver optimal downforce and efficiency for any condition.
cars.hero: Porsche's modern yet daring statement on the future of the sports car remains true to its racing roots.

cars.description: It was the Spyder variant of the Porsche Vision Gran Turismo, which originally made its debut in 2021. The sculpted surfaces and refined cabin fused artfully to heighten driver engagement. Beneath it all, the dual-motor setup and active aero system worked in concert to ensure performance remained as precise as it was exhilarating.
cars.hero: Porsche's modern-yet-daring statement on the future of the sports car.

cars.description: First sold in 1954, the 550/1500RS was a racing sports car featuring a lightweight aluminum body over a steel tube frame, powered by a 4-cam flat-4 engine producing 133.1 HP. It delivered impressive results on the track, securing class victories at the 24 Hours of Le Mans in both 1954 and 1955. This particular 1500RS is especially prized, still wearing the original paint it sported during the 1956 running of Le Mans.
cars.hero: This French blue Porsche wears the original livery from the 1956 24 Hours of Le Mans race.

cars.description: The Taycan marked Porsche’s first fully electric sports sedan. Equipped with electric motors on the front and rear axles, its advanced all-wheel-drive system was paired with a 2-speed transmission, delivering blistering acceleration and top-end performance. The overboost-equipped Turbo S variant produced 560 kW (750.5 HP). Notably, the Taycan was the first mass-produced vehicle to feature an 800V electrical system, enhancing both powertrain efficiency and reducing charging times.
cars.hero: With a total system voltage of 800V, this fully electric sedan boasts both comfort and remarkable performance.

cars.description: The Radical SR3 SL was a road-legal track machine that closely resembled a scaled-down Le Mans Prototype. Among its powertrain options was a 2.0-liter Ford EcoBoost inline-4 with direct injection and a turbocharger, producing 295.9 HP and paired with a 6-speed sequential paddle-shift transmission. With a curb weight of just 1709 lbs, the SR3 SL delivered remarkable performance, launching from zero to 59.7 mph in just 3.4 seconds and reaching a top speed of 159.7 mph.
cars.hero: The road-going racer that can handle both pleasure cruises and circuit laps.

cars.description: This machine was the winner of the 2014 Gran Turismo Award. A heavily customized 1970 Chevrolet Camaro SS, it was reimagined by Roadster Shop in Illinois, USA. The car’s structure was rebuilt from the ground up using lightweight carbon fiber and aluminum components, while under the hood sat a rear-offset 7.0-liter LS7 engine tuned to produce 739.6 HP. Its aggressive aesthetic was matched by performance, with wide overfenders, a bold front spoiler, and a prominent rear wing.
cars.hero: This 2014 GT Awards winner was a high-speed monster wearing the skin of a Camaro SS.

cars.description: The Amemiya µ Boost up 7 was a street machine built by RE Amemiya, the legendary rotary tuner known for their presence in Super GT and D1GP. This car was engineered to fully exploit the FD3S platform’s capabilities as a cornering specialist. Celebrated for its performance on winding roads, it was featured in the Japanese DVD magazine Hot Version, where it earned the nickname “demon-lord of mountain paths” for its unmatched speed.
cars.hero: The Amemiya FD3S was another stylish RX-7 created by master tuner, RE Amemiya.

cars.description: The Avantime was a specialty car penned by Patrick Le Quément of Renault Design. Its distinctive body blended the proven underpinnings of the third-generation Espace, a favorite across Europe, with a striking three-door fiberglass shell. Although coupe-like in silhouette, what set the Avantime apart were its B-pillarless side windows and large sunroof, which could be opened. A pure expression of Renault’s design philosophy, the Avantime was proof that the monoform concept need not be limited to minivans.
cars.hero: A unique coupe that tests the boundaries of monoform design.

cars.description: The Captur was a compact crossover SUV produced by Renault. The second-generation model, introduced in 2019, measured 13.9 ft in length, 5.9 ft in width and 5.2 ft in height, giving it the stance of an SUV while preserving the agility of a compact car. It offered a broad range of powertrain options, spanning conventional gasoline engines as well as diesel and hybrid variants. Most notable among them was the E-Tech PHEV system, which incorporated hybrid technology developed by Renault’s Formula 1 team.
cars.hero: A formidable vehicle that blurred the boundaries of the compact SUV class.

cars.description: The Clio R.S. 220 EDC Trophy is a high-performance variant of the fourth-generation Clio, developed by Renault Sport. This model, known as the R.S. Vision, introduced a distinctive new front bumper design inspired by the pattern of a checkered flag. It also featured updated LED headlights and taillights, along with various other design enhancements throughout.
cars.hero: This super fast Clio set the compact hatch lap record at the Nürburgring.
cars.name_long: Renault Sport Clio R.S. 220 EDC Trophy '15

cars.description: The Clio R.S. 220 EDC Trophy is a high-performance variant of the fourth-generation Clio, developed by Renault Sport. The 2016 model, known as the R.S. Vision, introduced a distinctive new front bumper design inspired by the pattern of a checkered flag. It also featured updated LED headlights and taillights, along with various other design enhancements throughout.
cars.hero: This Clio sports model, tuned by Renault Sport, excelled on the race track.
cars.name_long: Renault Sport Clio R.S. 220 EDC Trophy '16

cars.description: Originally developed for motorsports, the Renault Clio R.S. V6 possessed the 3.0-liter V-6 from the luxury Laguna, producing up to 229.8 HP. In 2002, the updated Phase 2 model raised output to 251.5 HP and introduced changes to the exterior, interior, and tire size.
cars.hero: Built by Tom Walkinshaw Racing, this sporty Lutecia featured a mid-mounted 3.0-liter V6.

cars.description: Ten years after the debut of Europe’s first minivan came the Renault Espace F1—an unprecedented creation that redefined the limits of imagination. At its heart resided the RS4 3.5-liter V-10 from the 1992 Formula 1 championship–winning FW14B, mounted amidships within a body crafted from aluminum and carbon fiber. Producing 788 HP, it rocketed from 0-62.1 mph in just 2.8 seconds and reached a top speed of 196.4 mph. This extraordinary machine was even driven on a real circuit by F1 legend Alain Prost, among others.
cars.hero: Renault's rebellious minivan carries an F1 engine.

cars.description: In French, small vans are called "fourgonnettes." And the Kangoo gained popularity for embodying that spirit, with sliding passenger doors and split-folding rear seats that made it ideal not only for commercial tasks but also for personal and recreational use. It became a pioneer of the ludospace segment—vehicles designed for leisure activity. While its engine delivered only modest power, the soft suspension gave it a surprisingly lively and enjoyable driving character.
cars.hero: This popular leisure activity vehicle began its life as a commercial van.

cars.description: This Gran Turismo Original is a Gr.4-spec version of Renault’s fastest hatchback, the Mégane. Having already proven itself with a blistering Nürburgring lap time, the Mégane's transformation into a race car felt like a natural progression. With outstanding traction and sharp cornering capabilities, it delivers such precise performance that you’ll forget it’s front-wheel drive at all.
cars.hero: This limited-edition Renault set a lap record at the Nürburgring.

cars.description: Based on the third-generation Mégane 3-door coupe, the Mégane R.S. was factory-tuned by Renault Sport for high performance. With bespoke ground effects and a newly developed chassis, it delivered exceptional cornering capability—earning its reputation as one of the fastest front-wheel-drive cars of its time. In 2011, the Mégane R.S. Trophy was introduced. With just 500 units produced worldwide, it made headlines by setting a new Nürburgring lap record for mass-produced front-wheel-drive cars, clocking in at 8 minutes and 7.97 seconds.
cars.hero: This limited-edition Renault set a lap record at the Nürburgring.

cars.description: This fictional safety car is based on that very Mégane R.S. Trophy. Developed by Renault Sport, the "R.S." was the high-performance version of the Mégane, but the Trophy edition pushed even further with increased engine output and finely tuned suspension, all in pursuit of becoming the fastest front-wheel-drive production car in the world.
cars.hero: This safety car version of the Mégane RS Trophy was created to patrol the race track.
cars.name_long: Renault Sport Mégane R.S. Trophy Safety Car

cars.description: The Renault Sport Mégane Trophy was developed specifically for the Mégane Trophy race series, which began in 2005. While retaining the overall silhouette of the production Mégane, the Trophy version featured far more aggressive styling and a mid-mounted 355 HP 3.5-liter V-6 in a lightweight 2194 lbs package. A 6-speed two-pedal manual transmission with paddle shifters delivered quick, precise gear changes. The suspension and brakes were full racing spec.
cars.hero: Aggressive looks topped off by gullwing doors highlight this Mégane Trophy.

cars.description: In the summer of 2014, Renault Sport unveiled the R.S.01 as its new contender for one-make racing, succeeding the Mégane Trophy. Measuring 164.2 inches in length and 78.7 inches in width, the R.S.01 boasted a lightweight body at just 2425 lbs. Beneath its sculpted exterior was a potent twin-turbo V-6 engine producing 542.4 HP. Every detail of the car—from its advanced aerodynamics to its efficient cooling systems—reflects Renault Sport’s deep expertise, making it an impressive race machine in every sense.
cars.hero: A French race car with a Japanese heart.

cars.description: Based on Renault Sport’s purpose-built one-make racer, the R.S.01, the Renault Sport R.S.01 GT3 was developed to compete in FIA GT championships. To comply with FIA GT3 regulations, the car underwent significant modifications. The power output was restricted, and the brake materials were replaced. Also, 110 lbs of ballast was added, and the ground effect aerodynamics were completely reengineered
cars.hero: Renault's special GT3 machine with Nismo power.

cars.description: The Renault 4 (Quatre), introduced in 1961, was designed to replace the best-selling 4CV. By 1978, the car reached its full potential with the GTL variant. This model added a plastic grille, a more powerful 1.1-liter engine, and a modernized instrument panel. Amassing more than 8.1 million units by the end of its production in 1992, the Renault 4 became a French cultural icon. It was a car for the people, a symbol of practical, efficient design from France.
cars.hero: The world's first hatchback found great success through utilitarian design.

cars.description: The Renault R5 ("Cinq") Turbo drew major attention when it was introduced at the 1978 Paris Motor Show. Initially developed as a prototype for the World Rally Championship (WRC), a production version followed in 1980. The transformation was dramatic, its front-engine/front-wheel-drive layout replaced with a mid-engine/rear-wheel-drive one. The new engine delivered 1.5 times the power and more than three times the torque compared to the standard model. Making its debut at the 1980 WRC Tour de Corse, the R5 Turbo dominated the field, establishing Renault as a serious WRC force.
cars.hero: The rear-mid-engine layout and ultra-wide rear fenders of this Renault hatchback set the 1980s auto industry on the right track.

cars.description: This high-performance version of the Renault 8 was tuned by Amédée Gordini, known as "The Sorcerer" for his remarkable engine tuning. Building on the strengths of the original 1108 cc compact sedan, Gordini transformed the modest Renault 8 into a formidable touring machine, blending precision engineering with motorsport spirit. In 1966, the engine was enlarged to 1300 cc and paired with a 5-speed transmission, further unlocking its performance potential. With its distinctive character and motorsport pedigree, this automotive gem holds a cherished place in the hearts of enthusiasts to this day.
cars.hero: A French icon of the '60s, the R8 Gordini is still popular half a century after its birth.

cars.description: The Twingo became known for its 3-door monospace design, with a near-continuous curve flowing from the truncated hood, over the roof and into the rear. The wheels were positioned at the extreme corners of the body, allowing for an unusually spacious interior despite its compact form. At launch, the engine delivered modest output, but paired with the lightweight body, it provided a lively and engaging drive in urban settings. It was also praised for bringing character to a practical vehicle, with sliding rear seats that enabled a variety of seating/cargo configurations.
cars.hero: Practical yet cute. A breath of fresh air for the A-segment.

cars.description: Released in 2007, the RUF CTR3 served as the successor to the iconic CTR and CTR2. Unlike its predecessors, which were based on the Porsche 930 and 993 Turbo, the CTR3 was designed entirely from the ground up by RUF. It adopted a mid-engine layout and was powered by a twin-turbocharged 3.8-liter flat-6 with intercooling. Performance was staggering, with a top speed of 236.1 mph and zero-62.1 mph acceleration in just 3.2 seconds.
cars.hero: The third-generation CTR was thoroughly re-engineered by Ruf, including being converted to a mid-engine layout.

cars.description: This RUF original was based on the 991-generation Porsche 911 GT3. Developed with the philosophy of blending GT3-level performance with refined road car comfort, it was powered by a naturally-aspirated Mezger engine—fitted with the legendary GT1 crankshaft—and enlarged from 3.8 to 4.2 liters. Riveted overfenders added a bold visual statement, emphasizing the car’s raw capability and presence. A true enthusiast’s machine, tailored for the gentleman driver.
cars.hero: The ultimate naturally-aspirated flat-6 machine, meticulously crafted by Ruf.

cars.description: Shelby developed the Cobra 427 with the goal of winning the FIA Speed World Challenge, where the team was actively competing at the time. The car was powered by a formidable 7.0-liter 427 “Side Oiler” V-8—a purpose-built race engine originally designed for stock car competition. To handle its impressive 493.1 HP output, the Cobra 427 replaced its signature side-mounted leaf springs with a modern double wishbone suspension, greatly enhancing its handling and stability.
cars.hero: Lightweight and powerful, the Cobra is an American sports car icon.

cars.description: The AC Cobra had already made a name for itself on the racing scene in the 1960s, and its closed-roof variant was the Shelby Cobra Coupe. While the open-bodied Cobra excelled in acceleration and handling, it lagged behind in top speed due to poor aerodynamics. That changed with a coupe body designed by Pete Brock, which dramatically improved the car’s airflow and added more than 18.6 mph to its top speed. With its full potential unlocked, the Cobra Coupe went on to win numerous races over the following two years.
cars.hero: Only 6 units of the legendary, and very successful, Shelby Daytona Coupe race car were ever made.

cars.description: This high-performance Mustang was developed by Ford in collaboration with Carroll Shelby to compete in the SCCA, a premier American sports car racing series. The lightened body was equipped with race suspension and an LSD, while at its heart sat the 289 engine, producing 301.8 HP. Beginning in 1965, it went on to dominate the series for three consecutive years.
cars.hero: This highly collectible Mustang earned a great track record in SCCA racing.

cars.description: The 2017 Falken Tire / Turn 14 Distribution BRZ was piloted by Formula Drift champion Daijiro Yoshihara. Based on the Rocket Bunny V3 aero kit, the car housed a 7.0-liter turbocharged V-8 that delivered approximately 986.2 HP. A 4-speed transmission and reinforced drivetrain components ensured it could handle the immense power.
cars.hero: This BRZ competition machine was piloted by Formula Drift champion Daijiro Yoshihara in 2017.

cars.description: Starting in 2012, Subaru entered the BRZ into Japan’s domestic Super GT series, competing in the GT300 class. After the release of the second-generation BRZ in 2021, Subaru transitioned to a new GT machine based on the updated model. The new car retained proven elements like the EJ20 engine, while incorporating enhancements to weight distribution and aerodynamics. That same year, the BRZ claimed the GT300 class championship, marking a historic first for Subaru.
cars.hero: Cornering better than ever before. A BRZ for the Super GT.

cars.description: The Toyota 86 and Subaru BRZ sports cars were developed through a collaborative effort between Toyota and Subaru. "BRZ" stood for "Boxer engine, Rear-wheel drive, Zenith." The car was powered by a Subaru 2.0-liter boxer engine paired with Toyota’s D-4S direct injection system. Following its 2012 debut, the car received near-annual updates. The 2015 model notably improved both handling and ride comfort.
cars.hero: Subaru's first FR sports car featured a boxer engine, giving it a low center of gravity and excellent handling.

cars.description: The Toyota 86 and Subaru BRZ, both rear-wheel drive sports cars powered by boxer engines, were developed through a close collaboration between Toyota and Subaru. The series evolved into its second generation with the ZD8 in 2020. The updated platform featured a lighter yet more rigid body, while the engine was an all-new 2.4-liter boxer unit. Its peak output reached 231.8 HP. The Subaru BRZ "S" grade was positioned as a premium trim, offering enhanced interior and exterior appointments.
cars.hero: The second-gen FR sports car features a larger 2.4-liter engine.

cars.description: In 2017, Subaru introduced the BRZ STI Sport as the flagship of the BRZ lineup. It was co-developed with Subaru’s motorsports division, STI (Subaru Tecnica International). The most notable upgrade was the revised chassis setup. Handling and stability were enhanced through STI’s proprietary Flexible V-Bar and Flexible Draw Stiffener components, while custom-developed suspension parts boosted overall agility.
cars.hero: Numerous chassis performance and visual enhancements by STI gave the BRZ sports car unprecedented flair.

cars.description: This limited-edition model, based on the Impreza WRX STi Version IV, featured wide blister fenders identical to those of the World Rally car and was powered by a 2.2-liter boxer engine producing 276.1 HP and 267.6 ft-lb of torque. Despite its five million yen price tag, all 400 units sold out within days, securing its status as one of the most coveted models among Subaru enthusiasts.
cars.hero: Essentially a road-going version of Subaru's WRC car, this car’s production was limited to only 400 units (and sold out immediately).

cars.description: Released in September 1999, this was the coupe version of the Impreza Version VI. In addition to its rally-inspired styling, it came equipped with the Driver’s Control Center Differential (DCCD), an intercooler water sprayer, specially tuned stiff suspension, and a reinforced rear axle—all as standard. Its iconic EJ20 engine was tuned to deliver 276.1 HP, making this one of the most complete and refined GC8 models ever produced.
cars.hero: After six years of evolution, this car represented the final form of the GC8 Impreza coupe.
cars.model: Impreza Coupe WRX Type R STi Ver.VI '99
cars.name_long: Subaru Impreza Coupe WRX Type R STi Version VI '99

cars.description: This WRC machine was based on the 2-door Impreza. Beginning with the 1997 model, this evolution introduced computer-controlled active differentials at the front, rear, and center. Although it didn’t secure Subaru a fourth consecutive constructors’ title, Colin McRae’s wins in Portugal, the Tour de Corse, and the Acropolis rallies proved its formidable potential.
cars.hero: Subaru's triple race winning Impreza World Rally car from the 1998 season.

cars.description: The first facelift of the GD-generation Impreza was marked by its distinctive teardrop-shaped “blob eye” headlights. Engine efficiency was improved with the adoption of equal-length, matched exhaust headers. Also, some manual variants featured a Driver's Control Center Differential with an automatic mode. A minor update in 2004 brought larger tires and boosted torque output to 303.8 ft-lb.
cars.hero: The second-generation Impreza was developed alongside the rally spec model.

cars.description: The SUBARU VIZIV GT Vision Gran Turismo is Subaru’s ultimate expression of a next-generation sports car, carrying forward the brand’s “VIZIV” philosophy—Vision for Innovation. Carbon materials have been used extensively throughout the body, keeping weight down to 3042 lbs. At its heart is a specially tuned horizontally-opposed 2.0-liter engine paired with high-output electric motors, delivering a combined output of 591.7 HP and a peak torque of 800Nm (593.1 ft-lb).
cars.hero: Subaru's most aggressive sports car ever is potent yet civilized.
cars.name_long: SUBARU VIZIV GT Vision Gran Turismo

cars.description: A Gran Turismo Original, Subaru’s high-performance WRX sedan has been modified to meet Gr.3 racing regulations. To reduce the frontal cross-sectional area, the lower chassis has been trimmed and the overall ride height lowered as much as possible. Equipped with a diffuser-style front splitter and a two-level rear wing, this 4-door sedan generates more downforce than many coupes.
cars.hero: The WRX STI continues its tradition of delivering potent 4WD performance.

cars.description: A Gran Turismo Original, Subaru’s high-performance WRX sedan has been modified to meet Gr.4 racing regulations. A front splitter and rear wing have been added to generate additional downforce. The base car’s 4-wheel-drive system is retained, giving it class-leading traction among the Gr.4 field.
cars.hero: The WRX STI continues its tradition of delivering potent 4WD performance.

cars.description: A Gran Turismo Original, Subaru’s high-performance WRX sedan has been modified to comply with Gr.B regulations. To enhance downforce and agility, the car’s track width has been significantly widened, while long-stroke suspension was fitted to improve off-road capability. The result is a cutting-edge rally machine.
cars.hero: The WRX STI continues its tradition of delivering potent 4WD performance.

cars.description: This is the homologation model of the WRX Gr.B, a variant of Subaru’s high-performance WRX sedan engineered to meet Gr.B regulations. Although rooted in rally car design, greater emphasis has been placed on on-road performance, with the addition of a race-inspired front splitter, side skirt winglets, and a rear diffuser.
cars.hero: This road-going version of the WRX Gr.B was modified to excel on the tarmac.

cars.description: In June 2016, a Subaru WRX STI set a new record for 4-wheeled vehicles during a time attack on the Isle of Man Tourist Trophy course. While Subaru had been competing in the event since 2011, the 2016 machine was specially prepared by Britain’s Prodrive, a team renowned for its multiple World Rally Championship titles. Thanks to their expertise, the record was lowered by nearly two minutes, with a final time of 17:35.139 and an average speed of 128.6 mph.
cars.hero: This celebrated WRX set the lap record on the holy ground of motorcycle racing, the Isle of Man.
cars.name_long: Subaru WRX STI Isle of Man Time Attack Car '16

cars.description: Introduced in the autumn of 2013, the Subaru WRX compact sedan emerged as a standalone model, separating itself from the Impreza lineup. Built on a platform closely related to that of the Levorg, the WRX featured significant structural reinforcements. The high-performance STI edition took things further, offering enhanced dynamics with newly developed suspension and a refined version of the EJ20 engine, delivering 303.7 HP and 311.0 ft-lb of torque.
cars.hero: The WRX STI continues its tradition of delivering potent 4WD performance.

cars.description: The Japanese Super Formula series transitioned to the Dallara SF19 chassis in 2019. Equipped with a halo system that met F1 safety standards, the SF19 also featured aerodynamic enhancements over its predecessor, the SF14, making overtaking easier and improving race action. Power came from a turbocharged 2.0-liter direct-injection inline-4, with separate versions independently developed by Toyota and Honda. Despite tight regulations, a fierce development battle unfolded between the two manufacturers.
cars.hero: Both Toyota and Honda provide engines for the Super Formula series. This is the one from Honda.

cars.description: The Japanese Super Formula series transitioned to the Dallara SF19 chassis in 2019. Equipped with a halo system that met F1 safety standards, the SF19 also featured aerodynamic enhancements over its predecessor, the SF14, making overtaking easier and improving race action. Power came from a turbocharged 2.0-liter direct-injection inline-4, with separate versions independently developed by Toyota and Honda. Despite tight regulations, a fierce development battle unfolded between the two manufacturers.
cars.hero: Both Toyota and Honda provide engines for the Super Formula series. This is the one from Toyota.

cars.description: The Dallara SF23 Super Formula made its debut in the spring of 2023 as the latest machine for the Super Formula series. Developed under the “SUPER FORMULA NEXT50” initiative, the car aimed to promote sustainability in motorsports. It incorporated biocomposite materials, while significantly reducing CO₂ emissions. Engines were supplied by Toyota and Honda.
cars.hero: The next evolution of Super Formula cars aims to bring sustainability to motorsports

cars.description: The Dallara SF23 Super Formula made its debut in the spring of 2023 as the latest machine for the Super Formula series. Developed under the “SUPER FORMULA NEXT50” initiative, the car aimed to promote sustainability in motorsports. It incorporated biocomposite materials, while significantly reducing CO₂ emissions. Engines were supplied by Toyota and Honda.
cars.hero: The next evolution of Super Formula cars aims to bring sustainability to motorsports

cars.description: The Cappuccino was Suzuki’s entry into the kei-class sports car segment, launched in November 1991. Alongside the Honda Beat and Mazda’s Autozam AZ-1, it helped define the two-seater kei sports car boom of the era. It featured a long-nose, two-seat convertible body paired with a front-mounted engine producing 63.1 HP—the maximum output allowed under kei-car regulations. With a near-perfect 51:49 front-to-rear weight distribution, the Cappuccino left no doubt that it was a true rear-wheel-drive sports car.
cars.hero: The rear-drive Cappuccino roadster kickstarted the two-seat kei-car trend.

cars.description: Japan’s micro-car segment, known locally as kei-cars, has become an indispensable part of everyday life throughout the country. The Suzuki Carry compact truck is a classic example of the commercial kei-car segment, which includes a wide range of cargo vans and mini trucks. Introduced in 1961, the Carry has built a long-standing reputation. The model shown here is the 2012 version, the final evolution of the 10th generation. With its endearing styling and everyday practicality, the Carry has begun to attract attention from enthusiasts and users overseas as well.
cars.hero: A quintessential example of the micro-truck trend that has become a hit all over the world.

cars.description: This 3-door model of the Jimny was lengthened and widened to better suit international markets. Now mated to a 1460 cc DOHC inline-4, the part-time 4WD system with a mechanical transfer case delivers uncompromising off-road performance. The third-generation JB74, counting from the original Sierra, earned widespread acclaim for its boxy, elongated design.
cars.hero: A stouter Jimny with an eye on global success.

cars.description: This was Japan’s premier micro off-roader. Since its debut in the 1970s, the Jimny consistently adhered to kei-car regulations, featuring a ladder frame chassis, 4-wheel drive with rigid axle suspension, and large-diameter tires. In 2018, the boxy fourth-generation model was introduced, maintaining its rugged charm while gaining popularity both as a leisure vehicle and as a reliable workhorse in Japan’s mountainous regions.
cars.hero: Japan's mighty micro off-roader boasts amazing all-terrain ability beyond its size.

cars.description: The SUZUKI Vision Gran Turismo harnesses the cutting-edge engine technology of the renowned Hayabusa sports bike, paired with advanced electrification and weight-saving innovations. Its powertrain combines the 1,340 cm³ (1340 cc) Hayabusa engine with three high-output electric motors in an all-wheel-drive layout. Together, they deliver a total system output of 426 HP at 9700 rpm, making this compact machine a true super sports car.
cars.hero: A super sports car combining the heart of the Hayabusa with electric motors.

cars.description: The SUZUKI Vision Gran Turismo harnesses the cutting-edge engine technology of the renowned Hayabusa sports bike, paired with advanced electrification and weight-saving innovations. Its powertrain combines the 1,340 cm³ (1340 cc) Hayabusa engine with three high-output electric motors in an all-wheel-drive layout. Together, they deliver a total system output of 426 HP at 9700 rpm, making this compact machine a true super sports car.
cars.hero: This Gr.3 Vision Gran Turismo possesses Suzuki's racing spirit.

cars.description: The Suzuki Swift Sport was the performance-focused variant of the second-generation Swift. At its heart was a naturally-aspirated 1.6-liter engine, tuned for high-revs and equipped with forged pistons and variable valve timing. A minor update in 2007 raised the rev limit from 7000 rpm to 7500 rpm. Paired with a close-ratio 5-speed manual gearbox, it delivered an exhilarating driving experience.
cars.hero: Suzuki's fun-to-drive Swift Sport was made even more lively with a high-revving engine and close-ratio gears.

cars.description: The Swift Sport was the high-performance variant of the fourth-generation Suzuki Swift, launched in 2016. Its aerodynamic body concealed a downsized turbocharged 1.4-liter engine, specially tuned to run on high-octane fuel. The suspension received dedicated tuning to sharpen handling. Notably, this iteration was 154 lbs lighter than its predecessor, contributing to its agility and dynamic driving feel.
cars.hero: Superb handling was just one of the fortes of this high-performance Japanese hatchback.

cars.description: This is the Gr.4 version of the KATANA Edition concept, a fusion of the ZC33 Swift Sport and the striking style and performance of the iconic KATANA sports bike. Enhancements include an extended front under spoiler and the addition of a GT-style rear wing, With staggered tire sizing, interior weight reduction, and the installation of a roll cage, the machine has been transformed into a true Gran Turismo Gr.4-spec race car.
cars.hero: A tuned up Gr. 4 version of the Swift Sport based on the 'KATANA Edition'.
cars.name_long: Suzuki Swift Sport KATANA Edition Gr.4

cars.description: The Pikes Peak International Hill Climb is the world’s most renowned hill climb race, covering a demanding 12.4 miles course with an elevation gain of 4721.1 ft. To take on this extreme challenge, Suzuki developed the V6 Escudo Pikes Peak Special—a purpose-built machine equipped with a mid-mounted twin-turbo 2.5-liter V-6 engine producing 981.3 HP. With its lightweight construction and advanced aerodynamics, Nobuhiro Tajima piloted the car to overall victory, becoming the first Japanese driver to win the prestigious event in 1995.
cars.hero: A monster made for the Pikes Peak Hillclimb.
cars.name_long: Suzuki V6 Escudo Pikes Peak Special '98

cars.description: The Tesla Model 3 is a compact battery-electric sedan. At the top of the lineup sat the Performance Dual Motor AWD variant, capable of accelerating from zero to 62.1 mph in just 3.3 seconds and reaching a top speed of 162.2 mph. Under WLTP testing—the global standard for electric and fuel efficiency—it offered an impressive maximum range of 339.9 miles. In 2023, it received its first major update, introducing refinements to the front fascia, overall length, and interior controls.
cars.hero: A best-seller from the company that changed the EV market forever.

cars.description: This vehicle marked Tesla’s second production model, following the Roadster. Its spacious sedan form incorporated a rear hatch, classifying it as a 5-door. Buyers could choose from three distinct battery capacities, each aligned with a specific price tier. At the top of the range, the Signature Performance variant delivered 410.3 HP and 441.2 ft-lb of torque, firmly placing it in supercar territory.
cars.hero: A stylish 5-door sedan introduced by Tesla, the pioneer of electric cars.

cars.description: Unveiled in 1967, the Toyota 2000GT blended engineering excellence with timeless design, instantly capturing the hearts of sports car enthusiasts. It made its mark on the track as well, setting a world record at 136.7 mph on the Yatabe test course. Global fame followed when it appeared as James Bond’s car in "You Only Live Twice."
cars.hero: Considered to be Japan's first supercar, this special car possessed originality in both style and mechanics.

cars.description: A Gran Turismo Original, this version of Toyota’s new sports car, the 86, has been specially modified to comply with Gr.4 racing regulations. While the 86 had already seen action in clubman-level motorsports across the globe, this iteration transforms it into a true race machine, with its power output raised to 364 horsepower. It excels through corners, where its lightweight and compact body can be fully exploited to deliver exceptional handling.
cars.hero: This is a Gran Turismo original version of the Toyota 86 FR sports car modified for Gr.4.

cars.description: A Gran Turismo Original, this version of Toyota’s new sports car, the 86, has been specially modified to comply with Gr.B racing regulations. The car has been transformed into a top-class rally machine, with its original rear-wheel-drive layout converted to 4-wheel drive, while aggressive aerodynamic elements such as canards and a two-level rear wing generated substantial downforce.
cars.hero: This off-road version of Toyota's 86 was modified for Gr.B competition.

cars.description: Available exclusively through online orders beginning in January 2016, the 86 GRMN was a fully tuned machine crafted by Toyota, based on its beloved 86 sports car. Beyond structural enhancements, its center of gravity was further lowered through the extensive use of lightweight materials. A host of additional refinements were made—not only was power output increased, but the car also received a newly developed close-ratio 6-speed manual transmission, upgraded brakes, and staggered tire sizing between the front and rear.
cars.hero: The "Nürburgring Meister" in the form of the Toyota 86.

cars.description: The Toyota 86 represents Toyota’s take on the compact, front-engine/rear-wheel-drive sports car co-developed with Subaru. Its front-mid-engine-mounted, naturally-aspirated 2.0-liter DOHC boxer engine produced 197.2 HP and 144.7 ft-lb of torque. Many components were freshly designed specifically for this model, resulting in precise, responsive handling that made the driver feel truly connected to the car. It was a next-generation lightweight sports car, created with driving enthusiasts at its core.
cars.hero: The rebirth of the AE86, Toyota creates an exciting 21st-century version of the ideal sports car.

cars.description: Released in 2012, the Toyota 86 was a sports car that combined a compact body with a rear-wheel-drive layout. The first minor update came in 2016, enhancing body rigidity and aerodynamics. Models equipped with the 6-speed manual transmission received engine retuning along with upgrades to numerous components, placing greater emphasis on performance rather than appearance. The GT Limited trim represented the highest grade in the 86 lineup. Its interior featured upscale materials such as leather and Alcantara, offering a more premium and mature cabin environment.
cars.hero: The "classic" Toyota 86 sports car takes on a more mature character.

cars.description: Since its original launch in 2002, the Toyota Alphard had continuously aimed to define the luxury minivan segment. The third-generation Alphard, launched in 2015, introduced the Executive Lounge trim, delivering exceptional comfort to second-row passengers. It offered a higher level of luxury and refinement than ever before. A 2017 facelift brought updates to the 4.5-liter V-6 engine and further enhancements to overall ride comfort.
cars.hero: Japan's premium minivan that evolved into a high-class luxury car.

cars.description: After making hybrids mainstream with the Prius, Toyota introduced the Aqua, a smaller, more fuel-efficient hybrid. Its hybrid system was a lighter, optimized version of that used in the third-generation Prius. In JC08 fuel economy tests conducted in Japan, it reached a maximum efficiency of 83.3 MPG. Internationally, the car was marketed as the Prius C.
cars.hero: More economical than the larger Prius, this model is helping to expand the hybrid vehicle market.

cars.description: Following a series of internationally-focused models such as the Corolla and Yaris, Toyota introduced the C-HR crossover SUV in 2016, designed as a global vehicle for the modern era. This distinctive SUV also hinted at sporting ambitions, with a prototype version taking part in the Nürburgring 24 Hours race. Built on Toyota’s next-generation TNGA platform, the C-HR came with a choice of a 1.8-liter hybrid powertrain or a turbocharged 1.2-liter inline-4. The C-HR would go on to earn broad acclaim, becoming a bestseller.
cars.hero: An unconventional crossover SUV that took on the Nürburgring 24 Hours.

cars.description: The sixth-generation Toyota Celica made its debut in October 1993. Its futuristic design was sharpened by the distinctive quad round headlights, while a larger body emphasized its identity as a front-wheel-drive specialty car. In 1994, the GT-FOUR (ST205) appeared as a homologation model for the WRC. Its 3S-GTE turbocharged 2.0-liter engine produced 251.5 HP.
cars.hero: This is the WRC base model of the popular sporty coupe, complete with aluminum hood and rear spoiler.

cars.description: The car followed the success of the previous ST185 model, which had secured both the manufacturers' and drivers' titles in the 1993 WRC. The ST205 entered the 1994 season aiming for another championship. However, during Round 7 in Catalonia, the car was disqualified for an engine regulation violation, and all championship points were revoked. In response, Toyota withdrew from the WRC, bringing the ST205’s competition career to an abrupt end after just one season. Despite its brief time on the stage, the ST205’s bold, rally-bred appearance won it a lasting place in the hearts of enthusiasts.
cars.hero: The rally machine that left an impression on many fans, though it only competed for a short time.

cars.description: The Chaser was Toyota’s midsize sedan, sharing the Mark II’s fundamental design but wearing different exterior styling. The Tourer V performance model was powered by the second-generation 1JZ-GTE engine with variable valve timing, and flooring the pedal launched this beast forward with ferocious boost. The front-engine/rear-wheel-drive layout provided excellent control, making the car responsive to the driver’s inputs.
cars.hero: This sister to the Toyota Mark II provides an intense drive.

cars.description: The fourth-generation Corolla Levin was introduced in 1983. It carried over the floor panel from the previous TE71 and was the only model of its generation to retain a rear-wheel-drive layout, while all other Corollas had transitioned to front-wheel drive. The 1.6-liter 4A-GEU DOHC engine and lightweight body delivered a sharp, responsive driving experience. After production ended, demand for affordable rear-wheel-drive cars only grew, securing this model’s legacy as one of the greatest sports cars ever produced by Toyota.
cars.hero: The now legendary AE86, a compact rear-drive coupe that emphasized driving excitement.

cars.description: In 2012, the Toyota Crown underwent a full model change, entering its 14th generation with a bold new front-end design. The lineup was split into two distinct versions: the more conservative "Royal" and the sportier "Athlete." The Royal featured design elements inspired by a crown, while the Athlete adopted a more aggressive look with lightning bolt motifs. Together, they introduced a fresh visual identity while preserving the core values that had defined the Crown nameplate for generations.
cars.hero: The 14th-generation Crown sported a bold front-end design, giving the sport sedan an extra dose of flair.

cars.description: In 2012, the Toyota Crown underwent a full model change, entering its 14th generation with a bold new front-end design. The lineup was split into two distinct versions: the more conservative "Royal" and the sportier "Athlete." Four different powertrains were offered across the series: a 3.5-liter V-6, a 2.5-liter V-6, a 2.5-liter inline-4 hybrid, and a 2.0-liter inline-4 turbo. This safety car version was a Gran Turismo Original design.
cars.hero: This Crown Athlete, converted into a safety car, was designed to patrol the race track.
cars.name_long: Toyota Crown Athlete G Safety Car

cars.description: The Toyota FT-1 is a concept car created by CALTY Design, Toyota’s North American design studio, offering a glimpse into the potential future of the brand’s sports car philosophy. Its projected dimensions are: overall length, 184.1 inches; width 77.6 inches; height 48.2 inches; with a wheelbase of 107.9 inches. The design draws inspiration from Toyota’s rich sports car heritage, beginning with the iconic Toyota 2000GT.
cars.hero: Toyota's sports design concept presented at the January 2014 Detroit Auto Show.

cars.description: The FT-1 Vision Gran Turismo itself was a racing adaptation of Toyota’s FT-1 sports design concept, developed by CALTY Design Research, the company’s North American design studio. The design drew heavily from data and practical experience, featuring oversized fenders, an expanded front air intake, a large rear wing, and aggressive front canards.
cars.hero: The FT-1 design concept transformed into a pure race car.

cars.description: This Gran Turismo Original is a Gr.3 specification version of Toyota’s next-generation racing concept, the FT-1 Vision Gran Turismo. The base FT-1 has been outfitted with wide fenders, a prominent rear wing, and a front splitter, transforming it into a cutting-edge race car.
cars.hero: The FT-1 design concept transformed into a pure race car.

cars.description: The GR Corolla was developed by Toyota’s high-performance GR division as a hot hatch aimed squarely at outperforming its rivals. Already the most powerful model in Corolla history, it was taken even further with the hardcore MORIZO Edition. At a time when the automotive world moves toward electrification and advanced systems, the GR Corolla stood out as a rare celebration of the pure, mechanical thrill of the internal combustion engine.
cars.hero: A 2-seat model that takes the GR Corolla to the extreme.

cars.description: The GR Supra marked the return of Toyota’s flagship sports car, 17 years after production ended. It retained a rear-wheel-drive layout and inline-6, but came wrapped in a modern two-seat body with advanced construction and a twin-scroll turbocharger. It made its Nürburgring 24 Hours debut in 2018 and, in 2019, finished 3rd in the SP8T class and 41st overall. This cementing its image as a true performance contender.
cars.hero: The Supra returned after a 17-year hiatus, with this racing version competing at the Nürburgring in 2019.

cars.description: The GR Supra Racing Concept reimagined the Supra as a race car, appearing 16 years after the model's production ceased in 2002. Its compact two-door coupe body, with classic long-nose, short-deck proportions, utilized cutting-edge materials and engineering to deliver outstanding aerodynamics and handling.
cars.hero: First seen at the 2018 Geneva Motor Show, this race Supra represented a preview of the production model.

cars.description: The Toyota Supra made its long-awaited return in 2019, following its discontinuation in 2002. The new model retained an inline-6 engine and rear-wheel-drive layout, embodying the essence of a pure sports car. It featured an ideal 50:50 front-to-rear weight distribution and a low center of gravity, delivering superb balance and driving dynamics. A twin-scroll turbocharger ensured strong, responsive acceleration, while its wide stance and short wheelbase contributed to nimble, agile handling, making it a truly compelling performance machine.
cars.hero: Toyota's flagship FR sports car returned after a 17-year absence with a completely new look.

cars.description: The Toyota Supra made its long-awaited return in 2019, following its discontinuation in 2002. The new model retained an inline-6 engine and rear-wheel-drive layout, embodying the essence of a pure sports car. It featured an ideal 50:50 front-to-rear weight distribution and a low center of gravity, delivering superb balance and driving dynamics. A twin-scroll turbocharger ensured strong, responsive acceleration, while its wide stance and short wheelbase contributed to nimble, agile handling, making it a truly compelling performance machine.
cars.hero: The 2020 Supra possessed a significant power boost compared to the past model.

cars.description: Developed by Toyota for the WRC, the GR Yaris may have appeared as a simple compact car, but underneath was a serious competition machine. With increased rigidity, reduced weight, and a dramatically lowered center of gravity, it was engineered for peak performance. The 4-wheel-drive RZ model featured a 1.6-liter 3-cylinder turbo engine paired with a 6-speed manual transmission. The RZ High Performance variant added a limited-slip differential, delivering rock-solid traction. In January 2020, the "1st Edition" was introduced as a special edition model, marking the launch with exclusive features.
cars.hero: This new WRC race car was created to carry the torch for Toyota's strong rallying tradition.
cars.name_long: Toyota GR Yaris 1st Edition RZ "High performance" '20

cars.description: The TOYOTA GR010 HYBRID 2021 succeeded the TS050, developed in response to the new regulations introduced that year. It featured a twin-turbo 3.5-liter V-6 engine producing 670.6 HP, paired with a 268.2 HP electric motor at the front in a 4-wheel-drive layout. Driver lineups including Kamui Kobayashi and Kazuki Nakajima went on to win all six rounds of the WEC season, including Le Mans, ushering in the beginning of the hypercar era.
cars.hero: Four consecutive wins at Le Mans for Toyota with this prototype race car

cars.description: Toyota’s lightweight 86, a front-engine/rear-wheel-drive sports car, was introduced in 2012 and sold more than 200,000 units worldwide. Nine years later, it was reborn as the GR86, now equipped with a larger naturally-aspirated 2.4-liter flat-4 DOHC engine producing 231.8 HP and 184.4 ft-lb of torque. With enhanced body rigidity, reduced weight, and an aerodynamic design shaped by motorsport experience, the GR86 delivered an even more engaging and dynamic driving experience.
cars.hero: This version of Japan's signature lightweight sports car boasts a bigger engine, but it remains true to its heritage.

cars.description: In 1998, Toyota developed the GT-One (TS020) with the singular goal of winning the 24 Hours of Le Mans. Designed by André de Cortanze, the car incorporated Formula 1-inspired aerodynamics and suspension. Although mechanical issues prevented a result in its debut year, the GT-One returned in 1999 as an evolved LM GTP machine. Ukyo Katayama and company finished 2nd overall—the highest-ever at Le Mans for a team composed entirely of Japanese drivers.
cars.hero: Toyota's endurance race machine that achieved a class win at Le Mans in 1999.

cars.description: The Hiace has long stood as Toyota’s flagship commercial vehicle, earning widespread support around the globe. Introduced in 2004 and continually refined, the fifth-generation H200 model became a record-setting seller. Offered in various configurations based on body size, it came with a choice of 2.0-liter or 2.7-liter gasoline engines, or a 2.8-liter diesel engine. The Van DX variant featured a standard roof height and rear-wheel drive. It accommodated up to nine passengers, or, with the seats folded, transforming into a spacious cargo carrier.
cars.hero: The cab-over commercial van was equally capable of moving people and cargo.

cars.description: Since the 1950s, Toyota had been producing ambulances based on specially adapted passenger and commercial vehicles. The most recent of these was the third-generation Himedic, a high-standard ambulance introduced in 2006. Its platform was built on the 200 Series HiAce Super Long. With improvements such as an expanded patient compartment, this vehicle was engineered for maximum functionality in critical, life-saving situations.
cars.hero: Saving lives faster and more safely.

cars.description: Renowned for its all-terrain performance and reliability, the Toyota Land Cruiser has become among the world’s most beloved off-road vehicles. Introduced in 1960, the third-generation “40” series also offered a surprising degree of on-road comfort. The 2-door hardtop variant shown here was powered by a 3.9-liter F-model gasoline engine, paired with a part-time 4-wheel-drive system. Its popularity only grew in 1974 with the introduction of the 3.0-liter B-model diesel engine. The 40 series went on to become a massive success, remaining in production until 1984.
cars.hero: A best-selling Land Cruiser with a 24-year production run.

cars.description: The Tourer V was a performance model added to the eighth-generation Mark II lineup. Its biggest selling point was its power unit: a turbocharged 2.5-liter inline-6 engine that produced 276.1 HP and 278.5 ft-lb of torque. A 5-speed manual transmission was also available, and the roar of the 6-cylinder engine, combined with tremendous boost, hit as soon as the throttle pedal was floored. Even so, the interior was lavish and comfortable, bringing two seemingly opposite characters together in the Tourer V.
cars.hero: This sports sedan's refined looks hide sharp teeth.

cars.description: Introduced in 1989, the second-generation MR2, designated SW20, succeeded the AW11, Japan’s first mass-produced mid-engine sports car. Its body dimensions were stretched to the upper limits of Japan’s Class 5 vehicle regulations, while its design adopted smoother, more aerodynamic lines to emphasize its mid-engine configuration. At launch, the car faced criticism for its challenging handling character, but subsequent refinements transformed it into a well-balanced performer.
cars.hero: The turbocharged model of Toyota's mid-engine sports car featured a rigid chassis that matched its extra power.

cars.description: The third-generation Prius remained synonymous with hybrid technology. This iteration sought to elevate not only its environmental credentials but also the pleasure of driving itself. Its newly sculpted body featured a sleek, aerodynamic silhouette that conveyed a sense of motion even at rest. The engine was upsized to 1.8 liters, and more than 90 percent of the hybrid system components were newly developed. Fuel efficiency reached an astonishing 89.4 MPG, introducing a new dimension to the driving experience, one where performance met the pure satisfaction of exceptional economy.
cars.hero: This Prius variant focused on both increased performance and delivering better overall driving pleasure.

cars.description: When it was introduced in 1994, the Toyota RAV4 pioneered an entirely new market segment, called the “crossover SUV.” With its compact body and high ground clearance, it quickly gained followers around the world and reached its fifth generation in 2018. The Adventure grade brought rugged off-road styling, highlighted by a custom grille, skid-plate bumpers, and 19-inch wheel rims. A 2.0-liter inline-4 Dynamic Force Engine was mated to a Direct Shift-CVT, delivering smooth acceleration and impressive fuel efficiency.
cars.hero: An adventurous SUV for active lifestyles.

cars.description: In the fall of 2015, at the Tokyo Motor Show, Toyota unveiled the S-FR lightweight sports car, conceived with the philosophy of delivering “perfect control in an entry model, allowing drivers to fully enjoy the car through everyday engagement." The design captured the spirit of the classic Toyota Sports 800, reimagined with a contemporary sensibility to suit modern tastes.
cars.hero: Toyota's exciting concept vehicle that carries on the lightweight sports-car torch established by the Sport 800.

cars.description: Unveiled at the 2015 Tokyo Motor Show, the S-FR Racing Concept was a track-focused evolution of Toyota’s S-FR. Fender width was extended by 0.8 inches on each side, while a prominent air outlet was integrated into the hood. A large rear wing and aggressive aerodynamic elements transformed the once-playful S-FR Concept into a car exuding the aura of a GT racer.
cars.hero: The racing version of the attention-getting S-FR concept car.

cars.description: The Toyota Sports 800, affectionately known as the “Yota-Hachi,” was a compact sports car distinguished by its fixed B-pillar Targa-style removable roof panel. Extensive use of aluminum and acrylic throughout the body kept its weight down to just 1279 lbs. While its 750 cc engine produced a modest 44.4 HP, the car’s featherlight construction allowed it to reach a top speed of 96.3 mph—comparable to many 1.500 cc-class vehicles of its era.
cars.hero: With its wide tread and low center of gravity, the "Yota-Hachi" was a capable sports car.

cars.description: In 1983, the Corolla and Sprinter lines largely transitioned to a front-wheel-drive layout, with the sole exception being the rear-wheel-drive AE86 variant—the Corolla Levin and Sprinter Trueno—affectionately known as the "Hachi-Roku." It was offered as a 3-door hatchback and a 2-door notchback coupe. Power came from a newly developed 1.6-liter DOHC 4A-GEU inline-4. While several rivals featured similar specifications, the Hachi-Roku continued to win over driving enthusiasts with its playful, rewarding handling.
cars.hero: The tossable nature of this original hatchback 86 more than compensated for its lack of structural rigidity.

cars.description: This car was the Trueno owned by Shuichi Shigeno, the creator of the acclaimed manga "Initial D," which prominently featured the "Hachi-Roku" AE86 Levin and Trueno models. Fitted with an HKS exhaust manifold and a Trust silencer, its engine was tuned to produce 207.1 HP. A TRD suspension kit was also installed, enabling agile handling and high cornering speeds.
cars.hero: This modified 86 was built to order for the author of the "Initial D" comic books.
cars.name_long: Toyota Trueno 3door 1600GT APEX (AE86 Shuichi Shigeno Version)

cars.description: Originally introduced as a variant of the Celica, the XX evolved into a standalone model in February 1986 with the debut of the Supra. Among its various trim levels, the most celebrated was the high-performance 3.0GT Turbo A—built for championship homologation—featuring the turbocharged 3.0-liter 7M-GTEU engine, producing 266.3 HP. It also featured a wider body, matching the North American specification at 68.7 inches, along with reinforced suspension.
cars.hero: This variant of the Supra was a homologation model with special equipment for Group A racing.

cars.description: The All Japan Grand Touring Championship (JGTC) ran until 2004, after which it evolved into the current Super GT series. Toyota entered the Supra into JGTC competition in 1994. During that era, the series was largely dominated by the Nissan Skyline GT-R; however, in 1997, the Supra finally broke through, capturing the season title with the No. 36 Castrol TOM'S Supra.
cars.hero: This car brought an end to the GT-R's domination by taking the title in 1997.

cars.description: In May 1993, the Toyota Supra was reborn, shedding its long-nose silhouette in favor of a bold, muscular new design. At the heart of the twin-turbo 3.0-liter DOHC model was the legendary 2JZ engine, delivering 276.1 HP. The highest-grade variant came equipped with a 6-speed manual transmission and Bilstein suspension. Structural reinforcements, along with carefully tuned dampers and bushings, transformed the car into a refined high-performance machine.
cars.hero: This Supra was all business, equipped with a 6-speed gearbox and Bilstein suspension.

cars.description: The TS030 Hybrid was developed to compete in the 2012 World Endurance Championship. Its THS-R powertrain was the result of a collaborative effort between Toyota’s production hybrid engineers and the motorsports division at the Higashi-Fuji Technical Center, built around a newly designed V-8 engine. Although it was forced to retire during its debut at the 24 Hours of Le Mans, the car went on to claim three victories over the season, ultimately securing 2nd place in the championship standings.
cars.hero: The revolutionary hybrid-powered racing prototype that waged war at Le Mans and the WEC.

cars.description: The TS050 - Hybrid was developed for competition in the 2016 World Endurance Championship. It featured motor generator units (MGUs) on both the front and rear axles, paired with a V-6 direct-injection twin-turbocharged engine. The combined output of the engine and electric motors reached 986.2 HP. While the car showed strong potential as a title contender, it ultimately finished 3rd in the drivers’ standings. It also secured 3rd place in the manufacturers’ rankings.
cars.hero: Toyota's hybrid LMP1 car was developed to dominate the World Endurance Championship.

cars.description: The Tundra was a full-size pickup truck developed by Toyota specifically for the North American market. Introduced in 2015, the TRD Pro variant featured a 5.7-liter V-8 and was specially tuned by Toyota’s motorsports division, TRD. Its suspension was refined with the addition of Fox dampers, while a newly designed hood scoop and BBS wheels enhanced its aggressive appearance.
cars.hero: Toyota's large pickup was equipped with a unique suspension system to maximize its sporting performance.

cars.description: Introduced in 2000 by British sports car manufacturer TVR, this two-door coupe featured a detachable roof and a distinctive exterior design that blended bold curves with aggressive lines. Power came from TVR’s in-house developed 4.0L inline-6, known as the Speed 6, which produced 359 HP. With a lightweight body tipping the scales at just 2425 lbs, the car delivered truly staggering performance.
cars.hero: This unique machine offers a classic sports car feel to enthusiast drivers of today.

cars.description: The Beetle Gr.3 is a racing variant of Volkswagen’s iconic compact, engineered to comply with Gr.3 regulations. The once-playful road car has been thoroughly reworked into a serious contender, with major changes including a switch from front- to rear-wheel drive and a lowered roofline to reduce frontal area and improve aerodynamics.
cars.hero: This Gr.3 race version of the Volkswagen Beetle is on an entirely different level to the road-going model.

cars.description: Released in 1974, the Volkswagen Golf quickly rose to popularity as a pioneer of the compact car segment. The sporty GTI variant featured a 1.6-liter inline-4 SOHC engine with Bosch fuel injection, producing 108.5 HP. Blending performance with everyday practicality, the GTI redefined the concept of sporty driving.
cars.hero: This grandfather of hot hatches balanced everyday usability with a fun-to-drive nature.

cars.description: Unveiled in 2012, the seventh-generation Golf was built on a new platform that introduced a host of advancements. Handling was notably enhanced through the use of XDS—an electronically controlled differential lock—alongside DCC adaptive chassis control and progressive steering. These technologies improved stability and allowed for much higher cornering speeds.
cars.hero: The GTI version of the 7th-generation Golf ups its handling performance.

cars.description: The GTI Roadster Vision Gran Turismo is a supercar that embodies the spirit and performance heritage of Volkswagen’s GTI lineage. At its heart beats a twin-turbocharged 3.0-liter VR6 TSI engine, delivering 502 HP and 484.6 ft-lb of torque. Power is routed through a 7-speed dual-clutch transmission to all four wheels, ensuring exceptional traction and rapid acceleration.
cars.hero: This supercar with the GTI's DNA possesses race car-like acceleration.
cars.name_long: Volkswagen GTI Roadster Vision Gran Turismo

cars.description: The GTI Supersport Vision Gran Turismo draws upon the DNA of Volkswagen’s legendary GTI lineage to create a supercar that was both technically advanced and visually striking. Its body, inspired by the iconic Golf silhouette, houses a 502 HP VR6 TSI engine. With a lowered center of gravity and the extensive use of lightweight components, the car exhibits an exceptional handling experience.
cars.hero: The ultimate GTI; there's a reason this car's name includes "Supersport."
cars.name_long: Volkswagen GTI Supersport Vision Gran Turismo

cars.description: Volkswagen’s prototype race car stood as a symbol of carbon reduction and future performance. Its carbon-fiber body featured prominent front and rear wings, while two electric motors powered both the front and rear axles for all-wheel drive. The car delivered astonishing performance, setting record-breaking times at Pikes Peak, the Nürburgring Nordschleife, and Goodwood.
cars.hero: The prototype EV that rewrote speed records around the world.

cars.description: This was the high-performance variant of the fifth-generation Polo, Volkswagen’s standout in the compact car segment. Initially powered by a 1.4-liter engine featuring both a supercharger and turbocharger, the 2014 update saw a switch to a 1.8-liter turbocharged unit, delivering 189.3 HP along with improved fuel efficiency. With performance worthy of the GTI badge, it stood as a strong contender among B-segment hot hatches.
cars.hero: The 'hot' version of the 5th generation Polo uses an advanced engine setup.

cars.description: Dr. Ferdinand Porsche’s Volkswagen was developed into a broad range of variants. One such version was the Sambabus, which reimagined the car as a van with generous luggage capacity. By positioning the horizontally-opposed engine at the very rear, designers were able to create a wide, low floor while preserving the vehicle’s compact footprint. This clever layout gave the model a number of advantages as a commercial vehicle, adding to its appeal and versatility.
cars.hero: With maximum interior space in a small body, this cute bus was highly efficient.

cars.description: A Gran Turismo Original, Volkswagen’s sleek Scirocco sports coupe has been reimagined to meet Gr.4 race standards. Its aerodynamic enhancements are subtle—a modest front splitter and a compact rear wing—underscoring a focus on preserving the strengths of the base model. The result is a front-wheel-drive machine with remarkable cornering prowess.
cars.hero: This attractive coupe possessed the sharp cornering ability of a full-fledged sports car.

cars.description: The Scirocco R was a high-performance sports coupe developed from the core architecture of the Golf. Its body sat lower, with a wider track for enhanced stability, and is fitted with unique bumpers, side skirts, and a roof-mounted spoiler. Significant upgrades were made to the suspension and braking systems. Lighter than the Golf R of the same era, the Scirocco R was refined into a nimble, high-spec sports machine with a sharp, responsive edge.
cars.hero: This attractive coupe possesses the sharp cornering ability of a fully-fledged sports car.

cars.description: Often referred to by its nicknames—most famously, the "Beetle"—the Volkswagen Type I was a rear-wheel-drive vehicle powered by an air-cooled, rear-mounted 4-cylinder engine. Produced from 1938 to 2003, it saw over 21 million units built. The Volkswagen 1200 was the official designation for the version produced between the mid-1950s and late 1960s, which featured a 1.2-liter engine.
cars.hero: Its cute silhouette and rear-engine layout made this car an icon in automobiledom.

cars.description: This Gran Turismo Original is a Gr.3 specification version of the GTI Vision Gran Turismo, a concept born from the collaboration between Volkswagen and Gran Turismo. Significant aerodynamic enhancements were made, including an extended front splitter and an enlarged rear wing.
cars.hero: This supercar with the GTI's DNA possesses race car-like acceleration.

cars.description: The Volvo 240 Estate became synonymous with the Swedish brand's image as a station wagon maker. Its boxy shape and long profile became design signatures that made the vehicle popular to all. Inside, it offered a minimalist Scandinavian interior with plush, sofa-like seating. Its production run ended in 1993, but the 240 remains a beloved classic, still seen in daily use, a rarity among vintage cars.
cars.hero: A historic model that epitomized the station wagon.

cars.description: The V40 was a 5-door hatchback positioned in the C-segment. Drawing inspiration from Volvo classics of the 1960s—such as the P1800 and 1800ES—its flowing silhouette blended cues of both a coupe and a wagon. The T5 R-Design was the sportiest model in the lineup. Powered by a turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-5 producing 210.1 HP, it was paired with a sport suspension and 18-inch wheels to deliver sharp, refined handling.
cars.hero: The globally successful Volvo that served as a sedan, estate and coupe.

cars.description: The Gran Turismo Award was presented to standout custom cars showcased at SEMA. In 2016, the 14th award went to the Wicked Fabrications GT 51—a 1951 Ford Custom Club Coupe crafted by a team of specialists for former racing driver Bruce Leven. The project required an estimated 10,000 hours to complete.
cars.hero: More than 10,000 labor hours went into this 2016 Gran Turismo Award winner.

cars.description: The Xiaomi SU7 Ultra was an extreme performance version of the first car from smart device maker Xiaomi, the SU7 sports sedan. The all-wheel-drive system, which used three electric motors spread across the front and rear axles, boasted a total system output of 1526.6 HP. The "V8" model motors located on the rear axle were the most powerful in any production car, able to rotate at speeds of up to 27,200 rpm. Also, extensive aerodynamic development resulted in the car being able to produce up to 628 lbs of downforce.
cars.hero: It's the smartphone giant’s expression of automotive innovation.

cars.description: This electric hypercar featured a teardrop-shaped cockpit embedded within a body sculpted with cutouts and air ducts. Its signature halo-shaped taillight served as both a visual icon and a massive air outlet. Together with numerous aerodynamic innovations, the car achieved a drag coefficient of 0.29, downforce of -1.2 and an aerodynamic efficiency rating of 4.1. Achieving both low drag and high downforce is a difficult aerodynamic challenge, but this car managed to balance the two at an exceptionally high level.
cars.hero: A Hypercar Sculpted by Wind and Intelligence.

cars.description: Released by Yangwang, BYD’s luxury brand, the U9 is a supercar aimed at delivering the ultimate in power, technology and speed in the electric era. It uses the proprietary e⁴ platform, featuring four electric motors that produce a total system output of 960 kW, or roughly 1286 HP. It accelerates from 0-62.1 mph in 2.36 seconds. In 2025, the high-performance U9 Xtreme variant attempted to set a world speed record, reaching 308.3 mph.
cars.hero: This rare electric super car broke world speed records.

cars.description: This Vision Gran Turismo was created by the famed Carrozzeria Zagato, drawing inspiration from the IsoRivolta, a grand tourer produced in the 1960s by the Italian sports-car brand ISO. It inherited the DNA of the IsoRivolta, a car with a rich motorsport history, and reimagined it through the lens of cutting-edge design and modern engineering.
cars.hero: This Vision Gran Turismo machine pays tribute to the legendary manufacturer, Zagato.

cars.description: With more than 130 years of heritage, Czech manufacturer Škoda made its Gran Turismo debut with a single-seater EV producing 800kW (1071 HP). The exterior design blended styling cues from Škoda’s classic forebears with a host of advanced technologies, including independent left and right rear wings that respond to driving conditions. It also incorporates onboard distance sensors that assess the position of other vehicles.
cars.hero: A single-seat all-wheel-drive EV from the distinguished Czech manufacturer.
